- [x] Decide how the guest sees Hyper-V's interface, and forward it (issue #27). The guest keeps CPUID's hypervisor-present bit and the leaves from `0x40000000`, and Aleph0 forwards Hyper-V's interface from root operation, so L0 Hyper-V serves it as an access of Aleph0's own virtual processor, the one the firmware set up before Aleph0 started; decided and documented in [docs/HYPERV_INTERFACE.md](docs/HYPERV_INTERFACE.md). Bring-up checks for the interface (CPUID.1:ECX bit 31, then `"Hv#1"` in CPUID.40000001H:EAX; `hyperv::offers_interface`, host-tested) and publishes the result to the exit handler. For the firmware and the OS, `decide` (host-tested) gives a VMCALL from CPL > 0 #UD, resumes Aleph0's own, now told apart by RCX values with reserved hypercall-input bits set (`vmx::vmcall`, so no hypercall Hyper-V takes is mistaken for one), forwards any other when Hyper-V is present (`Emulation::Hypercall`: VMCALL in root with the guest's RCX, RDX and R8; RAX, RCX, RDX and R8 back; RIP past it) and gives #UD otherwise; the test guest keeps its script. RDMSR and WRMSR of Hyper-V's synthetic MSRs, `0x40000000..=0x4000FFFF` (wider than `0xFF`: the crash MSRs, `0x40000118` and the nested SynIC's are past it), are forwarded under Hyper-V and get #GP without it (`MsrRoute::Synthetic`, host-tested). A forward Hyper-V refuses, #UD at the VMCALL or #GP at the RDMSR/WRMSR, no longer halts Aleph0: the host fault handler resumes it at the forwarder's recovery point (`hyperv::recovery`, host-tested against the assembled bytes), and the guest gets the exception at its own instruction (`ResumePlan::refused_with`, host-tested). The `forward-refusal-test` feature showed it on Hyper-V: `WRMSR 0xc0000102 <- 0x8000000000000000 -> Err(Refused); Aleph0 still runs.`, while `0x4000FFFF`, which Hyper-V does not define, read 0 and took the write. `VcpuStats` counts the forwards, `Forwarded` keeps them by call code and by MSR, a stop prints both, and the summary lines of VMCALL, RDMSR and WRMSR exits print that reason's tally. On Hyper-V, `-ProcessorCount 1`: `Hyper-V interface offered (... max leaf 0x4000000b vendor "Microsoft Hv", ... interface 0x31237648)`, then `RDMSR 0x40000020 (synthetic) forwarded to Hyper-V -> 0x00000000003b5321` at the RIP that got #GP before, `Firmware timer fired`, `hypercall 0x005d (rcx=0x1005d) forwarded to Hyper-V -> status 0x0` from the firmware's hypercall page at `0x7f60b000`, and 36 million exits in three minutes with no stop (`synthetic MSR reads: 0x40000020=16350` at the 16384th RDMSR, `hypercalls by call code: 0x5d=32` at the 32nd VMCALL); the console showed the firmware's "Virtual Machine Boot Summary", and Tab then Enter through `Msvm_Keyboard` pressed "Restart now": event 18514 "reset by the guest operating system", as in the control run without Aleph0. `-TestGuest` and `-InjectNmi`: 24 and 26 exits, `SUCCESS`, nothing forwarded. Option B, hiding Hyper-V from the OS, was tried without Aleph0: the Linux target built with `# CONFIG_HYPERVISOR_GUEST is not set` reaches its shell, calibrating the TSC against the ACPI PM timer, on clocksource `tsc`; kept for later, since the firmware needs A anyway and A keeps #17's kernel configuration.
- [ ] Hide Aleph0's own pages from the guest through EPT: code, stacks, VMXON region, VMCS, host GDT/TSS and the EPT tables themselves. The identity map shows the guest all of them, so a guest with kernel rights could read Aleph0, rewrite its EPT entries or its exit handler. Each page becomes not present (the access redirected or a #PF injected, rather than stopping the guest) or maps to a zero-filled shadow page. Aleph0 then has to track every page it allocates. EPT does not cover what Hyper-V does for a forwarded access (#27): a hypercall's output GPA and the GPAs of the overlay MSRs (hypercall page, SynIC message and event pages, VP assist page) must be checked against Aleph0's pages too, and refused with #GP ([docs/HYPERV_INTERFACE.md](docs/HYPERV_INTERFACE.md) section 8). Belongs with the persistence item below.
- [x] Decide how the hypervisor will own memory and persist after `ExitBootServices` (issue #23). After `ExitBootServices` the OS may reuse all `LOADER_CODE` (the `.efi` image, including its statics), `LOADER_DATA` (every page from `page.rs`) and `BOOT_SERVICES_DATA`. Decided and implemented, see [docs/RESIDENT.md](docs/RESIDENT.md): every page Aleph0 keeps is `RUNTIME_SERVICES_DATA` (`page::RESIDENT_DATA`), and bring-up prints each resident allocation's type from the memory map and refuses to launch if one is reclaimable (`resident::memory::is_reclaimable`, host-tested). The image stays an application: `main` copies it into `RUNTIME_SERVICES_CODE`, applies its base relocations for the new address (`resident::pe`, host-tested) and runs everything else from the copy, which `SetVirtualAddressMap` leaves alone, unlike a runtime driver's image. The test guest's pages are resident too, since EPT keeps its data page read-only for the firmware guest. An `ExitBootServices` event tells Aleph0 when boot services end (section 0b). On Hyper-V, `-TestGuest`: `Image copied to resident memory: 0x000000007eab2000 -> 0x000000007ea23000, 585728 bytes, 927 fixups applied`, 27 lines `Resident allocation at ...` (the copy and the test guest's code and data `RUNTIME_SERVICES_CODE`, the rest `RUNTIME_SERVICES_DATA`), `Resident memory checked: 325 pages, all kept by the OS after ExitBootServices.`, then the same 24 exits and statistics, teardown and `SUCCESS`, all from the copy. `-ProcessorCount 1`: the copy, `Resident memory checked: 324 pages`, `ExitBootServices event created`, the launch, and the unchanged stop at `RDMSR 0x40000020` (#27). The test harness `tools/ebs-harness` (`run-hyperv.ps1 -Harness`, `-SetVirtualAddressMap`) starts Aleph0, exits boot services as its guest, overwrites every reclaimable page but its own image, then makes CPUID, MSR and VMCALL exits and idles. Its first run loaded Aleph0 from `\EFI\BOOT\aleph0.efi` (`Resident memory checked: 324 pages`) and stopped at the same `RDMSR 0x40000020` before `StartImage` returned, so the checks this item needs waited for #27. With #27's forwarding, `-Harness -ProcessorCount 1`: COM1 `boot services exited`, `overwrote 2045 MiB in 22 ranges with 0xcccccccccccccccc`, `CPUID.1: ecx=0xf7fa3203, VMX hidden: Aleph0 answered.`, `IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE: wrote 0xffff8000eb5e0000, read back 0xffff8000eb5e0000: match.`, `test VMCALL (rcx=0x416c657068305453): resumed past it.`, `idling with HLT`; COM2 `VM exit #123091: VMCALL from Aleph0's ExitBootServices event (rcx=0x416c657068304542): boot services are over; output phase now runtime (serial only)`, then the VMBus drivers' own teardown, forwarded (`hypercall 0x005c` with status 0, WRMSRs of 0 to the synthetic timers `0x400000b0`-`0x400000b7`, `0x10000` (masked) to the SINTs from `0x40000090`), the harness's exits, `VM exit #123136: test VMCALL`, and 2 min of uptime with no stop (`reason=12 (HLT), 16777216 exits of this reason so far`). `-Harness -SetVirtualAddressMap -ProcessorCount 1`: the same, with `SetVirtualAddressMap: 5 runtime regions moved up by 0xffffff0000000000` before the overwrite, the ExitBootServices exit at #96973, the test VMCALL at #97018, and 2 min with no stop. The optional control run with the resident types set back to `LOADER_DATA` was not made.
- [ ] Expand to multiple vCPUs, scheduling, and an OS guest only after the single-vCPU lifecycle is reliable. Per-line output locking and CPU-numbered log lines are in section 0b.

## 6. End goal: anti-cheat research on top of the hypervisor

Once an OS guest boots reliably under Aleph0, the hypervisor becomes the base for research into game anti-cheat. Running below the guest OS, Aleph0 sees memory and CPU state that a kernel-mode cheat cannot hide from or tamper with. The design is not decided yet. The items below are candidate directions, not commitments.

The project is also a study of its own method: AI-driven development of low-level `unsafe` Rust, and AI-assisted reverse-engineering tooling for analysing the game and cheats the anti-cheat has to deal with.

Candidate directions:

- [ ] **Guest memory introspection.** Read a game process's memory from outside the guest by walking the guest's own page tables (from its CR3) and then EPT. `src/vmx/paging.rs` already walks 4-level tables; it would start from the guest's CR3 instead of the host's.
- [ ] **EPT-based protection.** Mark selected guest-physical pages read-only or execute-only in EPT, so writes to protected game code or anti-cheat data cause an EPT-violation exit (reason 48) that Aleph0 can log or block. Section 5 already does this for one page of its own guest.
- [ ] **EPT split views.** Map one guest-physical page to one host page for execution (execute-only, EPT/VPID capability bit 0, which Hyper-V reports) and to another for reads, switching on EPT violations, to watch or protect code without changing the bytes the guest can read.
- [ ] **Watching privileged changes.** Exit on writes to sensitive MSRs (for example `IA32_LSTAR`, the system-call entry point), to control registers, and to descriptor tables, to detect kernel hooks.
- [ ] **Detecting nested hypervisors.** Treat a guest `VMXON` (which always exits) as a signal that something in the guest is trying to run its own hypervisor.
- [ ] **Process tracking.** Follow guest CR3 changes to know which process is running, so protection applies to the game's address space only.

Open questions to settle before this section starts: which game or test target, which guest OS and version, what the anti-cheat reports and to whom, and how to keep Aleph0 itself hard to detect and to tamper with. Research only: no deployment against third-party services.

## How to verify each milestone

- Run `cargo build --target x86_64-unknown-uefi` after each change. It checks compilation, not VM-entry validity.
- Run `cargo test-host` for the host unit tests of pure logic (RFLAGS decoding, control selection, descriptor encoding). They do not execute VMX instructions. They live in `tests/unit/`, mirroring `src/`.
- Run `scripts/run-hyperv.ps1` from an elevated PowerShell session and inspect the VM console and the serial stream in the PowerShell window (also saved to `run\serial.log`). The runner turns off the named test VM and recreates its ESP VHDX; do not keep irreplaceable data there. VM-exit diagnostics appear only on serial.
- Record observed VMX instruction errors and VM-exit reasons as milestones are reached. QEMU without nested VMX can still test non-VMX diagnostics, but cannot validate `VMLAUNCH`.

Relevant code: `src/main.rs`, `src/resident/`, `src/bring_up/`, `src/serial.rs`, `src/port.rs`, `src/output.rs`, `src/vmx/segment.rs`, `src/vmx/vmxon.rs`, `src/vmx/vmcs/`, `src/vmx/region.rs`, `src/vmx/vmexit/`, `src/vmx/exit_decision/`, `src/vmx/exit_bitmaps.rs`, `src/vmx/ept/`, `src/vmx/mtrr/`, `src/vmx/guest.rs`, `src/vmx/paging.rs`, `src/vmx/guest_state.rs`, `src/vmx/page.rs`, `src/vmx/vmcall.rs`, `tools/ebs-harness/`, `scripts/run-hyperv.ps1`, and `scripts/read-serial.ps1`.
```

`docs/CLEAN_STOP.md`:

```md
# The clean stop: leaving VMX and returning to firmware

How Aleph0 stops its guest, leaves VMX operation, puts the firmware's CPU
state back, and returns from the EFI application with a `Status`, instead of
halting after the last VM exit (ROADMAP section 4). It covers how execution
gets from the VM-exit stub back into `bring_up::run`, the 64-bit stop value
that says why the guest stopped, the teardown order and the reasons for it,
and what the Hyper-V run printed.

Code: `src/vmx/vmcs/launch.rs` (launch stub and stop value),
`src/vmx/vmexit/` (exit stub and handler), `src/bring_up/teardown.rs`,
`src/bring_up/mod.rs` (`run`), `src/vmx/vmxon.rs` (`VmxOperation::leave`),
`src/main.rs` (timer check and return).

## 1. The problem

Before this change, `bring_up::run` ended with VMLAUNCH and never came back:

```
main ─▶ run ─▶ ... ─▶ VMLAUNCH ─▶ guest ─▶ VM exit ─▶ exit stub ─▶ handler ─▶ cli; hlt
                                                       (exit stack)
```

After VMLAUNCH, host code runs only when a VM exit starts the exit stub at
`HOST_RIP`, with `RSP = HOST_RSP` on the separate VM-exit stack. The frames
of `main` and `run` are still on the firmware stack, but nothing jumps back
to them, so the only option was to halt.

Returning to firmware needs two things:

1. **A way back into `run`'s frame** from the exit stub (section 2).
2. **Undoing what VMX and the VM exits changed** before firmware runs
   again (section 5). A VM exit loads host state with a few fixed values:

   | State | After every VM exit | Firmware expects |
   |---|---|---|
   | GDTR limit, IDTR limit | `0xFFFF` | the real table size |
   | TR limit | `0x67` | (unchanged for Aleph0's own TSS) |
   | RFLAGS | `0x2`, so IF = 0 | IF = 1 (timer interrupts) |
   | DR7, IA32_DEBUGCTL | `0x400`, `0` | the same values, unless a debugger is attached |
   | LDTR | null | null (UEFI uses no LDT) |

   On top of that the CPU is still in VMX root operation, with CR4.VMXE set
   and a current VMCS.

## 2. Getting back into `run`: a setjmp/longjmp

`vmx_launch` (in `launch.rs`) is a small assembly routine that saves its
caller's state *before* VMLAUNCH, like C's `setjmp`. When the guest should
stop, the exit stub jumps to `vmx_return_to_launcher`, which restores that
state and returns, like `longjmp`. To Rust, `vmcs::launch()` is an ordinary
call that returns a `GuestStop`.

### What gets saved

`vmx_launch` is called with the Microsoft x64 ABI (`efiapi`). A function
must give its caller back RBX, RBP, RDI, RSI, R12-R15 and RSP unchanged. So
the stub pushes those eight registers and writes RSP to a static,
`VMX_LAUNCH_RSP`:

```
firmware stack (grows down)

  │ ...                     │  launch()'s frame (Rust)
  │ return address          │  ◀ pushed by `call vmx_launch`
  │ rbx                     │
  │ rbp                     │
  │ rdi                     │
  │ rsi                     │
  │ r12                     │
  │ r13                     │
  │ r14                     │
  │ r15                     │  ◀ RSP here is saved in VMX_LAUNCH_RSP
  └─────────────────────────┘
```

`vmx_return_to_launcher` loads RSP from `VMX_LAUNCH_RSP`, pops the eight
registers in reverse order, and executes `ret`. The return address on the
stack takes it back into `launch()`, with the stop value in RAX, the
ordinary return register.

The ABI also makes XMM6-XMM15 callee-saved. The `x86_64-unknown-uefi`
target is soft-float with SSE disabled, so neither Aleph0 nor the guest
touches them.

### Why the saved frame survives the guest run

Three stacks are in play, and only the first one holds the saved frame:

| Stack | Who uses it | While the guest runs |
|---|---|---|
| firmware stack | `main`, `run`, `launch`, `vmx_launch` | frozen; nothing writes it |
| VM-exit stack (16 pages, `HOST_RSP`) | the exit stub and handler | every exit starts at its top again |
| guest stack page | the guest | the guest's RSP |

The guest runs with IF = 0, and every guest exception exits (exception
bitmap all ones), so no firmware handler runs on the firmware stack in the
meantime.

### The full path of one run

```
run ─▶ launch() ─▶ vmx_launch: push 8 regs, save RSP, VMLAUNCH
                                   │
          guest: mov eax,0xa1e0; vmcall ──▶ exit #1 ──▶ handler returns 0
                                   ◀── stub pops guest regs, VMRESUME
     guest: (wait loop) inc eax; vmcall ──▶ exit #2 ──▶ handler returns 0x4000_0000_0000_0002
                                                        │ stub: test rax,rax; jnz
                                                        ▼
                                   vmx_return_to_launcher: RSP = VMX_LAUNCH_RSP,
                                   pop 8 regs, ret
run ◀─ launch() returns GuestStop::Finished { exits: 2 }
 └─▶ teardown ─▶ main: timer check ─▶ return SUCCESS to firmware
```

## 3. The stop value

The stubs can pass one register back, so every way back carries one 64-bit
**stop value**. Bits 63:62 say which kind it is, and the rest is the payload:

| Bits 63:62 | Payload | Meaning | `GuestStop` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | RFLAGS right after VMLAUNCH | VMLAUNCH failed | `LaunchFailed` |
| 1 | number of exits | all planned exits arrived | `Finished` |
| 2 | exit number (bits 61:32), raw exit reason (bits 31:0) | an exit the handler does not resume | `Unexpected` |
| 3 | RFLAGS right after VMRESUME | VMRESUME failed | `ResumeFailed` |

Kind 0 is RFLAGS itself, unencoded: RFLAGS bits 63:22 are reserved and read
as 0, so the launch stub can return it as it is. RFLAGS bit 1 always reads
as 1, so **no stop value is 0**. That frees 0 to mean "resume the guest" as
the exit handler's return value.

Worked examples:

| Situation | Stop value | Decoded |
|---|---|---|
| the Hyper-V run: exit #2 was the last planned one | `0x4000_0000_0000_0002` | `Finished { exits: 2 }` |
| if exit #1 were a CPUID exit (reason 10) | `0x8000_0001_0000_000A` | `Unexpected { number: 1, reason: 10 }` |
| VMLAUNCH fails with ZF set (called with IF = 1) | `0x0000_0000_0000_0242` | `LaunchFailed { VmFailValid }` |
| VMRESUME fails with ZF set (IF = 0 after the exit) | `0xC000_0000_0000_0042` | `ResumeFailed { VmFailValid }` |

The exit number keeps only 30 bits, so an absurdly large number can never
spill into the kind bits. `encode_*` and `decode` are pure functions with
host tests in `tests/unit/vmx/vmcs/launch.rs`.

## 4. What the exit handler returns

`vmexit_handler` prints the exit, as before, then returns a `u64` to the
stub instead of halting:

| Exit | Handler action | Returns | Stub does |
|---|---|---|---|
| expected VMCALL, not the last one | writes GUEST_RIP = RIP + instruction length | `0` | pops guest registers, VMRESUME |
| expected VMCALL, the last planned one | prints `all 2 planned VMCALLs handled` | `encode_finished(number)` | jumps to `vmx_return_to_launcher` |
| anything else | prints `NOT an expected exit` | `encode_unexpected(number, reason)` | jumps to `vmx_return_to_launcher` |
| expected VMCALL, but GUEST_RIP cannot be advanced | prints why | `encode_unexpected(number, 18)` | jumps to `vmx_return_to_launcher` |

If VMRESUME itself falls through, the stub calls `vmresume_failed`, which
prints the reason and returns `encode_resume_failed(rflags)`; the stub then
jumps to `vmx_return_to_launcher` too. If VM_EXIT_REASON cannot be read, the
reason sent back is `0xFFFF`, which no real exit uses
(`exit_reason_name` prints it as `VM_EXIT_REASON unreadable`).

The stop path never restores the guest's registers: the exit stack is
simply abandoned, and the next launch would start it from the top again.

Since the NMI step, `exit_decision::decide` makes this decision, and the handler also resumes after NMI and NMI-window exits; see [NMI.md](NMI.md).

## 5. Teardown

`bring_up::teardown::teardown` runs in plain Rust on the firmware stack,
right after `launch()` returns. The order matters:

| # | Step | Why here |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | CR3, `lgdt` / `lidt` with the firmware's CR3, GDTR and IDTR | VM exits load Aleph0's own page tables, GDT and IDT ([HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md](HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md)); CR3 first, before anything can call firmware |
| 2 | VMCLEAR the VMCS (if one was created) | writes the CPU's cached VMCS data back to memory and makes it not current |
| 3 | VMXOFF, then CR0/CR4 as they were before VMXON | CR4.VMXE can only be cleared after VMXOFF; clearing it earlier is #GP |
| 4 | output phase back to `BootServices` | `log!` may use the firmware console again |
| 5 | STI, only if IF was 1 before VMXON | firmware's timer interrupts come back |
| 6 | read CR4, CR3, GDTR, IDTR, RFLAGS and print them | the `Teardown:` line on serial and console |

Worked example from the Hyper-V run: the guest-state line printed
`idtr=0x000000007ff2fcd0/0x0fff`, the firmware's IDT. After each VM exit the
CPU's IDTR was `0x7ff2fcd0/0xffff`; step 1 loads `/0x0fff` again. The same
line printed `cr4=0x2668`: CR4 in VMX operation, with bit 13 (`0x2000`,
VMXE) set. Step 3 writes back the CR4 value saved before VMXON, which has
VMXE clear, and the `Teardown:` line confirms `CR4.VMXE=0`.

### Why interrupts and the console come back last

When the guest ran, interrupts stay off from the first VM exit until step 5.
The firmware console can call `RestoreTPL`, which executes STI, so a console
`log!` during steps 1 to 3 would turn interrupts on too early. Until step 4
the phase is still `VmExit` (the exit handler set it), so `log!` writes to
serial only. On paths that never launched the guest, the phase is still
`BootServices` and IF was never cleared, so the problem does not arise.

IF is recorded in `run` right before VMXON (`FirmwareState`), not in the
launch stub. Nothing between VMXON and VMLAUNCH turns interrupts off, so the
value is the same, and the stub stays smaller.

### What teardown leaves as it is

- **TR** keeps Aleph0's TSS selector. LTR cannot load a null selector, and
  the TSS and GDT pages are never freed, so the CPU's cached TSS descriptor
  stays valid. The selector may lie past the firmware GDT's limit; only an
  LTR or a task switch would look it up again.
- **DR7, IA32_DEBUGCTL, LDTR** stay as the VM exit set them. Firmware
  normally runs with those values anyway; they matter only with a hardware
  debugger attached.
- **Memory**: no page is returned to UEFI. The TSS, GDT, VM-exit stack,
  guest pages, VMXON region and VMCS stay allocated.

### When a teardown step fails

Every step runs even if an earlier one failed. The exception: after a
failed VMXOFF, CR0/CR4 are not touched, because the CPU is still in VMX
operation. Each failure is printed when it happens. `run` returns the error
from before teardown if there was one, otherwise `BringUpError::Teardown`.

## 6. Error numbers are read early

For a VmFailValid, the reason number lives in the current VMCS
(`VM_INSTRUCTION_ERROR`). Errors used to read it while printing. Now they are
printed after teardown, and a VMREAD after VMXOFF raises #UD. So the number
is read when the error is created, while the VMCS is still current:
`vmcs_step` and `guest_state_error` (in `bring_up/error.rs`) and `launch()`
store it in the error value (`instruction_error: Option<u32>`), and
`report_vmcs_error` only prints what was stored.

## 7. Which failures reach teardown

| Where `run` fails | What is undone before returning |
|---|---|
| before the host tables are active (TSS/GDT allocation) | nothing was changed |
| after activation, before VMXON (allocation, page-table check, VMX unsupported, VMXON failed) | the firmware's GDTR is loaded again |
| after VMXON (VMCS setup, changed host tables, VMLAUNCH, unexpected exit, VMRESUME) | full teardown |

So once VMXON succeeds, firmware never gets the CPU back in VMX operation,
unless VMXOFF itself fails, which teardown prints.

## 8. Back in `main`

`main` maps the result to a `Status` (`SUCCESS` for the planned run,
`ABORTED` for any error), then runs `check_firmware_timer`: it creates a
one-shot UEFI timer event, arms it for 1 s, waits for it, and closes it. Only
the firmware's timer interrupt signals that event, so getting past the wait
shows that interrupts reach the firmware's handlers through the restored
IDT. If they did not, the wait would never end and `Waiting 1 s on a firmware
timer event...` would be the last line on serial.

The wait does not prove that teardown restored IF: WaitForEvent can turn
interrupts on by itself through `RestoreTPL`. That is why the `Teardown:`
line prints IF separately.

Then `main` returns the status, and the firmware's boot manager takes over.

## 9. The Hyper-V run

The tail of `run\serial.log` from the clean-stop step, before NMI exiting was added, with what each part shows. Its addresses and the exit #2 RIP match that older guest, not the current one:

> This log predates EPT and the emulated exits. Since then the guest first
> causes nine emulated exits (CPUID, four MSR, four I/O; see
> [EMULATED_EXITS.md](EMULATED_EXITS.md)), one HLT and one EPT violation, so
> in a current run its VMCALLs are exits #12 and #13: the numbers are eleven
> higher. The guest RIPs and addresses differ too. Since #22 the `Teardown:`
> line also reports `firmware CR3 restored=true`.

```text
VM exit #1: guest rip=0x000000007eb0f005 instruction length=3
VM exit #1: guest rax=0x000000000000a1e0 ...                      ◀ guest code ran up to VMCALL
VM exit #1: expected VMCALL (rax=0xa1e0); resuming the guest at rip=0x000000007eb0f008.
VM exit #2: guest rip=0x000000007eb0f005 instruction length=3
VM exit #2: guest rax=0x000000000000a1e1 ...                      ◀ resumed past VMCALL, ran inc eax
VM exit #2: expected VMCALL (rax=0xa1e1); all 2 planned exits handled.
VM exit #2: stopping the guest; returning to bring-up.            ◀ handler returned 0x4000_0000_0000_0002
Teardown: CR4.VMXE=0 firmware GDTR/IDTR restored=true IF=1.       ◀ back in run(), VMX off
Guest finished after 2 VM exits; VMX operation left.             ◀ GuestStop::Finished { exits: 2 }
Waiting 1 s on a firmware timer event...
Firmware timer fired: interrupts reach the firmware again.        ◀ IDT and timer work
Returning to firmware with SUCCESS.                               ◀ main returns
```

Under QEMU without VMX, bring-up stops in step 1 at an older check
(`IdtRequiresIst`: OVMF's IDT uses IST stacks), before any table is loaded.
The timer check still runs, and the last line is `Returning to firmware
with ABORTED.`

## 10. What is not covered yet

- Only the planned path ran on real VMX. The other stops (unexpected exit,
  failed VMLAUNCH or VMRESUME) go through the same teardown but have only
  been compiled. The `unexpected-exit-test` Cargo feature changes the
  expected guest RAX on purpose, which exercises `Unexpected` at main
  VMCALL #1 (exit #12), the stop report, teardown from exit context, and
  `ABORTED` (`run-hyperv.ps1 -Features unexpected-exit-test`).
- NMIs: since the NMI step, NMI exiting is on and NMIs are reinjected into
  the guest's own IDT; see NMI.md.
- After `ExitBootServices` Aleph0 must stay resident instead of returning
  ([RESIDENT.md](RESIDENT.md)). A stop then halts, as it does for the
  firmware guest; the OS-mode stop policy is #28.
- All of this is the test guest's path, the regression mode (Cargo feature
  `test-guest`). A default build virtualizes the firmware in place, which
  has no stop to return from: a stop of the firmware halts after its report,
  and no teardown runs. See [FIRMWARE_GUEST.md](FIRMWARE_GUEST.md).

## Cheat sheet

| Name | Where | What |
|---|---|---|
| `vmx_launch` | `vmcs/launch.rs` | push 8 callee-saved regs, save RSP, VMLAUNCH |
| `vmx_return_to_launcher` | `vmcs/launch.rs` | reload RSP, pop 8 regs, `ret` with the stop value in RAX |
| `VMX_LAUNCH_RSP` | `vmcs/launch.rs` | the saved RSP |
| `GuestStop` | `vmcs/launch.rs` | `Finished`, `Unexpected`, `LaunchFailed`, `ResumeFailed` |
| `RESUME_GUEST` (0) | `vmexit/handler.rs` | handler return value: resume |
| `stub_return` | `vmexit/handler.rs` | `ExitAction` to `0` or a stop value |
| `VmxOperation::leave` | `vmxon.rs` | VMXOFF, then CR0/CR4 from before VMXON |
| `load_gdtr`, `load_idtr` | `segment.rs` | LGDT/LIDT from a `DescriptorTable` |
| `teardown` | `bring_up/teardown.rs` | tables, VMCLEAR, VMXOFF + CRs, phase, STI, report |
| `check_firmware_timer` | `main.rs` | 1 s UEFI timer event before returning |

```

`docs/EMULATED_EXITS.md`:

```md
# Emulated exits: CPUID, RDMSR/WRMSR and port I/O

An operating system runs CPUID among its first instructions, and CPUID
always causes a VM exit. Until Aleph0 handles such exits, no real guest code
can run under it. This page explains how Aleph0 handles the exits every guest
needs: it executes the instruction itself and hands the result back
(**passthrough emulation**):
- one handler per exit reason;
- the flow of one emulated exit;
- CPUID, and the one value Aleph0 changes;
- the MSR bitmap, and which RDMSR/WRMSR exit;
- the I/O bitmaps, and which IN/OUT exit;
- the test the guest runs, and how it is checked;
- what the Hyper-V run printed;
- what is not covered yet.

Code:
- `src/vmx/exit_decision/mod.rs`: `decide`, the dispatch on the exit reason, and the shared exit types;
- `src/vmx/exit_decision/emulation.rs`: the handlers for CPUID, RDMSR, WRMSR and IN/OUT, and `cpuid_policy`;
- `src/vmx/exit_decision/scenario.rs`: the test guest's own exits (EPT write, VMCALLs, NMI);
- `src/vmx/exit_bitmaps.rs`: the MSR bitmap and the two I/O bitmaps;
- `src/vmx/vmexit/handler.rs`: `execute`, `prepare_resume`, `queue_exception`;
- `src/vmx/vmexit/guest_mtrrs.rs`: the guest's copy of its MTRRs, which its RDMSR and WRMSR of them reach;
- `src/vmx/vmexit/report.rs`: the report lines;
- `src/port.rs`: `in`/`out` of 1, 2 and 4 bytes;
- `src/vmx/guest.rs`: the guest code that causes the exits, and its checks;
- `src/bring_up/mod.rs`: `PassthroughState`.

## 1. One handler per exit reason

The exit handler (`vmexit/handler.rs`) reads an exit into an `ExitInfo`, calls
`exit_decision::decide`, and applies what comes back (`docs/NMI.md`
section 6). `decide` first handles what holds for every exit, whatever its
reason: a failed VM entry stops the guest. An exit that interrupted an
event's delivery (IDT-vectoring info valid) is still judged by its reason;
the handler then re-delivers the interrupted event on top of the plan
(`docs/NMI.md` section 8). `decide` dispatches on the basic exit reason:

```rust
pub fn decide(state: ExitState, exit: ExitInfo) -> (ExitEvent, ExitState) {
    if exit.reason.entry_failure {
        return (ExitEvent::Unexpected, state);
    }
    match exit.reason.basic {
        EXIT_REASON_CPUID => emulation::cpuid(state, &exit),
        EXIT_REASON_RDMSR => emulation::rdmsr(state, &exit),
        EXIT_REASON_WRMSR => emulation::wrmsr(state, &exit),
        EXIT_REASON_IO_INSTRUCTION => emulation::io(state, &exit),
        EXIT_REASON_EXCEPTION_OR_NMI => scenario::exception_or_nmi(state, &exit),
        EXIT_REASON_NMI_WINDOW => scenario::nmi_window(state, &exit),
        EXIT_REASON_EPT_VIOLATION => scenario::ept_violation(state, &exit),
        EXIT_REASON_VMCALL => scenario::vmcall(state, &exit),
        _ => (ExitEvent::Unexpected, state),
    }
}
```

Every handler has the same signature, `fn(ExitState, &ExitInfo) ->
(ExitEvent, ExitState)`: given the state kept between exits and what was
read about this exit, it returns what the exit is and the state for the next
one. None of them touches the CPU, so each can be tested on the host.

KVM keeps the same structure as a table of function pointers indexed by exit
reason (`kvm_vmx_exit_handlers[]`). Aleph0 uses a `match` instead, without
function pointers: each handler stays a separate pure function, and the list
of handled reasons is readable in one place. A reason without a handler lands
in the `_` arm, which is `Unexpected` and stops the guest.

The handlers live in two files:
- `emulation.rs`: instructions Aleph0 executes for **any** guest (CPUID,
  RDMSR, WRMSR, IN, OUT). It stays when an OS guest comes.
- `scenario.rs`: the test guest's own exits (its write to the protected data
  page, its VMCALLs, NMI reinjection). It goes when an OS guest comes.

## 2. Passthrough: the flow of one emulated exit

For these instructions Aleph0 does not model the device or the register file.
It runs the same instruction itself, in VMX root operation, and puts the
result where the guest expects it:

```text
guest: cpuid / rdmsr / wrmsr / in / out
  │  VM exit
  ▼
vmexit_entry (stub)    push the 15 general-purpose registers = RegisterFrame
  ▼
vmexit_handler(frame)
  ├─ read_exit    VMCS fields + frame (prints nothing) ─▶ ExitRead, with its ExitInfo
  ├─ judge        decide(state, exit)                  ─▶ ExitEvent::Emulated(Emulation), next state
  ├─ carry_out    event.action()
  │                 = Resume(ResumePlan { emulate: Some(emulation), advance_rip: true, .. })
  │    └─ prepare_resume
  │         1. execute(emulation, frame)   the real instruction, in root operation;
  │                                        result into frame.rax .. frame.rdx
  │         2. GUEST_RIP = RIP + VM_EXIT_INSTRUCTION_LEN
  └─ report_exit  the exit's lines, once its outcome is known
     returns RESUME_GUEST (0)
  ▼
vmexit_entry (stub)    pop the frame into the guest's registers, VMRESUME
  ▼
guest: the instruction after the emulated one, with the result in its registers
```

The plan comes from one arm of `ExitEvent::action`:

```rust
Self::Emulated(emulation) => ExitAction::Resume(ResumePlan {
    emulate: Some(emulation),
    ..ResumePlan::PAST_INSTRUCTION
}),
```

`PAST_INSTRUCTION` is the plan that advances RIP. The instruction is
executed **before** RIP moves, so the guest never runs past it without its
result. `VM_EXIT_INSTRUCTION_LEN` gives the length; Aleph0 does not decode
the instruction.

Where RIP will go is worked out before the instruction runs, with
`next_rip`. RIP is the guest's: for an instruction at the very top of the
address space `RIP + length` would wrap, and for one ending at the last
canonical byte of the lower half it would be `0x0000_8000_0000_0000`, which
VM entry refuses. In both cases the guest is stopped instead, before the
instruction takes effect (the same as when the length cannot be read).

The stub pushed the guest's registers into a `RegisterFrame` on the exit
stack, and `execute` takes it as `&mut RegisterFrame`. After the handler
returns 0 the stub pops that frame into the CPU, so what `execute` wrote
reaches the guest. The register rules are the instructions' own:

| Instruction | Result | What `execute` writes |
|---|---|---|
| CPUID | EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX | each as a 32-bit write, which zero-extends into the 64-bit register |
| RDMSR | EDX:EAX | `rax = value & 0xFFFF_FFFF`, `rdx = value >> 32` |
| WRMSR | — | no register |
| IN, 8 or 16 bits | AL or AX | only those bits; the rest of RAX stays |
| IN, 32 bits | EAX | zero-extends into RAX |
| OUT | — | no register |

The IN rule is `merge_in`:

```rust
pub fn merge_in(rax: u64, size: IoSize, value: u32) -> u64 {
    match size {
        IoSize::Dword => u64::from(value),
        _ => (rax & !size.mask()) | (u64::from(value) & size.mask()),
    }
}
```

For `rax = 0x1122_3344_5566_7788`:
- `in al, dx` reading `0xA5` gives `0x1122_3344_5566_77A5`;
- `in ax, dx` reading `0xBEEF` gives `0x1122_3344_5566_BEEF`;
- `in eax, dx` reading `0x1234_5678` gives `0x0000_0000_1234_5678`.

A worked exit: the guest runs `rdmsr` (`0F 32`, 2 bytes) with
`ecx = 0xC0000102`. The exit has reason 31; `emulation::rdmsr` returns
`Emulation::Rdmsr { msr: 0xC0000102 }`; `execute` runs the real RDMSR, gets
(say) `0x0000_7A1E_0000_0000` and writes `rax = 0`, `rdx = 0x7A1E`; GUEST_RIP
moves by 2; the guest continues after its `rdmsr`.

The emulation handlers hold for any guest, so they read only the exit
(`fn(&ExitInfo) -> ExitEvent`) and count nothing. The exit handler counts
what it carried out in the vCPU's exit statistics (`vmexit::stats`,
`VcpuStats`), the way KVM keeps `struct kvm_vcpu_stat`: one counter per
instruction executed for the guest (`cpuid_exits`, `msr_read_exits`,
`msr_write_exits`, `io_in_exits`, `io_out_exits`, and, forwarded to
Hyper-V, `hypercall_exits`, `synthetic_read_exits` and
`synthetic_write_exits`), plus `exits`, `halt_exits`, `nmi_injections` and
`exception_injections`. An exit counts
only once its resume was prepared, so a WRMSR whose next RIP was invalid,
and which never ran, is not counted. Section 6 uses them. Each counter is a
`u64`, which no exit rate overflows.

## 3. CPUID and its policy

CPUID always exits in VMX non-root operation; no control turns that off.
`emulation::cpuid` takes the leaf from the guest's EAX and the subleaf from
ECX, and `execute` runs `__cpuid_count(leaf, subleaf)` in root operation.
Under Hyper-V that returns what Hyper-V shows Aleph0.

Everything passes through except one bit:

```rust
const CPUID_1_ECX_VMX: u32 = 1 << 5;

pub fn cpuid_policy(leaf: u32, raw: CpuidResult) -> CpuidResult {
    match leaf {
        1 => CpuidResult {
            ecx: raw.ecx & !CPUID_1_ECX_VMX,
            ..raw
        },
        _ => raw,
    }
}
```

**CPUID.1:ECX bit 5 (VMX) is hidden.** A guest that saw it would try VMXON,
which always exits (reason 27) in non-root operation, and Aleph0 does not
emulate VMX. The report line prints both values, so the effect is visible:
`ecx=` is what the guest got, `processor ecx=` what the CPU returned.

What passes through:
- **ECX bit 31 (hypervisor present) and the leaves from 0x40000000.** Under
  nested Hyper-V they describe Hyper-V, and a guest that sees them uses
  Hyper-V's interface: hypercalls, which are VMCALLs and exit to Aleph0,
  and the synthetic MSRs. Decided in #27: the guest keeps them, and Aleph0
  forwards the hypercalls and the synthetic MSRs to Hyper-V
  ([HYPERV_INTERFACE.md](HYPERV_INTERFACE.md)).
- **Values that follow CR4 and XCR0**, still to be decided before an OS
  guest: CPUID.1:ECX.OSXSAVE and leaf 0xD
  (the XSAVE area size). They are right for the guest only while its CR4 and
  XCR0 equal the host's, as they do today.

## 4. The MSR bitmap

RDMSR and WRMSR cause a VM exit depending on one primary control:
- without "use MSR bitmaps" (bit 28), **every** RDMSR and WRMSR exits;
- with it, they exit only for MSRs whose bit is set in the MSR bitmap, and
  always for MSRs outside the two ranges the bitmap covers.

Aleph0 turns the control on (`DesiredControls::minimal_64_bit_guest`).
`ExitBitmaps::allocate` makes three zeroed pages (this one and the two I/O
bitmaps of section 5) and sets the bits of `INTERCEPTED_MSRS`, of every
address an MTRR MSR can have, and of `INTERCEPTED_PORTS`; `write_to_vmcs` writes the
MSR bitmap's address to
`MSR_BITMAP` (`0x2004`). The page has four quarters:

```text
MSR bitmap, one 4 KiB page (Intel SDM Vol. 3C, "MSR-Bitmap Address"):
offset 0x000  read,  MSR 0x00000000..=0x00001FFF
offset 0x400  read,  MSR 0xC0000000..=0xC0001FFF
offset 0x800  write, MSR 0x00000000..=0x00001FFF
offset 0xC00  write, MSR 0xC0000000..=0xC0001FFF
RDMSR/WRMSR of any other MSR always exits.
```

`msr_bit` finds an MSR's bit:

```rust
pub const fn msr_bit(msr: u32, access: MsrAccess) -> Option<(usize, u8)> {
    let (read_offset, index) = match msr {
        0..=0x1FFF => (0x000, msr),
        0xC000_0000..=0xC000_1FFF => (0x400, msr - 0xC000_0000),
        _ => return None,
    };
    let offset = match access {
        MsrAccess::Read => read_offset,
        MsrAccess::Write => read_offset + 0x800,
    };
    Some((offset + index as usize / 8, (index % 8) as u8))
}
```

For IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE (`0xC0000102`): index `0x102`, so byte
`0x400 + 0x102 / 8 = 0x420` and bit `0x102 % 8 = 2` for reads, byte `0xC20`
bit 2 for writes. `None` means the MSR is outside both ranges.

### Why not exiting is a correct passthrough

For an MSR whose bit is clear, the guest's own RDMSR/WRMSR runs in non-root
operation, and the CPU uses the guest's value. That holds even for MSRs
whose guest value is a VMCS field (IA32_GS_BASE, IA32_EFER, IA32_PAT,
IA32_SYSENTER_*): while the guest runs, the CPU holds the guest's value, so
the guest reads and writes its own.

That is correct for the guest. For Aleph0 it is safe only where VM exit
loads the host's value back. The SYSENTER MSRs and the FS and GS bases
always are (`HOST_*` fields). IA32_PAT is when the CPU allows "save
IA32_PAT" and "load IA32_PAT" on VM exit and "load IA32_PAT" on VM entry,
which `configure_controls` then turns on (`vmcs::pat_switch`): otherwise a
guest that made PAT entry 0 UC or WC would set the memory type of every one
of Aleph0's accesses, whose page tables select that entry. IA32_EFER is not
switched yet: its bits other than LME and LMA stay as the guest wrote them
([HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md](HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md) section 9).

### The trap: emulating an MSR the VMCS holds

An *intercepted* MSR is different. Aleph0 emulates it with a real
RDMSR/WRMSR in root operation, which reaches the **host's** value, not the
guest's. For IA32_GS_BASE, say, a VM exit loads `HOST_GS_BASE`, so an
emulated RDMSR would give the guest the host's GS base, and an emulated
WRMSR would overwrite the host's. Hence `VMCS_HELD_MSRS`, the MSRs whose
guest value is a VMCS field, and a compile-time check that no intercepted
MSR is on it, or lacks a bitmap bit:

```rust
pub const INTERCEPTED_MSRS: [u32; 1] = [IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE];

// Every intercepted MSR has a bitmap bit, and none is held in the VMCS.
const _: () = {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < INTERCEPTED_MSRS.len() {
        assert!(msr_bit(INTERCEPTED_MSRS[i], MsrAccess::Read).is_some());
        let mut j = 0;
        while j < VMCS_HELD_MSRS.len() {
            assert!(
                INTERCEPTED_MSRS[i] != VMCS_HELD_MSRS[j],
                "an intercepted MSR is held in the VMCS"
            );
            j += 1;
        }
        i += 1;
    }
};
```

IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE is safe because VM entry and exit do not switch it (it
has no VMCS field) and Aleph0 never runs SWAPGS: the CPU's value is the
guest's.

### The four routes

An RDMSR or WRMSR exit takes one of five routes, chosen by `route`:

| MSR | Route | Event |
|---|---|---|
| in `INTERCEPTED_MSRS` | emulate with the real RDMSR/WRMSR | `Emulated` |
| an MTRR MSR the guest has (`ExitInfo::mtrr`) | read or write the guest's copy; a WRMSR value the CPU would refuse gets #GP(0) | `Emulated(MtrrRead)`, `Emulated(MtrrWrite)`, `GuestGeneralProtection` |
| outside both ranges, one of Hyper-V's synthetic MSRs, Hyper-V present | forward it to Hyper-V ([HYPERV_INTERFACE.md](HYPERV_INTERFACE.md)) | `Emulated(SyntheticRead)`, `Emulated(SyntheticWrite)` |
| outside both ranges otherwise (`msr_bit` is `None`) | inject #GP(0) into the guest | `GuestGeneralProtection` |
| in range, bit clear | it should never have exited: the bitmap is broken; stop | `Unexpected` |

The MTRRs are the one intercepted MSR family Aleph0 does not pass through:
the CPU's still set the memory types of Aleph0's own accesses in root
operation, so the guest reads and writes a copy, and EPT follows the copy
([MTRR.md](MTRR.md) section 7).

The middle row is what hardware does for an MSR that does not exist.
Aleph0 does not know whether such an MSR exists, and a real RDMSR/WRMSR of a
missing one would #GP in the host, so the guest gets the #GP instead.

**WRMSR checks the value first.** Every intercepted MSR holds an address
(only IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE today), and a WRMSR of a non-canonical address
faults. In the guest that is correct; in exit context it would be a #GP in
the host, which Aleph0's host fault handler can only print before it halts
the CPU ([HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md](HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md) section 5). So
`wrmsr` calls `is_canonical_48` and, for a non-canonical value, injects the
guest's #GP instead of executing:

```rust
pub fn is_canonical_48(value: u64) -> bool {
    ((value as i64) << 16 >> 16) as u64 == value
}
```

`0xFFFF_8000_0000_0000` and `0x0000_7A1E_0000_0000` are canonical (bits
63:47 all equal); `0x0000_8000_0000_0000` is not (bit 47 set, bits 63:48
clear).

### Injecting #GP

The plan `INJECT_GP` leaves RIP where it is, as for any fault, and
`queue_general_protection` writes the event for the next VM entry:

```rust
unsafe fn queue_general_protection() -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX root operation with a current VMCS.
    unsafe {
        vmcs::vmwrite(VM_ENTRY_EXCEPTION_ERROR_CODE, 0)?;
        vmcs::vmwrite(
            VM_ENTRY_INTERRUPTION_INFO,
            InterruptionInfo::GENERAL_PROTECTION.0.into(),
        )
    }
}
```

```text
0x80000B0D = 1000 0000 0000 0000 0000 1011 0000 1101
bit 31    = 1   valid
bit 11    = 1   deliver an error code (0, from VM_ENTRY_EXCEPTION_ERROR_CODE)
bits 10:8 = 3   type: hardware exception
bits 7:0  = 13  vector: #GP
```

The CPU delivers it through the guest's own IDT, at the `rdmsr`/`wrmsr`
that faulted.

## 5. The I/O bitmaps

IN and OUT work the same way, with "use I/O bitmaps" (primary bit 25) and
two bitmap pages, one bit per port:

```text
I/O bitmaps, one bit per port:
A (one page): ports 0x0000..=0x7FFF    B (one page): ports 0x8000..=0xFFFF
An access to several ports exits if any of their bits is set.
```

While bit 25 is set, the CPU ignores bit 24 (unconditional I/O exiting).
`io_bit` finds a port's bit:

```rust
pub const fn io_bit(port: u16) -> (IoBitmap, usize, u8) {
    let page = if port < 0x8000 { IoBitmap::A } else { IoBitmap::B };
    let index = (port & 0x7FFF) as usize;
    (page, index / 8, (port % 8) as u8)
}
```

The bit of port *p* is bit `p % 8` of byte `(p & 0x7FFF) / 8` in its page.
Aleph0 intercepts one port, `0x3FF`, the COM1 scratch register (base `0x3F8`
+ 7): a byte with no effect on the UART. COM1 is the guest's; Aleph0 prints
on COM2. It is
bit 7 of byte `0x7F` in page A. `write_to_vmcs` writes the pages' addresses
to `IO_BITMAP_A` (`0x2000`) and `IO_BITMAP_B` (`0x2002`).

### The multi-port rule

A 2- or 4-byte access touches 2 or 4 consecutive ports, and it exits if
**any** of their bits is set. So `in ax, dx` with `dx = 0x3FE` exits, because
it covers `0x3FE` and `0x3FF`. The exit handler does not check the port
against `INTERCEPTED_PORTS`: it passes through the port and size from the
exit qualification, as the guest would have done itself. This is a known
property, not a bug in the test: a 4-byte access at `0x3FC` exits, and
Aleph0 then reaches the real COM1 registers `0x3FC` to `0x3FF` (modem
control, line status, modem status and scratch): the guest's own UART,
which it could reach without Aleph0 anyway. Aleph0's serial driver is on
COM2, out of reach of this rule. The test guest never does that. It is a
decision for the OS-guest step (section 8).

### The exit qualification

Aleph0 learns what the guest did from the exit qualification, not from
decoding the instruction (`IoQualification`):

```text
bits 2:0   size − 1: 0 = 1 byte, 1 = 2 bytes, 3 = 4 bytes
bit  3     direction: 1 = IN, 0 = OUT
bit  4     string instruction (INS/OUTS)
bit  5     REP prefix
bit  6     operand: 1 = immediate port, 0 = DX
bits 31:16 port
```

For `in al, dx` with `dx = 0x3FF` the qualification is `0x03FF0008`: port
`0x3FF` in bits 31:16, direction bit set, size 1. For `out dx, al` it is
`0x03FF0000`. An OUT sends the value in AL, AX or EAX of the guest's RAX
(`out_value`); an IN merges into RAX as in section 2. `execute` runs the
matching function of `src/port.rs` (`inb`, `inw`, `inl`, `outb`, `outw`,
`outl`).

The encoding 2 of the size field is unused, and a **string or REP form
(INS, OUTS, REP) stops the guest**. Those read or write guest memory through
the guest's page tables and EPT, and handling them would need a translation
of the guest's addresses, segment and direction-flag handling and page
crossings; Aleph0 has none. This is also why the `nomem` option in
`port.rs` is sound here: no emulated port access reaches RAM through
Aleph0.

## 6. The test

The guest begins with a block that causes the nine emulated exits, before
the EPT write and the VMCALLs (`src/vmx/guest.rs`):

```asm
guest_code_start:
    // CPUID always exits; Aleph0 executes it and hides VMX (CPUID.1:ECX
    // bit 5), so a guest never tries VMXON.
    mov eax, 1
    xor ecx, ecx
    cpuid
    bt ecx, 5
    jc guest_emulation_failed
    // IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE exits through the MSR bitmap; Aleph0 runs the
    // real RDMSR/WRMSR. Save it, write GUEST_MSR_VALUE, read it back,
    // restore it.
    mov ecx, {kernel_gs_base}
    rdmsr
    mov esi, eax
    mov edi, edx
    mov eax, {msr_low}
    mov edx, {msr_high}
    wrmsr
    xor eax, eax
    xor edx, edx
    rdmsr
    cmp eax, {msr_low}
    jne guest_emulation_failed
    cmp edx, {msr_high}
    jne guest_emulation_failed
    mov eax, esi
    mov edx, edi
    wrmsr
    // The COM1 scratch register exits through the I/O bitmap; Aleph0 runs
    // the real IN/OUT. Save it, write GUEST_IO_VALUE, read it back, restore
    // it.
    mov dx, {scratch_port}
    in al, dx
    mov sil, al
    mov al, {io_value}
    out dx, al
    xor eax, eax
    in al, dx
    cmp al, {io_value}
    jne guest_emulation_failed
    mov al, sil
    out dx, al
```

```asm
guest_emulation_failed:
    // An emulated instruction returned the wrong value: stop with a marker
    // in RAX, which the #UD exit prints.
    mov eax, {fail_marker}
    ud2
```

The placeholders are the constants of `guest.rs`:

| Placeholder | Value |
|---|---|
| `kernel_gs_base` | `IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE`, `0xC0000102` |
| `msr_low`, `msr_high` | the halves of `GUEST_MSR_VALUE`, `0x0000_7A1E_0000_0000`: `0` and `0x7A1E` |
| `scratch_port` | `GUEST_SCRATCH_PORT`, `0x3FF` |
| `io_value` | `GUEST_IO_VALUE`, `0xA5` |
| `fail_marker` | `GUEST_EMULATION_FAIL_MARKER`, `0xFA11` |

The nine exits, in the order they happen:

| # | Instruction | What it checks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `cpuid` leaf 1 | bit 5 of ECX is clear: VMX is hidden |
| 2 | `rdmsr` | saves the original IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE |
| 3 | `wrmsr` | writes `GUEST_MSR_VALUE` |
| 4 | `rdmsr` | reads back `GUEST_MSR_VALUE`, both halves |
| 5 | `wrmsr` | writes the original back |
| 6 | `in al, dx` | saves the original scratch byte |
| 7 | `out dx, al` | writes `GUEST_IO_VALUE` |
| 8 | `in al, dx` | reads back `GUEST_IO_VALUE` |
| 9 | `out dx, al` | writes the original back |

The guest's CPUID check only tests the VMX bit. The full CPUID result is
visible on serial, but the guest does not check it. The MSR and port are real
hardware, not a copy, so on success the guest saves what it writes and puts
it back. If a check fails after its first WRMSR or OUT, it jumps to
`guest_emulation_failed` and `ud2` **without** restoring; bring-up does not
restore either, and prints `restored=false` below.

Then the guest moves its last variable MTRR and puts it back, which reaches
only Aleph0's copy of its MTRRs and the EPT memory types ([MTRR.md](MTRR.md)
section 7). It reads `IA32_MTRRCAP`, which does not exit, for the number of
variable ranges, and MAXPHYADDR from CPUID to build the masks. Eleven more
exits follow, numbered here as under Hyper-V, where the last range is 7:

| # | Instruction | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | `cpuid` leaf 0x80000008 | MAXPHYADDR, in EAX bits 7:0 |
| 11, 12 | `rdmsr` of PHYSBASE7, PHYSMASK7 | saves the pair, from the copy |
| 13 | `wrmsr` PHYSMASK7 ← 0 | turns the range off |
| 14 | `wrmsr` PHYSBASE7 ← `GUEST_MTRR_BASE` | `0x200000`, type UC |
| 15 | `wrmsr` PHYSMASK7 ← 2 MiB, valid | EPT maps the region at 2 MiB as one UC page |
| 16 | `rdmsr` PHYSMASK7 | reads the mask back, all 64 bits |
| 17 | `wrmsr` PHYSMASK7 ← 4 KiB, valid | the region takes a spare PT: its first page UC, the rest WB |
| 18 | `wrmsr` PHYSMASK7 ← 0 | the region is one WB page again; its PT is spare again |
| 19, 20 | `wrmsr` PHYSBASE7, PHYSMASK7 | puts the pair back |

`hlt` is then exit #21, the EPT violation #22, and the main VMCALLs #23 and
#24.

### Two checks, because one is not enough

- **The guest checks the values.** A wrong result ends in `ud2` with
  `0xFA11` in EAX. The #UD is an exception exit (reason 0, vector 6), which
  `exit_decision` does not handle, so the guest stops and serial shows the
  marker in RAX.
- **Bring-up checks the exit statistics.** A guest that got the right
  value does not prove the exit happened: with a broken bitmap, `rdmsr`
  would run directly and return the same value. Once the guest has
  finished, bring-up compares the vCPU's statistics with
  `guest::expected_stats`, as a KVM selftest checks a vCPU's statistics
  after its run:

```rust
pub fn expected_stats(actual: &VcpuStats) -> VcpuStats {
    VcpuStats {
        cpuid_exits: 2,
        msr_read_exits: 2,
        msr_write_exits: 2,
        mtrr_read_exits: 3,
        mtrr_write_exits: 7,
        io_in_exits: 2,
        io_out_exits: 2,
        halt_exits: 1,
        exception_injections: 0,
        // How many exits and NMIs depends on whether an NMI arrived.
        ..*actual
    }
}
```

Any other count fails the run with `UnexpectedExitStats`, which prints both
sets of statistics, and the application returns `ABORTED`. MTRR accesses
have counters of their own, so one passed through to the CPU by mistake
would show as a wrong `msr_*_exits` and `mtrr_*_exits`, not as the right
total.

### What serial shows

Each emulated exit prints one line (`report_emulation`), after the usual
`reason=`, `qualification=` and register lines of `docs/EPT.md`:

```text
VM exit #N: CPUID leaf=0x1 subleaf=0x0 -> eax=... ebx=... ecx=... edx=... (processor ecx=...); resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: RDMSR 0xc0000102 -> 0x...; resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: WRMSR 0xc0000102 <- 0x00007a1e00000000; resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: IN port 0x3ff size=1 -> 0x...; resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: OUT port 0x3ff size=1 value=0xa5; resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: RDMSR 0x20f (IA32_MTRR_PHYSMASK7) -> 0x00003fffffe00800, from the guest's MTRRs; resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: WRMSR 0x20f (IA32_MTRR_PHYSMASK7) <- 0x0000000000000000, into the guest's MTRRs; the CPU's IA32_MTRR_PHYSMASK7 stays 0x0000000000000000.
VM exit #N: exit statistics: exits=... cpuid_exits=2 msr_read_exits=2 msr_write_exits=2 mtrr_read_exits=3 mtrr_write_exits=7 ...
```

An MTRR write that changes types adds the guest's MTRRs and the EPT
regions that changed ([MTRR.md](MTRR.md) section 7.6).

The last line comes with the stop report after the final VMCALL. The EPT
violation, which was exit #1 before this step, is now exit #10.

### What bring-up checks

The MSR and the port are real, so `bring_up` reads them before and after the
guest (`PassthroughState`, both the IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE value and the COM1
scratch byte) and prints whether they match:

```text
Passthrough state before the guest PassthroughState { kernel_gs_base: <hex>, com1_scratch: <hex> }, after it PassthroughState { ... }: restored=true.
```

`restored=true` shows the guest put both back; `restored=false` means its
check failed after a write.

The MTRRs are the opposite case: the guest must never reach the CPU's. So
bring-up reads them before and after the guest too, and stops with
`MtrrsChanged` if they differ:

```text
MTRRs after the guest: the CPU's unchanged=true; the guest's copy restored=true.
```

## 7. On Hyper-V

The first Hyper-V run of this work had the bitmaps on and the guest
unchanged. It printed `VMX primary: required=0x240065f2 allowed=0xf7f9fffe`
(bits 25 and 28 are allowed, and neither is required, so Aleph0 has to set
them), wrote and read back the three bitmap addresses, and showed the old
three exits and `SUCCESS`: turning the bitmaps on changed nothing for that
guest, which runs no MSR or port instruction.

Plain run (`.\scripts\run-hyperv.ps1`), twelve exits. This is an excerpt of
`run\serial.log`. The `[Aleph0 Virtualization Hypervisor]` prefix is
removed, and of the five lines each exit prints only the reason line and the
result line are kept.

Bring-up, before the guest:

```text
Exit bitmaps allocated: MSR=0x000000007eaf2000 I/O A=0x000000007eaf1000 I/O B=0x000000007eaf0000.
Intercepted MSRs (read and write): [c0000102]; intercepted ports: [3ff].
VMCS MSR and I/O bitmap addresses written and read back.
```

The nine emulated exits:

```text
VM exit #1: reason=10 (CPUID)
VM exit #1: CPUID leaf=0x1 subleaf=0x0 -> eax=0x00090672 ebx=0x00020800 ecx=0xf7fa3203 edx=0x1f8bfbff (processor ecx=0xf7fa3223); resuming at rip=0x000000007eaf5009.
VM exit #2: reason=31 (RDMSR)
VM exit #2: RDMSR 0xc0000102 -> 0x0000000000000000; resuming at rip=0x000000007eaf501a.
VM exit #3: reason=32 (WRMSR)
VM exit #3: WRMSR 0xc0000102 <- 0x00007a1e00000000; resuming at rip=0x000000007eaf502a.
VM exit #4: reason=31 (RDMSR)
VM exit #4: RDMSR 0xc0000102 -> 0x00007a1e00000000; resuming at rip=0x000000007eaf5030.
VM exit #5: reason=32 (WRMSR)

VM exit #6: reason=30 (I/O instruction)

VM exit #7: reason=30 (I/O instruction)
VM exit #7: OUT port 0x3ff size=1 value=0xa5; resuming at rip=0x000000007eaf504e.

VM exit #9: OUT port 0x3ff size=1 value=0x0; resuming at rip=0x000000007eaf5059.
```

- Exit #1: the processor returned `ecx=0xf7fa3223` and the guest got
  `0xf7fa3203`. They differ by `0x20`, bit 5, the VMX bit, which the
  nested Hyper-V shows to Aleph0 and the policy hides from the guest. The
  policy changes nothing else. The guest value still has bit 31 set
  (hypervisor present), one of the open decisions of section 3.
- Exits #2 to #5: IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE was `0x0`. The guest wrote
  `0x00007a1e00000000` (exit #3 shows it split as RDX = `0x7a1e`,
  RAX = `0x0`), read the same value back, and wrote `0x0` again.
- Exits #6 to #9: the exit qualification is `0x03ff0008` for the two INs and
  `0x03ff0000` for the two OUTs: port `0x3ff`, size 1, direction in bit 3.
  The scratch byte was `0x0`; `0xa5` written by exit #7 was read back by
  exit #8. So the scratch register of Hyper-V's UART works, and its absence
  (a read-back other than `0xa5`, which would stop the guest at `ud2` with
  `0xFA11` in EAX, section 6) did not happen. Exit #9 put `0x0` back.
- Each RIP in `resuming at` is the exit's RIP plus its instruction length
  (2 for `cpuid`, `rdmsr` and `wrmsr`, 1 for `in` and `out`), as in
  section 2.

The EPT write, the VMCALLs and the end of the run:

```text

- Exit #10 is the EPT violation that was exit #1 in `docs/EPT.md`, with the

  allocations moved.
- Exits #11 and #12 are the main VMCALL #1 and #2.
- `emulated exits: cpuid=1 rdmsr=2 wrmsr=2 in=2 out=2.` is
  `EXPECTED_EMULATION`. Aleph0's own count agrees with the guest's checks,
  so each of the nine instructions did cause an exit (section 6).
- `restored=true`: before and after the guest, IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE and the
  COM1 scratch byte are both `0`. The guest wrote other values in between
  (exits #3 and #7), so it put both back (exits #5 and #9).

flow of `docs/NMI.md`, with the emulated exits before it unchanged:
