The NMI is not an emulated exit, so the counts stay at 1, 2, 2, 2, 2.

> These runs predate the exit statistics. Since then the stop report
> prints `exit statistics: ...` in place of `emulated exits: ...`, and
> bring-up, not the last VMCALL, checks the counts.

## 8. Limits before an OS guest

- **The CPUID decisions of section 3**: OSXSAVE with leaf 0xD. The
  hypervisor-present bit and the leaves from 0x40000000 pass through, with
  Hyper-V's interface forwarded (#27).
- **Unconditional exits.** XSETBV (reason 55), INVD (13), GETSEC (11), the
  VMX instructions and task switches always exit. Aleph0 handles none of
  them (except the test guest's VMCALLs, in `scenario.rs`); they reach the
  `_` arm and stop the guest. An OS runs XSETBV early.
- **String and REP I/O** stop the guest (section 5).
- **Only one MSR, the MTRRs and one port are intercepted.** Every other
  MSR inside the bitmap's ranges and every other port reaches the hardware
  without Aleph0 seeing it (MSRs outside the ranges get a #GP, section 4). The
  multi-port rule (section 5) also lets a wide access that touches `0x3FF`
  reach its neighbours, COM1's other registers, which are the guest's.
- **The #GP and #UD paths are tested on the host only.** They are
  delivered through the guest's own IDT, which in the test guest has only
  vector 2, so they would find no gate. The test guest never triggers them.
  The decisions (`GuestGeneralProtection`, `GuestInvalidOpcode`) and the
  encodings (`0x80000B0D`, `0x80000306`) are host tests; delivery needs a
  guest with an IDT of its own (section 9).
- **MSRs held in the VMCS cannot be intercepted.** They would need an
  emulation path that reads and writes the VMCS guest-state field
  (VMREAD/VMWRITE) instead of using RDMSR/WRMSR. `VMCS_HELD_MSRS` lists ten;
  newer CPUs have more fields (IA32_RTIT_CTL, IA32_S_CET and IA32_PKRS, for
  example), which belong on the list before Aleph0 intercepts them.

## 9. Idle and exceptions: HLT, MWAIT, MONITOR and the exception bitmap

Two VMCS settings would stop a real guest at its first idle and its first
fault (issue #19).

**HLT, MWAIT and MONITOR always exit under Hyper-V.** The primary-control
capability Hyper-V reports, `required=0x240065f2`, has bits 7 (HLT exiting),
10 (MWAIT exiting) and 29 (MONITOR exiting) among its must-be-1 bits, so
`ControlCapability::choose` sets them whatever Aleph0 asks for. Aleph0 also
requests bit 7 itself, so a guest HLT exits on any CPU.

| Exit | Reason | Decision | Resume |
|---|---|---|---|
| HLT | 12 | `Halted`, counted in `halt_exits` | past the instruction |
| MWAIT | 36 | `GuestInvalidOpcode` | inject #UD (`0x80000306`), RIP unchanged |
| MONITOR | 39 | `GuestInvalidOpcode` | inject #UD, RIP unchanged |

HLT is resumed at once rather than parked in the HLT activity state: a
halted vCPU waits for an interrupt, and the guest gets its interrupts when it
next runs anyway. The cost is one exit per round of an idle loop. The HLT
activity state would avoid it, but needs `IA32_VMX_MISC` bit 6 and a rule
for NMI exits taken in that state.

MWAIT and MONITOR get #UD, as on a CPU without them: Hyper-V reports
CPUID.1:ECX bit 3 (MONITOR/MWAIT) clear (`0xf7fa3223`), and `cpuid_policy`
passes that through, so a guest that checks CPUID never runs them.

**Ending the interrupt shadow.** STI and MOV SS block interrupts until the
end of the next instruction (interruptibility bits 0 and 1). An idle loop
runs `sti; hlt`, so the HLT exit reports blocking by STI. The CPU never
completes that HLT, so it never ends the shadow; Aleph0 must. Whenever it
moves RIP past an instruction, the handler clears both bits
(`after_skipped_instruction`), as KVM does when it skips an instruction. It
writes `GUEST_INTERRUPTIBILITY_STATE` only when one of them was set, so exits
outside a shadow cost no extra VMWRITE.

**The exception bitmap depends on the guest** (`vmcs::exception_bitmap`):

| `GuestKind` | Bitmap | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `BuiltInTest` | all ones | its IDT has only the NMI gate; its `ud2` paths rely on the #UD exit |
| `Firmware` | 0 | the firmware takes its own faults, as an OS will (Linux builds its early page tables from #PF) |

With a bitmap of 0, NMIs still exit (the NMI-exiting pin control, not the
bitmap), and a fault the guest cannot handle ends in a triple fault (reason
2), which stops it. Bring-up selects `GuestKind::SELECTED`: `Firmware` by
default, `BuiltInTest` with the `test-guest` Cargo feature (#21, see
[FIRMWARE_GUEST.md](FIRMWARE_GUEST.md)).

**The test.** The test guest runs one `hlt` after its I/O checks, with
IF = 0, so no interrupt could end the halt; only Aleph0 moving RIP past it
lets the guest go on. The HLT is exit #10, so the EPT violation becomes exit
#11 and the run has 13 exits (15 with `-InjectNmi`), whose statistics
include `halt_exits=1`. The HLT line,
`HLT; going on at rip=...`, deliberately avoids the text `resuming the
guest`, which arms the `-InjectNmi` job after main VMCALL #1.

## Cheat sheet

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Primary control bit 28 | use MSR bitmaps |
| Primary control bit 25 | use I/O bitmaps (bit 24 is then ignored) |
| `MSR_BITMAP` | `0x2004` |
| `IO_BITMAP_A` / `IO_BITMAP_B` | `0x2000` / `0x2002` |
| Exit reason 10 / 31 / 32 / 30 | CPUID / RDMSR / WRMSR / I/O instruction |
| MSR bitmap quarters | `0x000` read low, `0x400` read high, `0x800` write low, `0xC00` write high |
| I/O bit of port *p* | bit `p % 8` of byte `(p & 0x7FFF) / 8`, page A below `0x8000` |
| Intercepted | `IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE` (`0xC0000102`), every MTRR address (a copy of the MSRs the CPU has, #GP for the others; never passed through), port `0x3FF` |
| I/O qualification | 2:0 size − 1, 3 IN, 4 string, 5 REP, 6 immediate, 31:16 port |
| CPUID policy | CPUID.1:ECX bit 5 (VMX) cleared |
| Injected #GP | `0x80000B0D`, error code 0, RIP unchanged |
| Injected #UD (MWAIT, MONITOR) | `0x80000306`, no error code, RIP unchanged |
| Exit reason 12 / 36 / 39 | HLT / MWAIT / MONITOR |
| Exception bitmap | all ones for the test guest, 0 for the firmware |
| `GUEST_MSR_VALUE` / `GUEST_IO_VALUE` | `0x0000_7A1E_0000_0000` / `0xA5` |
| `GUEST_EMULATION_FAIL_MARKER` | `0xFA11` in EAX at the `ud2` |
| `guest::expected_stats` | cpuid 2, MSR reads 2, MSR writes 2, MTRR reads 3, MTRR writes 7, in 2, out 2, halt 1, exceptions 0 |

```

`docs/EPT.md`:

```md
# EPT: a second translation that Aleph0 controls

How Aleph0 turns on Extended Page Tables (EPT), and what that changes:
- why the guest needs a translation stage it cannot touch;
- the EPT entries and the EPT pointer;
- how Aleph0 checks support and builds an identity map of the whole
  guest-physical address space, with the memory types of the MTRRs for RAM
  and UC 1 GiB pages above it;
- the Local APIC, the device page the test guest reads through it;
- the guest's read-only data page and the EPT violation it causes on purpose;
- how Aleph0 handles that violation (grant write, INVEPT, retry), and how
  it stops on any other EPT exit with a walk of the GPA through the tables;
- what the Hyper-V runs printed;
- what the identity map does *not* hide, and what is not covered yet.

Code:
- `src/vmx/ept/mod.rs`: support check, entry encodings, the map's layout (`MapLayout`), identity map, `ProtectedPage::grant_write`, INVEPT;
- `src/vmx/ept/walk.rs`: what the CPU refuses in an entry (`check_entry`), and the walk of a GPA (`walk`);
- `src/vmx/apic.rs`: IA32_APIC_BASE, and the check that the test guest can read the Local APIC;
- `src/vmx/mtrr/mod.rs`: the memory type of each address, from the MTRRs (see [MTRR.md](MTRR.md));
- `src/vmx/guest.rs`: the data page and the guest code that writes it;
- `src/vmx/exit_decision/`: which EPT violation is accepted (`scenario.rs`, reached from `decide` in `mod.rs`);
- `src/vmx/vmexit/`: the handler that reports and applies it;
- `src/vmx/vmcs/mod.rs` and `fields.rs`: secondary controls, `EPT_POINTER`;
- `src/bring_up/mod.rs`: where EPT is checked, built and enabled.

## 1. Why EPT

Before this step the guest used the host's page tables (guest CR3 = host
CR3), and nothing came after them. A guest-physical address *was* a
host-physical address. Aleph0 could not protect or hide any memory from the
guest: whatever the page tables mapped, the guest could reach, and the
guest can edit its own page tables.

With EPT on, every guest memory access is translated twice:

```text
guest linear ──(guest page tables, guest CR3)──▶ guest-physical (GPA)
GPA          ──(EPT tables, built by Aleph0)───▶ host-physical  (HPA)
```

The guest owns the first stage and may change it as it likes. The second
stage lives in memory Aleph0 chooses, and the CPU walks it on **every**
guest access, including the CPU's own reads of the guest's page tables
(those tables sit at GPAs too). If an EPT entry does not allow the access,
the CPU does not perform it: it exits to Aleph0 with **exit reason 48, EPT
violation**.

This is the basis for everything later:
- an OS guest gets memory isolated from Aleph0;
- Aleph0 can hide its own pages from the guest;
- for anti-cheat (ROADMAP section 6), it can make a game's pages read-only
  or execute-only and see every write to them.

## 2. EPT entries and the EPT pointer

EPT tables have the same shape as ordinary 4-level page tables: PML4, PDPT,
PD, PT; one 4 KiB table holds 512 entries of 8 bytes, and each level takes
9 bits of the address (`docs/PAGE_TABLE_WALK.md` explains the walk). The
entry bits differ:

```text
 63    52 51               12 11   8  7   6  5   3  2  1  0
┌────────┬───────────────────┬──────┬───┬────┬─────┬──┬──┬──┐
│ ignored│ address of next   │ ign. │ PS│IPAT│ type│ X│ W│ R│
│        │ table or the page │      │   │    │(leaf)  │  │  │
└────────┴───────────────────┴──────┴───┴────┴─────┴──┴──┴──┘
```

| Bits | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0, 1, 2 | **R, W, X**: read, write, execute allowed. No separate "present" bit: R = W = X = 0 means not present. |
| 5:3 | memory type, in leaf entries only: 0 = UC, 6 = write-back (WB), the type of ordinary RAM; Aleph0 copies it from the MTRRs ([MTRR.md](MTRR.md)) |
| 6 | IPAT: ignore the guest's PAT. Aleph0 leaves it 0. |
| 7 | in a PDPT or PD entry: this entry maps a 1 GiB or 2 MiB page directly (no table below) |
| 51:12 | physical address of the next table, or of the page |

Some combinations are not just "forbidden" but invalid, for example W = 1
with R = 0. The CPU reports those as **exit reason 49, EPT
misconfiguration**. Aleph0 makes no such entry, so one stops the guest with
a walk of the GPA that names the bad entry (section 6).

The encodings Aleph0 uses (`ept/mod.rs`, all host-tested). `EptEntry<L>` is
generic over its table level (`Pml4`, `Pdpt`, `Pd`, `Pt` in `ept::level`),
so each constructor exists only where the entry is valid: calling
`large_page` on a PT entry, or `table` on one, does not compile.

| Function | Levels | Value | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EptEntry::table(addr)` | PML4, PDPT, PD | `addr \| 0b111` | `0x7e00_1007` |
| `EptEntry::large_page(addr, type)` | PD | `addr \| RWX \| type << 3 \| 1 << 7` | `0x4020_00B7` (WB) |
| `EptEntry::page(addr, R, type)` | PT | `addr \| R \| type << 3` | `0x7eb1_d031` (read-only, WB) |
| `Eptp::new(pml4)` | — | `pml4 \| 6 \| 3 << 3` | low bits always `0x1E` |

The **EPT pointer** (EPTP, VMCS field `0x201A`) tells the CPU where the
PML4 is:

```text
EPTP = PML4 address | bit 6: accessed/dirty flags (0) | bits 5:3: walk length - 1 (3 = 4 levels) | bits 2:0: memory type of the tables (6 = WB)
```

EPT is switched on by **secondary control bit 1** ("enable EPT"). The
secondary controls are a fourth control field (`0x401E`), read by the CPU
only while **primary control bit 31** ("activate secondary controls") is
set. `configure_controls` sets both when `DesiredControls::secondary` asks
for anything.

## 3. Checking support

Two MSRs answer whether EPT is usable, and each exists only if the one
before says so (reading a missing MSR raises #GP):

```text
IA32_VMX_PROCBASED_CTLS (primary) allows bit 31
  └─▶ IA32_VMX_PROCBASED_CTLS2 (0x48B, secondary) allows bit 1 (EPT) or bit 5 (VPID)
        └─▶ IA32_VMX_EPT_VPID_CAP (0x48C)
```

`ept::check_support` requires these bits of `IA32_VMX_EPT_VPID_CAP`:

| Bit | Meaning | Why Aleph0 needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 4-level page walk | the EPTP Aleph0 writes |
| 14 | WB for the EPT tables | the EPTP's memory type |
| 16 | 2 MiB pages | the identity map uses them |
| 20 | INVEPT | `ProtectedPage::grant_write` |
| 25 or 26 | single- or all-context INVEPT | single-context is preferred |

It also reads two bits it does not require, into `EntryRules` with
MAXPHYADDR:

| Bit | Meaning | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | execute-only pages | whether X = 1 with R = W = 0 is a misconfiguration (section 6) |
| 17 | 1 GiB pages | the map above RAM (section 4) |

Hyper-V (nested) reported:

```text
VMX secondary: required=0x00000000 allowed=0x065018ae; EPT/VPID capabilities=0x00000f0106f34041
EPT supported: 4-level walk, WB, 2 MiB pages, INVEPT single-context.
```

Decoded, `0x06f34041` (low half) has bits 0, 6, 14, 16, 17, 20, 21, 22, 23,
25 and 26 set. Beyond what Aleph0 requires, that means:
- execute-only pages (bit 0), which EPT split views need later;
- 1 GiB pages (bit 17), which the map above RAM uses;
- accessed/dirty flags (bit 21);
- advanced EPT-violation information (bit 22, see section 6).

The high half, `0x00000f01`, is about INVVPID, unused so far.

## 4. The identity map

Aleph0 builds an **identity map**: GPA = HPA everywhere. The guest then
runs exactly as before, because every address it used still reaches the
same memory. Only the permissions can now differ.

The map covers the whole guest-physical address space:
`[0, 2^min(MAXPHYADDR, 48))` (`address_space_end`). MAXPHYADDR is
CPUID.80000008H:EAX[7:0] (`cpuid::physical_address_bits`), and a 4-level
walk translates 48 bits whatever MAXPHYADDR says. Device memory can be
anywhere in that space: the Local APIC at `0xFEE00000`, the IOAPIC, PCI
BARs, the VMBus windows Hyper-V puts above RAM. A GPA without an entry
would stop the guest at its first access to it (section 6).

`MapLayout` lays the map out GiB by GiB:

```text
0 ── PDs (2 MiB and 4 KiB pages) ── pd_end ── 1 GiB pages, UC ── end
     the GiBs the UEFI memory map        no RAM above the memory map
     reaches: RAM, retyped when the
     guest writes its MTRRs
```

- The GiBs the UEFI memory map reaches keep a PD each, even a GiB of one
  type, so the guest's MTRR writes can retype its RAM 2 MiB or 4 KiB at a
  time (section 7, [MTRR.md](MTRR.md) section 7) without splitting a 1 GiB
  page.
- Above them there is no RAM, so every GiB is UC whatever the MTRRs say
  (`EptTypes`, [MTRR.md](MTRR.md) section 5), and is never retyped: one UC
  1 GiB page each, in a PDPT entry.
- One PDPT per 512 GiB, each in its own PML4 entry: 128 for a 46-bit space.
- Without 1 GiB pages (capability bit 17 clear), a PD per GiB of a 46-bit
  space would take 256 MiB of tables, so the PDs stop at
  `max(memory map end, 4 GiB)` instead. The 32-bit device window, with the
  Local APIC and the IOAPIC, is still mapped; an access above it stops the
  guest with the walk of section 6.

`Ept::build` (before VMXON, while boot services run):

1. Reads the UEFI memory map and takes the highest address any region
   reaches, rounded up to 1 GiB (`memory_map_end`). Every region counts,
   whatever its type. `MapLayout::new` refuses a memory map that reaches
   past the address space.
2. Gathers the memory map's RAM into sorted, merged ranges (`RamMap`):
   RAM takes the MTRRs' memory type, and everything else (MMIO, reserved
   memory, holes) is UC (`EptTypes`, [MTRR.md](MTRR.md) section 5).
   Counts the 2 MiB regions that need a PT (`split_regions`): those whose
   pages differ in memory type or are only partly RAM, and the one holding
   the guest's data page.
3. Allocates one PML4, the PDPTs, one PD per GiB below `pd_end`, and those
   PTs, plus spare PTs for regions the guest's MTRR writes split later
   (`spare_pts`), and a stack of the free PTs' indices.
4. Points PML4 entry *k* at PDPT *k*, and PDPT entry *g* at PD *g* below
   `pd_end`; above it, PDPT entry *g* is a UC 1 GiB page.
5. Fills every PD entry with a 2 MiB page, RWX, of the region's memory
   type, except for the regions counted in step 2. Their PD entry points to
   the next PT, which maps the region in 512 pages of 4 KiB, all RWX and
   each of its own memory type, **except the data page, which gets R only**.

2 MiB pages keep the tables small. Only the regions that need a 4 KiB
exception pay for a PT.

Aleph0's own page tables (HOST_CR3) map only up to the memory map's end
(`Ept::memory_map_end`, [HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md](HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md)): root
operation needs Aleph0's memory and the EPT tables, never device memory.

`Ept::build` also returns the `TypeTables` the exit handler keeps: the PDs,
the PTs with the spare ones, and the free stack. When the guest writes its
MTRRs, `TypeTables::apply` rewrites the entries whose memory type changed,
takes a spare PT for a region whose pages come to differ in type, gives the
PT of a region of one type again back, and runs INVEPT (section 7,
[MTRR.md](MTRR.md) section 7).

On Hyper-V (2 GiB of RAM), before the memory types came from the MTRRs
(every page was WB, and the data page's region had the only PT):

```text
EPT built: identity 0x0..0x80000000 (2 GiB) with 2 MiB pages, 5 table pages; data page 0x000000007eb01000 read-only (R=1 W=0 X=0).
VMCS EPT pointer 0x000000007eafc01e (WB, 4-level) written and read back.
```

The 5 pages are the PML4, the PDPT, 2 PDs and the PT. For the data page
`0x7eb01000`:

```text
PDPT index = bits 38:30 = 1       (second GiB)
PD index   = bits 29:21 = 0x1F5   (PD entry 1 * 512 + 0x1F5 = 0x3F5 across both PDs: the split)
PT index   = bits 20:12 = 0x101   (the read-only entry)
```

### The Local APIC

The Local APIC is the device every OS, and the firmware once it is the
guest (#21), touches first. In xAPIC mode its registers are a 4 KiB page of
MMIO at IA32_APIC_BASE (MSR `0x1B`), `0xFEE00000` unless the firmware moved
it: above RAM on the test VM, so in a UC 1 GiB page. `vmx/apic.rs` decodes
the MSR: the page's address (bits MAXPHYADDR-1:12), the BSP flag, and the
mode from bits 11:10, named as KVM's `enum lapic_mode` names them
(disabled, xAPIC, x2APIC, invalid).

Before VMXON, bring-up checks that the test guest can read the page
(`check_local_apic`). Only xAPIC mode (EN = 1, EXTD = 0) has one: in x2APIC
mode the registers are MSRs and the page decodes nothing, so in any other
mode bring-up prints that the guest skips its read, and the guest jumps
past it. In xAPIC mode bring-up stops with `LocalApic` unless:
- the page tables the guest shares with bring-up (the firmware's) map the
  page to itself, since the guest reads it through that linear address;
- the walk of the page through EPT (section 6) maps it to itself, UC and
  readable.

The test guest then reads it, after its MTRR writes and before its `hlt`:

```text
mov ecx, 0x1b                ; IA32_APIC_BASE, which the MSR bitmap passes through
rdmsr
mov ecx, eax
and ecx, 0xc00               ; EN and EXTD
cmp ecx, 0x800               ; xAPIC mode, or straight to the hlt
...
and rax, r10                 ; bits below MAXPHYADDR (R10, from the MTRR part)
and rax, -0x1000             ; the register page
mov eax, [rax + 0x30]        ; the version register: no exit
cmp al, 0x10 / cmp al, 0x15  ; an integrated APIC, or ud2 (0xFF: nothing answered)
hlt                          ; the HLT exit shows the register in RAX
```

The read adds no exit: with the page mapped RWX, it never leaves the
guest. A missing entry would be an EPT violation, and the walk would show
which level lacks it.

## 5. The guest's data page

The guest gets one more page: the **data page**, allocated together with
the code page as two contiguous `RUNTIME_SERVICES_CODE` pages (`LOADER_CODE`
until #23, [RESIDENT.md](RESIDENT.md) section 2). Contiguity lets the
copied guest code find it RIP-relative, without being told an address.
Aleph0 writes a seed, `0xDA7A`, at its start before launch.

New guest code, before main VMCALL #1 (offsets in the code page):

```text
+0   xor ebx, ebx
+2   lea rdi, [rip + guest_code_start]   ; start of the code page
+9   add rdi, 0x1000                     ; data page (its GPA, under identity)
+16  mov ecx, [rdi]                      ; read: R=1, allowed -> ecx = 0xda7a
+18  mov dword ptr [rdi], 0x455054       ; write: W=0 -> EPT violation
+24  mov edx, [rdi]                      ; read back -> edx = 0x455054 ("EPT")
+26  mov eax, 0xa1e0
+31  vmcall                              ; main VMCALL #1
     ... the NMI wait loop, VMCALL #2 and the NMI handler, unchanged ...
```

At main VMCALL #1 the registers prove each part: RCX shows the allowed
read went through EPT, RDX shows the retried write landed, and the EPT exit
before it shows the protection caught the write.

`check_mappings` also requires the data page to be **writable in the
guest's page tables**. Otherwise the write would fault in the first
translation stage (#PF, an exception exit) and never reach EPT, and the
test would prove nothing.

## 6. The EPT violation

When the guest writes the data page, the CPU stops before the write and
exits. Three VMCS fields describe the violation:

| Field | Encoding | Hyper-V value |
|---|---|---|
| `GUEST_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS` | `0x2400` | `0x7eb01000`: the data page |
| `GUEST_LINEAR_ADDRESS` | `0x640A` | `0x7eb01000`: the same, under identity |
| `EXIT_QUALIFICATION` | `0x6400` | `0x58a` |

The exit qualification, bit by bit:

```text
0x58a = 0101 1000 1010
bit 0  = 0  not a read
bit 1  = 1  a write
bit 2  = 0  not an instruction fetch
bit 3  = 1  the EPT entries allow reads    ─┐
bit 4  = 0  ... but not writes              ├─ R=1 W=0 X=0, as built
bit 5  = 0  ... nor execution              ─┘
bit 7  = 1  GUEST_LINEAR_ADDRESS is valid
bit 8  = 1  the access was to the address the guest used, not to its page tables
bit 9  = 0  a supervisor-mode address            ─┐ advanced information
bit 10 = 1  the guest's page tables allow writes  ├─ (cap bit 22)
bit 11 = 0  ... and execution                    ─┘
bit 12 = 0  not during an IRET that ended NMI blocking
```

Bit 10 confirms directly what `check_mappings` checked: as far as the
guest's own page tables go the page is writable, so EPT alone refused the
write.

`exit_decision::decide` (through `scenario::ept_violation`) accepts exactly
one EPT violation, and only if all
of these hold:
- the GPA's page is the protected page;
- bits 1, 3, 7 and 8 are set and bit 4 is clear: a write to a readable,
  non-writable page, through the guest's own address;
- bit 12 is clear (after such an IRET, resuming would need NMI blocking set
  again by hand, which Aleph0 does not do);
- no write was granted yet (a second violation would mean the grant did not
  work).

Any other EPT violation stops the guest as `EptViolation`, with a walk of
the GPA (below). And if main VMCALL #1 arrives **before** any violation, the
guest's write went through unnoticed: EPT did not protect the page, and the
guest stops with a message saying so (`EptWriteMissing`).

### Grant and retry

For the accepted violation, the handler:
1. sets W = 1 in the data page's PT entry (`ept::ProtectedPage::grant_write`);
2. runs INVEPT (section 7);
3. resumes **without advancing RIP**.

The guest then runs the same `mov dword ptr [rdi], 0x455054` again, and
this time the write is allowed.

Not advancing RIP is the only option anyway: for an EPT violation the CPU
does not report the instruction's length (`instruction length=0` in the
log), because the instruction did not complete. Skipping a write would
require decoding it.

### Any other EPT exit: the walk

The map allows every access to every GPA it covers, but one write. So any
other EPT violation, and every EPT misconfiguration (exit reason 49: an
entry the CPU refuses to use at all), means the map is wrong, not that an
access needs emulating. Each stops the guest as its own event,
`ExitEvent::EptViolation` or `ExitEvent::EptMisconfig`, and the report
prints the GPA's walk through the tables, the way KVM prints the hierarchy
of an EPT entry with reserved bits set (`get_mmio_spte`). Unlike KVM, which
misconfigures entries on purpose for MMIO and emulates those accesses in
`handle_ept_misconfig`, Aleph0 passes devices through, so it makes no
misconfigured entry.

`ept::walk` (`ept/walk.rs`) follows a GPA from the EPTP down, one entry
per level, as the CPU does, until an entry maps a page, is not present, or
is one the CPU refuses. It returns every entry it read, with what the CPU
refuses in it, and how the walk ended: mapped (with the HPA, page size,
access and memory type), not present, misconfigured, a pointer outside
the tables, or a GPA above the 48 bits a 4-level walk translates, which
it does not walk: its levels would index it like the GPA 2^48 below. It reads entries through a function its caller gives it.
`TypeTables::walk`, which the exit handler uses, gives it one that reads
only the table pages `Ept::build` allocated, so a corrupt pointer is
reported, never followed into memory that is not EPT. The walk starts from
the EPTP the VMCS holds.

`check_entry` names what the CPU refuses in an entry (Intel SDM Vol. 3C,
"EPT Misconfigurations"), as KVM's `is_rsvd_spte` does with the masks
`__reset_rsvds_bits_mask_ep` builds:

| Entry | Bits reserved (must be 0) |
|---|---|
| any | 51:MAXPHYADDR |
| PML4 | 7:3: no memory type, IPAT or page size |
| PDPT or PD pointing to a table | 6:3: no memory type or IPAT |
| PDPT mapping a 1 GiB page | 29:12, below the page's alignment; and 7 itself on a CPU without 1 GiB pages |
| PD mapping a 2 MiB page | 20:12 |
| PT | nothing more |

Besides reserved bits: bits 2:0 must not allow writes without reads (010b,
110b), nor execution alone (100b) on a CPU without execute-only pages; and
a page's memory type must not be 2, 3 or 7. An entry with bits 2:0 = 000b
is not present: a walk reaching it is an EPT violation, never a
misconfiguration.

The test-only `ept-misconfig-test` Cargo feature (`run-hyperv.ps1
-Features ept-misconfig-test`) plants one on purpose: before VMLAUNCH,
bring-up clears R in the PDPT entry of the Local APIC's GiB
(`TypeTables::misconfigure`), so the guest's read of the version register
is an EPT misconfiguration. On Hyper-V the CPU refused the same entry the
walk names:

```text
ept-misconfig-test: the PDPT entry of GiB 0x3 is now W without R.
...
VM exit #21: reason=49 (EPT misconfiguration)
VM exit #21: EPT misconfiguration at GPA 0x00000000fee00030: an EPT entry for it is invalid.
VM exit #21: guest rip=0x000000007eaa613f instruction length=2
VM exit #21: EPT walk of GPA 0x00000000fee00030 from EPTP 0x7eaa101e:
VM exit #21:   PML4 entry 0x0 at 0x7eaa1000 = 0x000000007ea21007: ok
VM exit #21:   PDPT entry 0x3 at 0x7ea21018 = 0x00000000c0000086: write without read
VM exit #21:   the CPU refuses the last entry: an EPT misconfiguration.
VM exit #21: stopping the guest; returning to bring-up.
...
Guest stopped at VM exit #21: reason=49 (EPT misconfiguration); Aleph0 did not resume the guest.
```

The walk ran in exit context, on Aleph0's own page tables, from the EPTP
the VMCS holds. The entry is the 1 GiB UC page at `0xc0000000`, RWX
(`0x87`) less R: `0x86`. The run then tears down as for any stop, and
returns `ABORTED`.

The host tests check each rule at each level, every entry `Ept::build`
makes, walks through hand-built tables and through the full Hyper-V map,
and the bounds-checked reader on real page-aligned tables, with a planted
pointer it must not follow.

## 7. INVEPT

The CPU caches EPT translations (TLB, paging-structure caches), tagged by
EPTP. After changing an EPT entry, the cached copy may still be used.
**INVEPT** drops them:

```text
invept type, [descriptor]       descriptor = { EPTP, 0 }  (128 bits)
type 1 = single-context: only translations from this EPTP
type 2 = all-context:    translations from every EPTP
```

Like other VMX instructions it reports failure through CF/ZF;
`ProtectedPage::grant_write` returns the failure (`VmxFail`) and the guest stops if it fails.

Strictly, this INVEPT is not needed: an EPT violation already drops the
cached translations for the address that caused it, so the retried write
would see W = 1 anyway. It is still the architectural way to publish an
EPT change, and changes not caused by a violation need it. The first such
change is a guest MTRR write: `TypeTables::apply` changes the memory types
of entries the CPU may have cached, then runs the same INVEPT.

## 8. The Hyper-V runs

> Since the emulated-exits step the guest first causes nine emulated exits
> (CPUID, four MSR, four I/O; see [EMULATED_EXITS.md](EMULATED_EXITS.md)), so
> in a current run these lines come with exit numbers nine higher. The guest
> RIPs and addresses differ too.

Plain run (`.\scripts\run-hyperv.ps1`), three exits:

```text
VM exit #1: reason=48 (EPT violation)
VM exit #1: qualification=0x000000000000058a
VM exit #1: EPT violation at GPA 0x000000007eb01000 (linear 0x000000007eb01000): write; page R=1 W=0 X=0.
VM exit #1: guest rip=0x000000007eb00012 instruction length=0
VM exit #1: guest rax=0x0000000000000000 rbx=0x0000000000000000 rcx=0x000000000000da7a rdx=0x0000000000000000
VM exit #1: write to the protected data page: write granted (W=1), INVEPT single-context; retrying the write at rip=0x000000007eb00012.
VM exit #2: reason=18 (VMCALL)
VM exit #2: guest rax=0x000000000000a1e0 rbx=0x0000000000000000 rcx=0x000000000000da7a rdx=0x0000000000455054
VM exit #3: expected VMCALL (rax=0xa1e1); all 2 planned VMCALLs handled; no NMI arrived.
VM exit #3: EPT: 1 write violation(s) on the protected data page, write granted.
```

- Exit #1, RIP `+0x12` (18): the write. RCX already holds `0xda7a`, so the
  read before it passed through EPT without an exit. RDX is still 0.
- The retry resumes at the same RIP.
- Exit #2, VMCALL #1 at `+0x1f` (31): RDX = `0x455054`, the retried write
  landed.
- Exit #3: VMCALL #2, the EPT summary, teardown, `SUCCESS`.

With `-InjectNmi`, five exits: the same EPT violation and VMCALL #1, then
the NMI flow from `docs/NMI.md`, unchanged under EPT:

```text
VM exit #3: reason=0 (exception or NMI)
VM exit #3: guest rip=0x000000007eb0002d ...
VM exit #3: NMI (interruption info=0x80000202); reinjecting it into the guest at rip=0x000000007eb0002d.
VM exit #4: guest NMI handler ran (rax=0x4e4d49); the reinjected NMI was delivered; resuming the guest at rip=0x000000007eb00041.
VM exit #5: expected VMCALL (rax=0xa1e1); all 2 planned VMCALLs handled; NMIs: 1 reinjected, 1 handled by the guest.
VM exit #5: EPT: 1 write violation(s) on the protected data page, write granted.
```

The NMI arrived at `+0x2d` (45, `dec ecx` in the wait loop, 24 bytes later
than before because of the new instructions). The CPU delivered it through
the guest IDT at `0x7eafe000` and ran the handler on the guest stack
`0x7eaff000`, both reached through EPT.

### The whole address space (#20)

```text
EPT supported: 4-level walk, WB, 2 MiB pages, INVEPT single-context; 1 GiB pages=true; MAXPHYADDR 46 bits.
EPT built: identity 0x0..0x400000000000 (65536 GiB), 142 table pages: 128 PDPT(s); 2 PD(s), for 0x0..0x80000000, with 2 PTs for 2 MiB regions mapped in 4 KiB pages and 9 spare PTs for the guest's MTRR writes; 65534 GiB above as 1 GiB pages; data page 0x000000007eaa7000 read-only (R=1 W=0 X=0).
EPT 0x000000000000..0x000000200000: 4 KiB pages (a PT each)
EPT 0x000000200000..0x00007ea00000: 2 MiB pages, WB
EPT 0x00007ea00000..0x00007ec00000: 4 KiB pages (a PT each)
EPT 0x00007ec00000..0x000080000000: 2 MiB pages, WB
EPT 0x000080000000..0x400000000000: 1 GiB pages, UC
Local APIC: IA32_APIC_BASE=0xfee00900 (xAPIC, BSP); its registers at 0xfee00000 are mapped to HPA 0xfee00000 by a 1 GiB page, UC, R=1 W=1 X=1; the test guest reads the version register at 0xfee00030.
Host page tables: identity 0x0..0x80000000 (2 GiB), 1 GiB pages, 2 table pages; HOST_CR3=0x7ea10000 (firmware CR3=0x4401000).
...
VM exit #21: reason=12 (HLT)
VM exit #21: guest rax=0x0000000000050014 rbx=0x0000000000000000 rcx=0x0000000000000800 rdx=0x0000000000000000
```

- The 142 table pages are the PML4, 128 PDPTs, 2 PDs and 11 PTs: the
  first 2 MiB's, the data page region's and the 9 spare ones.
- Host CR3 still maps only the memory map's 2 GiB.
- RAX at the HLT is the version register: version `0x14` (bits 7:0), and
  bits 23:16 = 5, so 6 LVT entries. RCX is `0x800`, the xAPIC mode bits
  the guest checked. Nested Hyper-V let the guest read the VM's own Local
  APIC through Aleph0's EPT, and the read added no exit: the run ended
  after 24 exits with `SUCCESS`, and the `-InjectNmi` run after 26, the
  same as before #20.
- No EPT stop came. `-Features ept-misconfig-test` shows the
  misconfiguration stop and its walk on real VMX (section 6); an
  `EptViolation` stop prints the same walk after its own line, and is
  host-tested only.

## 9. What the identity map does not hide

Identity means the guest sees **all** physical memory up to the map's end,
including Aleph0's own pages: its code and statics in the `.efi` image,
the VM-exit stack, the VMXON region and VMCS, the host GDT and TSS, **and
the EPT tables themselves**. In the run above the PML4 sits at
`0x7eafc000`, in the same 2 MiB region as the guest pages, mapped RWX by
the very PT Aleph0 built.

So a guest that wanted to could:
- scan memory and find Aleph0;
- rewrite the PT entry of the data page itself, making it writable without
  any exit;
- change the exit handler's code or stack, and run its own code in VMX root
  operation at the next exit.

The tiny guest here is Aleph0's own code, so this does not matter yet. For
an OS guest, and above all for anti-cheat, where the adversary has kernel
rights, Aleph0's pages must be removed from the guest's view (see
section 10).

## 10. What is not covered yet

- **Hiding Aleph0's own pages** (section 9). Each of them must become not
  present in EPT, with the access redirected or a #PF injected, or be
  mapped to a zero-filled shadow page. Aleph0 then has to track every page
  it allocates.
- **EPT split views** (ROADMAP section 6): one GPA mapped to one host page
  for execution (execute-only, cap bit 0, which Hyper-V has) and to another
  for reads.
- **1 GiB pages for RAM**: the GiBs the memory map reaches keep their PDs,
  so MTRR writes retype them 2 MiB or 4 KiB at a time. A GiB of RAM of one
  type mapped as one 1 GiB page would have to be split, with spare PDs, when
  an MTRR write gives part of it another type.
- **The guest's MAXPHYADDR**: CPUID passes it through. On a CPU that reports
  more than 48 bits, the guest could use GPAs a 4-level walk does not
  translate; KVM caps the guest's physical-address width for that (#25).
- **VPID**: tags TLB entries per guest so VM entries and exits need not
  flush them. A performance feature, independent of EPT.
- **INVEPT before VMXOFF**: the EPT pages are never freed, so cached
  translations of them cannot point at reused memory.
- **Hiding the tables**: since #23 the EPT tables are
  `RUNTIME_SERVICES_DATA`, which the OS keeps ([RESIDENT.md](RESIDENT.md)),
  but the identity map still shows them to the guest.

## Cheat sheet

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Primary control bit 31 | activate secondary controls |
| Secondary control bit 1 | enable EPT |
| `SECONDARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL` | `0x401E` |
| `EPT_POINTER` | `0x201A`; low bits `0x1E` = WB, 4 levels |
| `IA32_VMX_PROCBASED_CTLS2` | `0x48B` |
| `IA32_VMX_EPT_VPID_CAP` | `0x48C`; bits 6, 14, 16, 20, 25/26 required; 0 (execute-only) and 17 (1 GiB pages) read |
| EPT entry bits | 0 R, 1 W, 2 X, 5:3 type (from the MTRRs for RAM, UC for the rest; 0 = UC, 6 = WB), 6 IPAT, 7 1 GiB or 2 MiB page |
| The map | `[0, 2^min(MAXPHYADDR, 48))`: PDs up to the memory map's end, UC 1 GiB pages above |
| Exit reason 48 | EPT violation: `GUEST_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS` `0x2400`, `GUEST_LINEAR_ADDRESS` `0x640A`; any but the accepted one stops with the walk |
| Exit reason 49 | EPT misconfiguration: stops with the walk, which names the bad entry |
| IA32_APIC_BASE | `0x1B`; xAPIC registers at its bits MAXPHYADDR-1:12, the version register at `+0x30` |
| Qualification | 0 read, 1 write, 2 fetch, 3/4/5 R/W/X allowed, 7 linear valid, 8 translated access, 12 NMI-unblocking IRET |
| Accepted violation | write to the protected page, `0x58a` on Hyper-V |
| After it | W = 1, INVEPT, resume at the same RIP |
| `GUEST_DATA_SEED` / `GUEST_EPT_VALUE` | `0xDA7A` / `0x455054` ("EPT") |
| Hyper-V map (before the MTRR types) | `0x0..0x80000000`, 5 table pages, EPTP `0x7eafc01e` |

```

`docs/FIRMWARE_GUEST.md`:

```md
# The firmware as the guest: virtualizing in place

Until issue #21 Aleph0 ran a separate test guest, stopped it after its
scripted VMCALLs, left VMX and returned to the firmware, which then ran as
before, outside any VM. Now a default build makes the firmware itself the
guest: the code after Aleph0's own VMLAUNCH goes on in VMX non-root
operation, returns through `bring_up::run` and `main`, and the boot manager
or the UEFI shell that started Aleph0 keeps running virtualized. The test
guest stays, as a regression mode.

Code: `src/vmx/vmcs/launch.rs` (`launch_in_place`), `src/vmx/guest_state.rs`
(`GuestEntry`), `src/vmx/vmcs/mod.rs` (`GuestKind`, the exception bitmap),
`src/vmx/exit_decision/mod.rs` (`decide`), `src/vmx/vmexit/handler.rs` (the
stop), `src/bring_up/mod.rs` (`launch_guest`), `src/main.rs`.

## 1. The two paths

```text
test guest (`test-guest` feature):
  run ─▶ vmx_launch ─▶ VMLAUNCH ─▶ guest code page ─▶ ... ─▶ exit ─▶ handler ─▶ stop value
                ▲                                                                  │
                └──────────────── vmx_return_to_launcher ◀─────────────────────────┘
  run ─▶ teardown (VMXOFF) ─▶ main ─▶ firmware, outside VMX

firmware (default):
  run ─▶ launch_in_place ─▶ VMLAUNCH ─┐   root operation
  ════════════════════════════════════╪══════════════════════════════════════
                                      └▶ the next instruction ─▶ ret ─▶ run ─▶ main ─▶ firmware ─▶ ...
                                         non-root operation, until the next exit
  every exit ─▶ handler ─▶ VMRESUME, back to wherever the firmware was
  a stop     ─▶ handler ─▶ report ─▶ halt
```

`GuestKind::SELECTED` picks one at build time: `Firmware`, or `BuiltInTest`
with the `test-guest` Cargo feature. Everything that differs between the two
hangs off that one value:

| | `BuiltInTest` | `Firmware` |
|---|---|---|
| guest state (`GuestEntry`) | `At`: its code page, stack top, RFLAGS `0x2`, its IDT | `InPlace`: written at VMLAUNCH, the firmware's IDT |
| launch | `vmcs::launch`, returns at the stop | `vmcs::launch_in_place`, returns as the guest |
| exception bitmap | all ones | 0 |
| VMCALL | the script (`scenario::vmcall`) | Aleph0's own (`vmx::vmcall`, [RESIDENT.md](RESIDENT.md)) resume; any other is a Hyper-V hypercall, forwarded ([HYPERV_INTERFACE.md](HYPERV_INTERFACE.md)) |
| EPT violation | the protected-page write, once | stops, with the walk of the GPA |
| a stop | returns to bring-up, teardown, `SUCCESS` or `ABORTED` | halts after the report |

Everything else is the same for both: CPUID, RDMSR/WRMSR (MTRRs to the
guest's copy, Hyper-V's synthetic MSRs forwarded, #GP for any other MSR
outside the MSR bitmap), IN/OUT, HLT, #UD for MWAIT and MONITOR, NMI
reinjection, the EPT misconfiguration stop.

## 2. The guest state: the running context

The guest state is already a copy of the running CPU (`GuestState::from_current`):
CR0, CR3, CR4, the selectors, GDTR (Aleph0's GDT copy with its TSS, since
VM entry needs a busy TSS in TR and Hyper-V's firmware never loads one),
SYSENTER, PAT. For the firmware only four fields differ from the test
guest's:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| GUEST_RIP | the instruction after VMLAUNCH in `launch_in_place` |
| GUEST_RSP | RSP at VMLAUNCH |
| GUEST_RFLAGS | RFLAGS at VMLAUNCH, so IF is the firmware's (1) |
| GUEST_IDTR | the firmware's IDT, recorded when the GDT copy was activated |

RIP, RSP and RFLAGS only exist at VMLAUNCH, so `GuestEntry::InPlace` writes
placeholders (0, 0, `0x2`), bring-up prints that, and `launch_in_place`
writes the real ones in the same asm block as the VMLAUNCH:

```text
lea     rax, [rip + 2f]        ; RIP the guest starts at: label 2 below
vmwrite GUEST_RIP, rax
jbe     3f                     ; CF = 1 or ZF = 1: VMfailInvalid or VMfailValid
vmwrite GUEST_RSP, rsp         ; RSP right now: nothing below moves it
jbe     3f
pushfq
pop     rax
vmwrite GUEST_RFLAGS, rax      ; RFLAGS right now, IF included
jbe     3f
vmlaunch                       ; success never falls through
3:  pushfq                     ; failure: return its RFLAGS
    pop rax
    jmp 4f
2:  xor eax, eax               ; the guest starts here: return 0
4:
```

VM entry loads RIP, RSP and RFLAGS from the VMCS but leaves RAX to R15
alone, so at label 2 every register holds what it held at VMLAUNCH. To the
compiler the block is one instruction that returned 0 in RAX, with RSP
unchanged: the `ret`s that follow walk back up the same firmware stack, now
in non-root operation. `decode_in_place` turns the value into `Ok` (0) or
the failure (never 0: RFLAGS bit 1 always reads as 1).

An interrupt that arrives between the PUSHFQ and VMLAUNCH runs the
firmware's handler in root operation, on the stack below RSP, and is over
before VMLAUNCH. With IF = 1 and external-interrupt exiting off, the
firmware's own interrupts then go through its own IDT, with no VM exit.

## 3. A stop

The test guest's stop jumps back into the frame `vmx_launch` saved
(`VMX_LAUNCH_RSP`, [CLEAN_STOP.md](CLEAN_STOP.md)). `launch_in_place` saves
none: by the time the firmware stops, it has returned from that frame long
ago and reused the stack. So for the firmware (`GuestKind::stop_returns_to_bring_up`
is false) the handler prints the whole stop (the exit, the guest's state and
registers, the statistics, the exits by reason, the last exits), then halts
this CPU with `cli; hlt`. The line before the dump says so:

```text
VM exit #N: NOT an exit Aleph0 handles for the firmware.
VM exit #N: stopping the guest; halting: the firmware has nothing to return to.
```

A failed VMRESUME halts the same way. Teardown never runs for the firmware
once it has launched: CR4.VMXE stays set, the GDT stays Aleph0's copy, and
the CPU stays in VMX operation for good.

## 4. Output

The exit handler sets the `VmExit` output phase first, so nothing in exit
context reaches the firmware console. In place, the guest is Aleph0's own
code too until `main` returns, and it may print with `log!`; so the handler
puts back the phase it found when it resumes the guest, and the console
works again in non-root operation. `vmresume_failed` sets `VmExit` again
itself. After the launch `main` prints
`The firmware runs as the guest: Aleph0 returns to it in VMX non-root operation.`,
then waits on a firmware timer event, which shows that the timer interrupt
reaches the firmware's handler through its own IDT.

## 5. Running it

```powershell
.\scripts\run-hyperv.ps1 -ProcessorCount 1   # the firmware
.\scripts\run-hyperv.ps1 -TestGuest          # the regression mode
.\scripts\run-hyperv.ps1 -InjectNmi          # the regression mode, with an NMI
```

`-TestGuest` adds the `test-guest` feature, and so does `-InjectNmi`, whose
job waits for a line only the test guest's VMCALLs print. The
`host-nmi-test`, `unexpected-exit-test` and `ept-misconfig-test` features
turn it on themselves; `host-fault-test` and `trace-exits` work in both
modes.

On Hyper-V Gen 2, the keyboard, disk and video are VMBus devices: the
firmware's hypercalls are VMCALLs, which stopped it, and its reads and
writes of the synthetic MSRs (`0x40000000` and up) lie outside the MSR
bitmap, so they got a #GP. The first Hyper-V run showed which comes first:

```text
Launching the firmware in place with VMLAUNCH; its VM exits are reported on serial only.
VM exit #1: CPUID leaf=0x1 subleaf=0x1 -> ... resuming at rip=0x000000007ff1b167.
   (#2 to #6: CPUID leaves 0 and 1 at the same RIP)
VM exit #7: reason=31 (RDMSR)
VM exit #7: MSR 0x40000020 is outside the MSR bitmap, or the WRMSR value is not canonical; injecting #GP(0) at rip=0x000000007ff1d9c8.
VM exit #8: reason=2 (triple fault)
VM exit #8: guest rip=0x00000000047466e4 instruction length=0
VM exit #8: NOT an exit Aleph0 handles for the firmware.
VM exit #8: stopping the guest; halting: the firmware has nothing to return to.
VM exit #8: guest gdtr=0x000000007eaba000/0x004f idtr=0x0000000000000000/0x0000; ...
VM exit #8: exits by reason: 2 (triple fault)=1, 10 (CPUID)=6, 31 (RDMSR)=1.
```

The launch itself worked: the console showed the tag of `main`'s line
after it, so Aleph0's own code ran on as the guest. Drawing that line, the
firmware read `0x40000020`, `HV_X64_MSR_TIME_REF_COUNT` (the partition
reference counter its timer code uses), got the #GP, and its fatal-error
path loaded a zero IDT (the stop's `idtr=0/0`) and triple-faulted on
purpose. The test guest's runs printed the same exits as before: 24 and
`SUCCESS`, and 26 with `-InjectNmi`.

Since #27 Aleph0 forwards the firmware's hypercalls and synthetic MSRs to
Hyper-V ([HYPERV_INTERFACE.md](HYPERV_INTERFACE.md)). The same RDMSR at
`0x7ff1d9c8` now reads the reference counter, and the firmware runs on:
its timer fires, its VMBus drivers signal the host with hypercall `0x5d`,
it draws its "Virtual Machine Boot Summary" screen, and Tab then Enter on
its keyboard press "Restart now", which resets the VM as it does without
Aleph0 (HYPERV_INTERFACE.md section 7). Left alone at that screen, it ran
5 min 21 s under Aleph0 with no stop: 67 million exits, nearly all HLT
(`reason=12 (HLT), 67108864 exits of this reason so far` at exit
#67319478).

## 6. Not covered yet

- Its idle loop: HLT exits and resumes at once, so the exit counts grow
  quickly: about 36 million exits in three minutes at the Boot Summary
  screen, nearly all HLT, with the print policy keeping the first 16 of
  each reason in full and then one summary line per power of two.
- CR0/CR4 masks, so the firmware sees CR4.VMXE today (#24); re-delivering
  interrupted events and the interrupt policy for an OS (#26).
- The firmware guest still gets the test guest's pages, because `Ept::build`
  protects their data page. Nothing in the firmware touches it, and since
  #23 they are resident, so no OS reuses them either.
- Staying resident after `ExitBootServices` (#23): since #27 the harness
  runs past `0x40000020`, exits boot services as Aleph0's guest and
  overwrites every reclaimable page, and Aleph0 still handles its exits
  ([RESIDENT.md](RESIDENT.md) section 7).

| Name | Where | What |
|---|---|---|
| `GuestKind::SELECTED` | `vmcs/mod.rs` | `Firmware`, or `BuiltInTest` with `test-guest` |
| `GuestEntry::InPlace` | `guest_state.rs` | RIP/RSP/RFLAGS placeholders, the firmware's IDTR |
| `launch_in_place` | `vmcs/launch.rs` | writes RIP/RSP/RFLAGS, VMLAUNCH, returns `Ok` as the guest |
| `decode_in_place` | `vmcs/launch.rs` | 0 → `Ok`, RFLAGS → the failure |
| `decide(GuestKind, ..)` | `exit_decision/mod.rs` | only the test guest has VMCALLs and a protected page |
| `halt_unless_returnable` | `vmexit/handler.rs` | a stop of the firmware halts |
| `GuestRun::Virtualized` | `bring_up/mod.rs` | `run` returned in non-root operation; no teardown |

`docs/HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md`:

```md
# The host environment: what Aleph0 runs on in VMX root operation

Every VM exit switches the CPU to the *host state* in the VMCS: a CR3, a
GDT, a TSS, an IDT and the selectors that index them. This page explains
the host state Aleph0 builds for itself (`src/vmx/host/`), why it no longer
borrows the firmware's, and how NMIs and faults that arrive in root
operation are handled.

Code: `src/vmx/host/` (`mod.rs`, `page_tables.rs`, `gdt.rs`, `idt.rs`,
`handlers.rs`), the TSS in `src/vmx/context_tables.rs`, the NMI fold in
`src/vmx/exit_decision/mod.rs`, and teardown in `src/bring_up/teardown.rs`.
Issue #22.

## 1. Why not the firmware's

Until this step the VMCS host fields came from the running firmware:

| Field | Before | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| HOST_CR3 | the firmware's CR3 | its page tables are `BOOT_SERVICES_DATA`, which the OS may reuse after `ExitBootServices` |
| HOST_IDTR_BASE | the firmware's IDT | an NMI in root operation ran the firmware's NMI handler, which dead-loops; a fault ran a firmware handler from exit context |
| HOST_GDTR_BASE, HOST_TR_BASE | a copy of the firmware's GDT, with a TSS appended | no interrupt stacks, and the copy is shared with the guest |

Now every one of them comes from `HostEnvironment`, built during bring-up
and never freed:

| Field | Now |
|---|---|
| HOST_CR3 | Aleph0's identity map (section 2) |
| HOST_GDTR_BASE, host selectors | Aleph0's GDT (section 3) |
| HOST_TR_BASE, HOST_TR_SELECTOR | Aleph0's TSS with three interrupt stacks (section 4) |
| HOST_IDTR_BASE | Aleph0's IDT, 256 gates (section 5) |

Only VM exits load them. Bring-up and the test guest keep running on the
firmware's page tables and IDT and on the GDT copy (`context_tables.rs`), and
teardown switches back to the firmware's (section 7).

The pages come from `page.rs` as `RUNTIME_SERVICES_DATA`, which the OS keeps
after `ExitBootServices` (#23, [RESIDENT.md](RESIDENT.md)).

## 2. The page tables

An identity map (linear = physical) of every address the UEFI memory map
reaches, rounded up to 1 GiB (`Ept::memory_map_end`). That range holds the
image with the exit handler, every allocation (the EPT tables included),
and the firmware stack that `vmx_return_to_launcher` returns to after a
stop. EPT maps more for the guest, the whole guest-physical address space
([EPT.md](EPT.md) section 4), but root operation never touches the device
memory above the memory map.

```text
with 1 GiB pages (CPUID.80000001H:EDX bit 26):
CR3 ─▶ PML4[0] ─▶ PDPT[0..gibs] = 1 GiB pages                     2 table pages

without:
CR3 ─▶ PML4[0] ─▶ PDPT[0..gibs] ─▶ PD[0..512] = 2 MiB pages        2 + gibs table pages
```

On the Hyper-V test VM the map is `0x0..0x80000000` (2 GiB): with 1 GiB
pages that is a PML4, a PDPT and two PDPT entries.

Every entry is:

| Bit | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P (0), R/W (1) | 1 | present, writable |
| U/S (2) | 0 | supervisor only |
| PWT (3), PCD (4), PAT (12) | 0 | PAT entry 0, WB; the MTRRs still make device memory UC |
| A (5), D (6 in a leaf) | 1 | set in advance, so the CPU never writes the tables |
| PS (7) | 1 in a leaf | 1 GiB or 2 MiB page |
| XD (63) | 0 | the host does not switch IA32_EFER on VM exit, so the tables must work with EFER.NXE either way |

A table entry for the PDPT at `0x7f000000`, for example, is
`0x7f000023`; a 1 GiB page at 1 GiB is `0x400000e3`.

The entries are typed like EPT's (`HostEntry<L>` over the levels in
`ept::level`): a PDPT entry has `huge_page`, a PD entry `large_page`, and
only the levels above PT have `table`. Bring-up refuses CR4.LA57: HOST_CR4
is the running CR4, and these tables have 4 levels.

## 3. The GDT

A VM exit loads GDTR (with limit 0xFFFF) and the selectors from the VMCS,
and gives CS, SS and the data segments fixed flat attributes without
reading the GDT. The GDT still matters: IRETQ reloads CS and SS from it, as
does any interrupt return in firmware later.

The descriptors sit at the firmware's selector indices. On Hyper-V the
firmware runs with CS = `0x28` and SS = DS = ES = FS = GS = `0x08`:

```text
index  selector  descriptor
  0     0x00     null
  1     0x08     data: flat, read/write          0x00cf93000000ffff
  2-4            null
  5     0x28     code: flat, 64-bit, execute/read 0x00af9b000000ffff
  6-7   0x30     TSS (16 bytes)
```

Why the firmware's indices: after a stop, teardown loads the firmware's
GDTR, but CS keeps the selector the VM exit loaded until something reloads
it, which takes a far return. When both tables hold the code and data
descriptors at the same indices, a later interrupt return in firmware
reloads CS = `0x28` from the firmware's own GDT and finds its own code
descriptor. No segment register needs reloading.

`gdt::layout` refuses what would break that: a null CS, a selector with RPL
or TI set (VM entry requires both clear), or a data selector in CS's slot.

## 4. The TSS and the interrupt stacks

In long mode the TSS holds stack pointers only. Aleph0's has IST1-IST3,
each the top of its own 8 KiB stack:

| IST | Vector | Why its own stack |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | NMI (2) | can arrive at any instruction, including mid-push |
| 2 | #DF (8) | follows a fault while delivering a fault, for example a stack overflow |
| 3 | #MC (18) | can arrive at any time |

RSP0-2 stay 0 (the host never changes privilege level), and the I/O-map
base lies past the limit, so there is no I/O permission bitmap. VM exits
load TR with limit `0x67` and never mark the descriptor busy.

## 5. The IDT and the handlers

256 gates, one page. Every vector has a handler:

```text
vector 2 (NMI)     ─▶ host_nmi_entry ─▶ host_nmi_handler   (section 6), IRETQ
every other vector ─▶ stub n ─▶ host_exception_common ─▶ host_exception_handler: print, halt
                                                         (or resume a forward Hyper-V refused, below)
```

The stubs are 16 bytes apart, from `host_vector_stubs`. Each pushes a 0
where the CPU pushes no error code, then its vector, so every frame looks
alike:

```text
rsp+0   vector          (stub)
rsp+8   error code / 0  (CPU / stub)
rsp+16  RIP, CS, RFLAGS, RSP, SS (CPU)
```

The CPU pushes an error code for vectors 8, 10-14, 17, 21, 29 and 30
(`idt::has_error_code`). A host test reads the assembled stubs and checks
every one against that list.

A fault in root operation is a bug in Aleph0, so the handler prints and
halts:

```text
HOST EXCEPTION in VMX root operation: vector 13 (#GP general protection).
HOST EXCEPTION: error code 0x0.
HOST EXCEPTION: rip=0x... cs=0x0028 rflags=0x... rsp=0x... ss=0x0008 cr2=0x....
HOST EXCEPTION: halting this CPU.
```

One kind of fault is not a bug: Hyper-V refusing an access Aleph0 forwards
for the guest, #UD at the hypercall forwarder's VMCALL or #GP at its RDMSR
or WRMSR. `hyperv::recovery` names those three instructions; for one of
them the handler moves the frame's RIP to the forwarder's recovery point
and returns, and `host_exception_common`, which kept RSP in RBP, drops the
vector and error code and returns with IRETQ. The guest then gets the
exception ([HYPERV_INTERFACE.md](HYPERV_INTERFACE.md) section 5).

Maskable interrupts never arrive: a VM exit loads RFLAGS as `0x2` (IF = 0),
and nothing in root operation sets IF. Their gates exist so a stray `int n`
prints instead of hitting a missing gate.

## 6. NMIs in root operation

An NMI belongs to the guest wherever it lands: had the guest been running,
it would have caused an NMI exit. One that arrives while Aleph0 runs goes
through the host IDT instead.

```text
NMI in root ─▶ host_nmi_handler: NMI_PENDING = true; NMI-window exiting on; IRETQ
                     │
next exit's judge ───┴─▶ ExitState::with_host_nmi: nmi_pending = true
                         decide(...) as usual
                         ResumePlan::keeping_pending_nmi: NMI-window exiting stays on
NMI-window exit ──────▶ scenario::nmi_window injects it (0x80000202)
```

The handler cannot inject the NMI itself: whether VM_ENTRY_INTERRUPTION_INFO
is free depends on the exit being handled. So it marks the NMI pending, and
the guest gets it through the same NMI-window path as an NMI the guest
blocked.

**The late NMI.** Turning NMI-window exiting on in the handler covers an NMI
that arrives after the exit handler last looked at `NMI_PENDING` and before
VMRESUME. The exit handler orders its work so that no write can undo it:

1. The exit handler takes `NMI_PENDING` (`take_pending_nmi`) just before
   `judge` calls `decide`.
2. `prepare_resume` writes the VMCS, including the NMI-window bit
   (VMREAD, change, VMWRITE).
3. `keep_nmi_window_for_host_nmi` runs last: if `NMI_PENDING` is set again,
   it turns NMI-window exiting on.

An NMI between steps 1 and 3 may have its window bit overwritten by step 2,
but step 3 sees its flag and sets the bit again. An NMI after step 3 sets
the bit itself, and nothing writes the primary controls after that.

**NMI blocking after an NMI exit.** An NMI-caused VM exit blocks NMIs until
the next IRET or VM entry (Intel SDM Vol. 3C, "Architectural State Before a
VM Exit"). The exit handler never executes IRET, so the next VMRESUME
unblocks them. An NMI that arrives in between is held by the CPU and causes
an NMI exit right after the entry, so it is not lost. If the guest stops at
an NMI exit, NMIs stay blocked until firmware's next interrupt handler runs
IRET, as before.

NMIs that arrive after the guest stopped, before teardown loads the
firmware's IDT, set the flag and reach no guest.

## 7. Teardown

After a stop, bring-up keeps running on the host CR3, GDT and IDT the last
VM exit loaded, until teardown's first step loads the firmware's CR3, GDTR
and IDTR, in that order and before anything can call firmware. Both page
tables identity-map the running code and stack, so the CR3 switch moves
nothing. The line now reads:

```text
Teardown: CR4.VMXE=0 firmware CR3 restored=true firmware GDTR/IDTR restored=true IF=1.
```

TR keeps Aleph0's TSS selector, as before (see `teardown.rs`).

## 8. Testing it

Host tests (`tests/unit/vmx/host/`):
- the page tables, walked with `paging::walk`;
- the GDT layout and encoding;
- the gates and the IST assignment;
- the bytes of all 256 stubs;
- the NMI fold (`tests/unit/vmx/exit_decision.rs`).

On Hyper-V, bring-up prints the environment before VMXON:

```text
Host page tables: identity 0x0..0x80000000 (2 GiB), 1 GiB pages, 2 table pages; HOST_CR3=0x... (firmware CR3=0x4401000).
Host GDT at 0x... (limit 0x003f): code 0x0028, data 0x0008, TSS 0x0030 at 0x...; IDT at 0x... (256 gates).
Host interrupt stack: NMI IST1 top=0x....
Host interrupt stack: #DF IST2 top=0x....
Host interrupt stack: #MC IST3 top=0x....
```

Two test-only Cargo features, off by default, exercise the handlers
(`run-hyperv.ps1 -Features ...`):

| Run | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `-Features host-fault-test` | the exit handler reads a non-canonical address at exit #1; serial shows the `HOST EXCEPTION` lines for vector 13 and the VM stays halted |
| `-Features host-nmi-test -InjectNmi` | after main VMCALL #1 the exit handler waits in root operation; the job's NMI reaches the host NMI handler, then the guest through an NMI-window exit |

The expected lines of the second run:

```text
VM exit #12: expected VMCALL (rax=0xa1e0); resuming the guest at rip=...
VM exit #12: host-nmi-test: waiting in VMX root operation for an NMI.
VM exit #12: host-nmi-test: the host NMI handler ran (1 NMI(s) in root operation so far).
VM exit #12: an NMI arrived in root operation during this exit; NMI-window exiting on.
VM exit #13: reason=8 (NMI window)
...
VM exit #13: an NMI arrived while Aleph0 ran in root operation (1 so far); pending for the guest.
VM exit #13: NMI window open; reinjecting the pending NMI at rip=...
VM exit #14: guest NMI handler ran (rax=0x4e4d49); ...
VM exit #15: ... NMIs: 1 reinjected, 1 handled by the guest.
```

## 9. Not covered yet

- **The memory type of these pages**, and keeping the image with the
  handlers loaded after `ExitBootServices`: #23.
- **The guest's own tables** once the firmware runs as the guest: #21.
- **Hiding these pages from the guest** through EPT: after the first boot.
- **Per-CPU tables** for several vCPUs: after the first boot.
- **Host EFER**: the exit controls do not load it, so the bits of the
  guest's value other than LME and LMA (NXE, SCE) still apply to host
  accesses. IA32_PAT is switched when the CPU allows the controls for it
  (`vmcs::pat_switch`: VM exit saves the guest's and loads `HOST_IA32_PAT`,
  VM entry loads the guest's); on a CPU without them the guest's PAT still
  applies to host accesses too.

## Cheat sheet

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Host page-table entry bits | table `0x23` (P, R/W, A); leaf `0xE3` (+ D, PS) |
| 1 GiB pages | CPUID.80000001H:EDX bit 26 |
| Host GDT on Hyper-V | data `0x08`, code `0x28`, TSS `0x30`, limit `0x3f` |
| `CODE_64` / `DATA` | `0x00af9b000000ffff` / `0x00cf93000000ffff` |
| IST1 / IST2 / IST3 | NMI / #DF / #MC, 8 KiB each |
| Vectors with an error code | 8, 10-14, 17, 21, 29, 30 |
| Stub address | `host_vector_stubs + 16 * vector` |
| Host NMI | `NMI_PENDING`, NMI-window exiting on, folded by `ExitState::with_host_nmi` |
| Test features | `host-fault-test`, `host-nmi-test` |

`docs/HYPERV_INTERFACE.md`:

```md
# Hyper-V's interface: kept, and forwarded

Aleph0 runs nested under Hyper-V, and its guest ran on Hyper-V before
Aleph0 started: the firmware Aleph0 virtualizes in place had already set up
its hypercall page and its SynIC, because on a Gen 2 VM the keyboard, the
disk and the video are VMBus devices. Until issue #27 the guest still saw
Hyper-V in CPUID, but the parts of the interface that exit did not work:

- a hypercall is a VMCALL, which always exits, and Aleph0 stopped the
  firmware at any VMCALL that was not its own;
- Hyper-V's synthetic MSRs lie outside both MSR-bitmap ranges, so every
  RDMSR and WRMSR of them exited, and Aleph0 gave the guest a #GP.

The firmware's first synthetic MSR, `0x40000020`, got that #GP, and its
fatal-error path triple-faulted on purpose ([FIRMWARE_GUEST.md](FIRMWARE_GUEST.md)
section 5). Now Aleph0 repeats each hypercall and each synthetic-MSR access
in root operation, so L0 Hyper-V serves it as an access of Aleph0's own
virtual processor, the one the guest ran on before Aleph0 started.

Code: `src/vmx/hyperv.rs` (detection, the range, the forwarders and their
recovery points), `src/vmx/exit_decision/mod.rs` (`firmware_vmcall`),
`src/vmx/exit_decision/emulation.rs` (`route`, `MsrRoute::Synthetic`),
`src/vmx/vmexit/handler.rs` (`execute`, `prepare_resume`),
`src/vmx/host/handlers.rs` (the recovery in the host fault handler),
`src/vmx/vmexit/stats.rs` (`Forwarded`, `Tally`), `src/vmx/vmcall.rs`.

## 1. The decision: forward, everywhere

The issue weighed two options:

| | A: forward | B: hide Hyper-V from the OS |
|---|---|---|
| CPUID | passes through: ECX bit 31, the leaves from `0x40000000` | bit 31 cleared, the leaves answer zeros |
| the firmware | works: its VMBus drivers keep their hypercalls and SynIC | needs A anyway while boot services run |
| the OS | takes its Hyper-V paths (`ms_hyperv`, hypercall page, SynIC, the TSC and APIC frequencies from MSRs) | takes its bare-metal paths |

**Decision: A, for the firmware and the OS.** The firmware needs A whatever
the OS gets, and with A the first-boot kernel keeps the configuration #17
proved (`CONFIG_HYPERVISOR_GUEST=y`), so #28 boots the same kernel under
Aleph0 that already boots without it. B stays possible: the experiment
below shows the Linux target boots on the bare-metal paths too, so an OS
guest that must not see Hyper-V can get B later, in `cpuid_policy`, with A
left in place for the firmware.

What each experiment printed (section 7 has the lines):

- **A, firmware mode, 1 vCPU, Hyper-V.** The firmware ran on for minutes,
  36 million exits and no stop: synthetic MSR `0x40000020` read 16350 times,
  hypercall `0x5d` made at least 32 times, all forwarded. It drew its "Virtual
  Machine Boot Summary" screen, and Tab then Enter pressed "Restart now":
  Hyper-V logged event 18514, "reset by the guest operating system", as in
  the control run without Aleph0.
- **B, a kernel without Hyper-V guest support, without Aleph0.** Linux
  6.18.58 from `scripts/linux/build.sh` with `# CONFIG_HYPERVISOR_GUEST is
  not set` reached its shell. Without Hyper-V's frequency MSRs the fast
  TSC calibration and the PIT failed (the VM has no PIT), the TSC was
  calibrated against the ACPI PM timer (3168.264 MHz, where Hyper-V's MSR
  says 3187.199), the clocksource was `tsc-early` at the shell and `tsc`
  after the refinement at 1.19 s (3187.198 MHz); the TSC deadline timer is
  available for the LAPIC timer. Compared with #17's run, the CPU flags lack
  `constant_tsc`, `nonstop_tsc`, `tsc_reliable` and `tsc_known_freq`, which
  the kernel's Hyper-V code brings: it writes `0x40000118` to expose the
  invariant TSC and reads the frequency from `0x40000022`.

## 2. Whose VMCALL

A VMCALL means something different to each guest kind:

| Guest | CPL | RCX | Event | What Aleph0 does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| test guest | any | any | `scenario::vmcall` | its script, by RAX markers, as before |
| firmware or OS | > 0 | any | `GuestInvalidOpcode` | #UD, as Hyper-V gives (KVM's emulation of Hyper-V too) |
| firmware or OS | 0 | `BOOT_SERVICES_ENDED`, `TEST` | `BootServicesEnded`, `TestVmcall` | resumes past it |
| firmware or OS | 0 | anything else, Hyper-V present | `Emulated(Hypercall)` | forwards it |
| firmware or OS | 0 | anything else, no Hyper-V | `GuestInvalidOpcode` | #UD, as on hardware without a hypervisor |

**Aleph0's own VMCALLs moved from RAX to RCX.** A hypercall's input value
is RCX:

```text
 63:60  59:48        47:44  43:32      31      30:27  26:17        16    15:0
┌─────┬────────────┬──────┬──────────┬───────┬──────┬────────────┬─────┬───────────┐
│ res │ rep start  │ res  │ rep count│ nested│ res  │ var. header│ fast│ call code │
└─────┴────────────┴──────┴──────────┴───────┴──────┴────────────┴─────┴───────────┘
```

`"Aleph0EB"` read big-endian is `0x416c657068304542`: its top nibble, 4,
sets bit 62, reserved, so Hyper-V would refuse it as a hypercall, and no
hypercall it takes is ever mistaken for Aleph0's. RAX, which a hypercall
ignores, could hold the signature by chance; RCX cannot hold it in a valid
hypercall. A compile-time assert in `vmcall.rs` checks both values.

**The CPL comes from SS.DPL** (`cpl_from_ss`, GUEST_SS_ACCESS_RIGHTS bits
6:5), read for VMCALL exits only. Without the check, a VMCALL from user
mode would reach Hyper-V from Aleph0's CPL 0.

**Hyper-V present** means CPUID.1:ECX bit 31, a highest hypervisor leaf of
at least `0x40000001`, and `"Hv#1"` in CPUID.40000001H:EAX, the interface
signature the TLFS says to check (`offers_interface`). Bring-up reads the
leaves once (`Detection::read`), prints them, and publishes the result
(`hyperv::publish`); every exit carries it as `ExitInfo::hyperv`.

## 3. Which MSRs

`SYNTHETIC_MSRS` is `0x40000000..=0x4000FFFF`, wider than the
`0x40000000`-`0x400000FF` the issue named: Hyper-V puts MSRs past `0xFF`
too, among them the crash MSRs (`0x40000100`-`0x40000105`),
`HV_X64_MSR_TSC_INVARIANT_CONTROL` (`0x40000118`, which the Linux target
writes at boot) and the nested SynIC's (`0x40001080` and up). An MSR
Hyper-V does not define reads 0 and ignores writes (section 5 shows
`0x4000FFFF`), as it does for the guest without Aleph0, so the wider range
forwards nothing the guest could not reach anyway.

`route` checks the range only outside the bitmap's ranges:

| MSR | Route | Event |
|---|---|---|
| in `INTERCEPTED_MSRS` | the real RDMSR/WRMSR | `Emulated(Rdmsr)`, `Emulated(Wrmsr)` |
| an MTRR MSR the guest has | its copy | `Emulated(MtrrRead)`, `Emulated(MtrrWrite)` |
| an MTRR address the CPU has no MSR at | #GP(0) | `GuestGeneralProtection` |
| outside both ranges, in `SYNTHETIC_MSRS`, Hyper-V present | forward | `Emulated(SyntheticRead)`, `Emulated(SyntheticWrite)` |
| outside both ranges otherwise | #GP(0) | `GuestGeneralProtection` |
| in range, bit clear | the bitmap is broken: stop | `Unexpected` |

A forwarded WRMSR is not checked for a canonical value: Hyper-V checks
what it takes.

## 4. Forwarding

`execute` (`vmexit/handler.rs`) runs the forwarders in `hyperv.rs`, small
`global_asm!` functions:

```text
hyperv_forward_hypercall(registers):        hyperv_forward_rdmsr(msr, value):
    push registers                              mov r8, value
    rcx, rdx, r8 <- registers               hyperv_rdmsr_instruction:
hyperv_hypercall_instruction:                   rdmsr
    vmcall               ; to L0 Hyper-V        [value] <- edx:eax
    pop r9                                      return 0
    registers <- rcx, rdx, r8, rax          hyperv_rdmsr_refused:
    return 0                                    return 1
hyperv_hypercall_refused:
    pop r9
    return 1
```

`hyperv_forward_wrmsr` is the RDMSR's twin. The registers in and out:

- **Hypercall:** in, the guest's RCX (the input value), RDX and R8 (the
  input and output GPAs, or a fast hypercall's data); out, RAX (the result:
  status in bits 15:0, reps done in 43:32), and RCX, RDX and R8 written
  back too, since Hyper-V updates RCX's rep start index when it continues a
  rep hypercall, and a fast hypercall can return data in RDX and R8. RIP
  then moves past the VMCALL. A fast hypercall's XMM0-XMM5 pass unchanged:
  Aleph0 never touches vector state (the target is soft-float, see
  `vmx::vmexit`).
- **RDMSR / WRMSR:** EDX:EAX, as for every emulated MSR.

**Why the GPAs stay valid:** EPT is an identity map, so a GPA the guest
passes names the same page for Hyper-V. The pages Hyper-V overlays at GPAs
the guest chose (the hypercall page, the reference TSC page, the SynIC's
message and event pages) appear in Aleph0's address space, and the guest
sees them through the same map. In the run below the guest's VMCALL is at
`0x7f60b000`, the start of its hypercall page, which the firmware placed
there before Aleph0 started.

A hypercall from L1 in VMX root operation reaches L0 as a hypercall of
L1's virtual processor; that is how a nested hypervisor talks to Hyper-V
(MiniVisor and hvpp forward their guests' hypercalls the same way).

## 5. When Hyper-V refuses

Hyper-V raises #UD for a hypercall it does not take (none enabled yet, for
example) and #GP for an MSR value that is refused. Raised in root
operation, either would land in the host IDT's fault handler, which prints
and halts: a guest could stop Aleph0 with one WRMSR. So each forwarding
instruction has a recovery point:

```text
fault at RIP ─▶ stub ─▶ host_exception_common ─▶ host_exception_handler
                                                   │
             hyperv::recovery(RIP, vector) ────────┤ Some(resume): frame.RIP = resume, return
                                                   │ None: print, halt (a bug, as before)
host_exception_common: RSP from RBP, drop vector and error code, IRETQ ─▶ _refused: return 1
```

`recovery` matches the RIP exactly and the vector too (#UD at the VMCALL,
#GP at the RDMSR and the WRMSR); any other fault stays a bug. A host test
reads the assembled bytes at each label (`0F 01 C1`, `0F 32`, `0F 30`), so
the label is the instruction the CPU reports.

The forwarder returns 1, `execute` returns `EmulationOutcome::Refused` with
the guest's registers unchanged, and `prepare_resume` turns the plan into
the exception's (`ResumePlan::refused_with`, host-tested): RIP stays on
the guest's instruction, and #UD or #GP(0) is injected there, as Hyper-V
would have done without Aleph0. The plan it returns is the one carried
out, so the statistics count the forwarded access and the injected
exception both.

The `forward-refusal-test` Cargo feature checks the path on Hyper-V: at the
first exit it forwards an RDMSR and a WRMSR of 0 to `0x4000FFFF`, which
Hyper-V does not define, and a WRMSR of a non-canonical value to
IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE, which faults on any CPU:

```text
forward-refusal-test: RDMSR 0x4000ffff -> Ok(0), WRMSR 0x4000ffff <- 0 -> Ok(()); WRMSR 0xc0000102 <- 0x8000000000000000 -> Err(Refused); Aleph0 still runs.
```

The #GP reached the host fault handler, which resumed the forwarder at its
recovery point, and the firmware ran on for 6 million more exits. So an
undefined synthetic MSR is no refusal at all; only a value Hyper-V or the
CPU checks is. Hyper-V refused no hypercall in any run, so the VMCALL's #UD
recovery has the host test of its label only.

## 6. What it prints

Bring-up, after the exit bitmaps:

```text
Hyper-V interface offered (CPUID.1:ECX=0xf7fa3223, leaf 0x40000000: max leaf 0x4000000b vendor "Microsoft Hv", leaf 0x40000001: interface 0x31237648): the guest keeps it; Aleph0 forwards its hypercalls and its synthetic MSRs 0x40000000..=0x4000ffff to Hyper-V.
```

Each forwarded exit printed in full, within the print policy's first 16 of
its reason:

```text
VM exit #N: hypercall 0x005d (rcx=0x1005d) forwarded to Hyper-V -> status 0x0 (rax=0x0); resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: RDMSR 0x40000020 (synthetic) forwarded to Hyper-V -> 0x00000000003b5321; resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: WRMSR 0x40000001 (synthetic) <- 0x... forwarded to Hyper-V; resuming at rip=...
VM exit #N: Hyper-V refused the forwarded SyntheticWrite { msr: ..., value: ... } with #GP(0); injecting it at rip=...
VM exit #N: VMCALL (rcx=...) from CPL 3, which Hyper-V refuses too; injecting #UD at rip=...
```

The counts cost no line per exit. `VcpuStats` counts `hypercall_exits`,
`synthetic_read_exits` and `synthetic_write_exits`, and `Forwarded` keeps
them by call code (RCX bits 15:0) and by MSR, the first 32 keys each, the
rest in `other`. They are kept apart from `VcpuStats`, which bring-up
compares and returns in an error, so that stays a few words. A stop prints
both:

```text
VM exit #N: exit statistics: exits=... hypercall_exits=... synthetic_read_exits=... synthetic_write_exits=....
VM exit #N: forwarded to Hyper-V: hypercalls by call code: 0x5d=...; synthetic MSR reads: 0x40000020=...; synthetic MSR writes: none.
```

The firmware never stops when all goes well, so the summary line of a
VMCALL, RDMSR or WRMSR exit (the 32nd, 64th, ... of its reason) adds that
reason's tally:

```text
VM exit #101685: reason=18 (VMCALL), 32 exits of this reason so far.
VM exit #101685: forwarded to Hyper-V so far: hypercalls by call code: 0x5d=32.
```

## 7. The Hyper-V runs

**Firmware mode, `-ProcessorCount 1`.** From bring-up to the first
forwarded exits:

```text
Launching the firmware in place with VMLAUNCH; its VM exits are reported on serial only.
The firmware runs as the guest: Aleph0 returns to it in VMX non-root operation.
Waiting 1 s on a firmware timer event...
VM exit #1: HLT; going on at rip=0x000000007ff26114.
   (#2 to #7: CPUID)
VM exit #8: reason=31 (RDMSR)
VM exit #8: guest rip=0x000000007ff1d9c8 instruction length=2
VM exit #8: guest rax=0x0000000040000020 rbx=0x0000000040000020 rcx=0x0000000040000020 rdx=0x0000000000090004
VM exit #8: RDMSR 0x40000020 (synthetic) forwarded to Hyper-V -> 0x00000000003b5321; resuming at rip=0x000000007ff1d9ca.
   (the same RDMSR every few exits: HV_X64_MSR_TIME_REF_COUNT, 100 ns units, counting up)
VM exit #1675: reason=31 (RDMSR), 32 exits of this reason so far.
VM exit #1675: forwarded to Hyper-V so far: synthetic MSR reads: 0x40000020=32.
Firmware timer fired: interrupts reach the firmware again.
VM exit #101124: reason=18 (VMCALL)
VM exit #101124: guest rip=0x000000007f60b000 instruction length=3
VM exit #101124: guest rax=0x000000007f60b000 rbx=0x000000007ff21140 rcx=0x000000000001005d rdx=0x000000000000200d
VM exit #101124: hypercall 0x005d (rcx=0x1005d) forwarded to Hyper-V -> status 0x0 (rax=0x0); resuming at rip=0x000000007f60b003.
VM exit #101685: reason=18 (VMCALL), 32 exits of this reason so far.
VM exit #101685: forwarded to Hyper-V so far: hypercalls by call code: 0x5d=32.
...
VM exit #36639479: reason=31 (RDMSR), 16384 exits of this reason so far.
VM exit #36639479: forwarded to Hyper-V so far: synthetic MSR reads: 0x40000020=16350.
```

The exit at `0x7ff1d9c8` is the one that got #GP before (FIRMWARE_GUEST.md
section 5). `0x5d` with bit 16 is a fast `HvCallSignalEvent`, the VMBus
drivers' doorbell to the host, with the connection ID in RDX; it returned
`HV_STATUS_SUCCESS`. No WRMSR exit came: the firmware's SynIC was set up
before Aleph0 started. Between the timer reads the firmware idles in HLT,
which made most of the 36 million exits. Every hypercall seen was `0x5d`;
a stop would print the whole tally, and none came.

The console showed the firmware's "Virtual Machine Boot Summary" ("No
operating system was loaded", the "Restart now" button): Aleph0 had
returned to it, and it found no other boot option. The keyboard, through
Hyper-V's `Msvm_Keyboard.TypeKey`:

| Run | Keys | Result |
|---|---|---|
| control: `-TestGuest`, the firmware no longer virtualized after `SUCCESS` | Enter | nothing visible, as under Aleph0 in the first run |
| control | Tab, Enter | the VM reset, event 18514 "was reset by the guest operating system" at 19:10:40 |
| firmware under Aleph0 | Tab, Enter | the VM reset at the Enter (uptime 12 s before, 8 s after), event 18514 at 19:11:31 |

A triple fault in root operation would have reset the VM as well, but
Hyper-V logs that as event 18560; both resets were 18514. So the firmware,
as Aleph0's guest, read Tab and Enter from its VMBus keyboard and restarted
the VM through its own reset path.

Left alone at that screen in a third run, the firmware ran 5 min 21 s
with no stop: 67 million exits, the last summary lines

```text
VM exit #36592027: forwarded to Hyper-V so far: synthetic MSR reads: 0x40000020=16350.
VM exit #48865745: reason=10 (CPUID), 131072 exits of this reason so far.
VM exit #67319478: reason=12 (HLT), 67108864 exits of this reason so far.
```

**`-TestGuest` and `-InjectNmi`.** The same exits as before: 24 and
`SUCCESS`, 26 with the NMI reinjected at #24 and handled at #25, and
`SUCCESS`. The stop lines now end with the new counters, all zero:

```text
VM exit #26: exit statistics: exits=26 cpuid_exits=2 msr_read_exits=2 msr_write_exits=2 mtrr_read_exits=3 mtrr_write_exits=7 io_in_exits=2 io_out_exits=2 halt_exits=1 nmi_injections=1 exception_injections=0 hypercall_exits=0 synthetic_read_exits=0 synthetic_write_exits=0.
VM exit #26: forwarded to Hyper-V: hypercalls by call code: none; synthetic MSR reads: none; synthetic MSR writes: none.
```

`guest::expected_stats` requires those zeros: the test guest's VMCALLs are
its script's.

**Option B, without Aleph0.** `-Kernel <the build> -WithoutAleph0
-ProcessorCount 1`, from COM1:

```text
[    0.000000] tsc: Fast TSC calibration failed
[    0.000000] TSC deadline timer available

No `Hypervisor detected` line, as expected. The build took a copy of
