/// Prints what VMX root operation will run on: the host page tables next to
/// the firmware's CR3 they replace, the GDT, TSS and IDT, and the interrupt
/// stacks.
pub(super) fn host_environment(host: &HostEnvironment, firmware_cr3: u64) {
    let tables = host.page_tables();
    log!(
        "Host page tables: identity 0x0..{:#x} ({} GiB), {}, {} table pages; HOST_CR3={:#x} (firmware CR3={firmware_cr3:#x}).",
        tables.end(),
        tables.end() >> 30,
        tables.page_size().name(),
        tables.table_pages(),
        tables.cr3(),
    );
    let selectors = host.selectors();
    log!(
        "Host GDT at {:#018x} (limit {:#06x}): code {:#06x}, data {:#06x}, TSS {:#06x} at {:#018x}; IDT at {:#018x} (256 gates).",
        host.gdt_base(),
        host.gdt_limit(),
        selectors.cs,
        selectors.ss,
        selectors.tr,
        host.tss_base(),
        host.idt_base(),
    );
    for stack in InterruptStack::ALL {
        let (name, ist, top) = (stack.name(), stack.ist(), host.interrupt_stack_top(stack));
        log!("Host interrupt stack: {name} IST{ist} top={top:#018x}.");
    }
}

/// Prints one resident allocation with the type the memory map gives it
/// (`None`: no region holds it).
pub(super) fn resident_allocation(allocation: Allocation, memory_type: Option<MemoryType>) {
    let Allocation { address, pages } = allocation;
    match memory_type {
        Some(memory_type) => log!("Resident allocation at {address:#018x}: {pages} page(s), {memory_type:?}."),
        None => log!("Resident allocation at {address:#018x}: {pages} page(s), in no memory-map region."),
    }
}

/// Prints how the current page tables, which the guest will share, map the
/// guest pages. Only called once all permission checks have passed.
pub(super) fn guest_mappings(guest: &GuestMemory, mappings: &GuestMappings) {
    let stack_base = guest.stack_top() - vmx::page::PAGE_SIZE as u64;
    for (name, virtual_address, mapping) in [
        ("code", guest.code_base(), mappings.code),
        ("stack", stack_base, mappings.stack),
        ("IDT", guest.idt().base, mappings.idt),
        ("data", guest.data_page(), mappings.data),
    ] {
        log!(
            "Guest {name} page: virt={virtual_address:#018x} phys={:#018x} identity={} size={:?} writable={} user={} xd={}",
            mapping.physical,
            mapping.physical == virtual_address,
            mapping.size,
            mapping.writable,
            mapping.user,
            mapping.execute_disable,
        );
    }

    // The guest shares these tables, so a guest EFER.NXE that differs from
    // the host's would turn any XD bit in them into a reserved-bit fault.
    // SAFETY: IA32_EFER exists on every x86_64 CPU, and reading it has no
    // side effects.
    let nxe = unsafe { vmx::msr::rdmsr(vmx::msr::IA32_EFER) } & vmx::msr::EFER_NXE != 0;
    let cr4 = vmx::cr::read_cr4();
    log!(
        "Guest code page executable, stack and data pages writable; host EFER.NXE={nxe} CR4.SMEP={} CR4.SMAP={}.",
        cr4 & vmx::cr::CR4_SMEP != 0,
        cr4 & vmx::cr::CR4_SMAP != 0,
    );
}

/// Prints where the exit bitmaps are and what they intercept: the MSRs
/// passed through, every MTRR address, of which the guest's copy holds
/// those `mtrr` lists, and the ports.
pub(super) fn exit_bitmaps(bitmaps: &ExitBitmaps, mtrr: MtrrCapabilities) {
    log!(
        "Exit bitmaps allocated: MSR={:#018x} I/O A={:#018x} I/O B={:#018x}.",
        bitmaps.msr_address(),
        bitmaps.io_a_address(),
        bitmaps.io_b_address(),
    );
    log!("Intercepted MSRs (read and write): {INTERCEPTED_MSRS:x?}; intercepted ports: {INTERCEPTED_PORTS:x?}.");
    let addresses = vmx::mtrr::every_msr_address().count();
    match mtrr.msrs().count() {
        0 => log!("Intercepted MTRR addresses (read and write): all {addresses}, which get #GP: the CPU has no MTRRs."),
        count => log!(
            "Intercepted MTRR addresses (read and write): all {addresses}. The guest reads and writes a copy of the {count} MSRs the CPU has (IA32_MTRR_DEF_TYPE, {} fixed-range MSRs and {} variable ranges); the other {} get #GP.",
            if mtrr.fixed() { vmx::mtrr::FIXED_MSRS } else { 0 },
            mtrr.variable_count(),
            addresses - count,
        ),
    }
}

/// Prints what CPUID says of Hyper-V's interface (`detection`), and so what
/// the guest's hypercalls and synthetic MSRs get.
pub(super) fn hyperv(detection: &Detection) {
    let vendor = detection.vendor_bytes();
    let vendor = core::str::from_utf8(&vendor).unwrap_or("not ASCII");
    let line = format_args!(
        "CPUID.1:ECX={:#010x}, leaf {VENDOR_LEAF:#x}: max leaf {:#x} vendor \"{vendor}\", leaf {INTERFACE_LEAF:#x}: interface {:#010x}",
        detection.leaf1_ecx, detection.vendor.eax, detection.interface,
    );
    if detection.offers_interface() {
        log!(
            "Hyper-V interface offered ({line}): the guest keeps it; Aleph0 forwards its hypercalls and its synthetic MSRs {:#x}..={:#x} to Hyper-V.",
            SYNTHETIC_MSRS.start(),
            SYNTHETIC_MSRS.end(),
        );
    } else {
        log!("No Hyper-V interface ({line}): the guest's VMCALLs other than Aleph0's get #UD, its synthetic MSRs #GP.");
    }
}

/// Prints whether the CPU's MTRRs read the same after the guest
/// (`before`, `after`), and whether the guest left its copy (`guest`) as
/// it found it. Still in the exit phase, so serial only.
pub(super) fn mtrrs_after_guest(
    before: &Result<MtrrRegisters, MtrrError>,
    after: &Result<MtrrRegisters, MtrrError>,
    guest: Option<&MtrrRegisters>,
) {
    match (before, after) {
        (Ok(before), Ok(after)) => log!(
            "MTRRs after the guest: the CPU's unchanged={}; the guest's copy restored={}.",
            before == after,
            guest == Some(before),
        ),
        (Err(error), _) | (_, Err(error)) => log!("MTRRs after the guest: the CPU's could not be read: {error}."),
    }
}

/// Prints the host state the guest reached through passthrough emulation,
/// before and after its run. Still in the exit phase, so serial only.
pub(super) fn passthrough_state(before: PassthroughState, after: PassthroughState) {
    log!(
        "Passthrough state before the guest {before:x?}, after it {after:x?}: restored={}.",
        before == after
    );
}

/// Prints the guest state that was written to the VMCS. If VM entry later
/// fails with "invalid guest state" (exit reason 33), these are the values
/// the CPU rejected.
pub(super) fn guest_state(state: &GuestState, entry: GuestEntry) {
    state.report(format_args!("Guest"));
    if let GuestEntry::InPlace { .. } = entry {
        log!(
            "Guest rip, rsp and rflags are placeholders: VMLAUNCH writes its own, and the code after it goes on as the guest."
        );
    }
    log!("VMCS guest fields written and read back; VM entry not attempted.");
}

`src/bring_up/teardown.rs`:

```rs
//! Leaving VMX operation and handing the CPU back to firmware.
//!
//! Runs after the guest stopped, and after any failure once VMXON has
//! succeeded, so firmware gets the CPU back outside VMX operation. The one
//! exception is a failing VMXOFF: the CPU is then still in VMX root
//! operation with CR4.VMXE set, and teardown prints that.
//!
//! The order matters:
//!
//! 1. Load the firmware's CR3, GDTR and IDTR again. A VM exit loads
//!    Aleph0's own page tables and descriptor tables (`vmx::host`), and the
//!    code after a stop keeps running on them until here. CR3 comes first,
//!    before anything can call firmware. The segment selectors need no
//!    reload: the host GDT keeps the firmware's selectors (`vmx::host`'s
//!    `gdt.rs`).
//! 2. VMCLEAR the VMCS, so the CPU writes any VMCS data it caches back to
//!    memory.
//! 3. VMXOFF, then CR0/CR4 as they were before VMXON
//!    (`VmxOperation::leave`). CR4.VMXE can only be cleared after VMXOFF.
//! 4. Switch the output phase back to boot services.
//! 5. Turn interrupts back on, if firmware had them on.
//! 6. Check and print the result.
//!
//! When the guest ran, interrupts are off until step 5: a VM exit loads
//! host RFLAGS as 0x2. The phase changes late for the same reason. The
//! firmware console can call RestoreTPL, which executes STI, so a console
//! line during steps 1 to 3 could turn interrupts on early. Until step 4
//! the exit handler's phase keeps `log!` on serial. On paths that never
//! launched, the phase is still boot services and interrupts were never
//! turned off, so neither concern applies.
//!
//! TR keeps Aleph0's TSS selector. LTR cannot load a null selector, and the
//! TSS and GDT pages are never freed, so the CPU's cached TSS descriptor
//! stays valid. The selector may lie past the firmware GDT's limit; only an
//! LTR or a task switch would look it up again.
//!
//! Three more things a VM exit changes are intentionally not restored: DR7 is
//! set to 0x400, IA32_DEBUGCTL is cleared, and LDTR is made null. Firmware
//! then runs with those values, which only matters while a hardware debugger
//! is attached; UEFI uses no LDT.

use core::arch::asm;

use crate::output::{self, Phase};
use crate::vmx::cr::{self, CR4_VMXE};
use crate::vmx::instruction::VmxFail;
use crate::vmx::segment::{self, DescriptorTable};
use crate::vmx::vmcs::{VmcsError, VmcsRegion};
use crate::vmx::vmxon::VmxOperation;

/// RFLAGS.IF, bit 9: maskable interrupts are delivered.
const RFLAGS_IF: u64 = 1 << 9;

/// Firmware state from before bring-up changed it, for [`teardown`] to put
/// back.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
pub(super) struct FirmwareState {
    pub(super) cr3: u64,
    pub(super) gdtr: DescriptorTable,
    pub(super) idtr: DescriptorTable,
    pub(super) interrupts_enabled: bool,
}

/// Which teardown step failed.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum TeardownError {
    /// VMCLEAR failed, so the VMCS data may not have been written back.
    Vmclear(VmcsError),
    /// VMXOFF failed: the CPU is still in VMX operation, with CR4.VMXE set.
    Vmxoff(VmxFail),
}

/// Whether maskable interrupts are on right now.
pub(super) fn interrupts_enabled() -> bool {
    read_rflags() & RFLAGS_IF != 0
}

fn read_rflags() -> u64 {
    let rflags: u64;
    // SAFETY: PUSHFQ and POP only use the stack below RSP, which `asm!`
    // allows once `nostack` is left out, and change nothing else.
    unsafe { asm!("pushfq", "pop {0}", out(reg) rflags, options(preserves_flags)) };
    rflags
}

/// Leaves VMX operation and restores the firmware's CPU state, in the order
/// the module docs give.
///
/// Every step runs even if an earlier one failed, except restoring CR0/CR4
/// after a failed VMXOFF. Each failure is printed when it happens; the
/// first one is returned.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// `vmx_operation` must be this CPU's VMX operation and `vmcs` its only
/// VMCS, if one was created. The guest must not be running, and `firmware`
/// must describe the firmware's live descriptor tables.
pub(super) unsafe fn teardown(
    vmx_operation: VmxOperation,
    vmcs: Option<&VmcsRegion>,
    firmware: &FirmwareState,
) -> Result<(), TeardownError> {
    let mut result = Ok(());

    // SAFETY: `firmware` holds the firmware's own page tables and
    // descriptor tables, which boot services keep live (the caller's
    // obligation). Both page tables identity-map the code and stack running
    // here, so the CR3 switch changes no address it uses.
    unsafe {
        cr::write_cr3(firmware.cr3);
        segment::load_gdtr(&firmware.gdtr);
        segment::load_idtr(&firmware.idtr);
    }

    if let Some(vmcs) = vmcs
        // SAFETY: still in VMX operation, with `vmcs` this CPU's VMCS;
        // VMXOFF comes next.
        && let Err(error) = unsafe { vmcs.vmclear() }
    {
        log!("Teardown: VMCLEAR failed: {error:?}.");
        result = Err(TeardownError::Vmclear(error));
    }

    // SAFETY: the VMCS was cleared above (or its failure printed, which only
    // leaves that VMCS's memory stale), and no VMX instruction runs after
    // this.
    if let Err(fail) = unsafe { vmx_operation.leave() } {
        log!("Teardown: VMXOFF failed: {fail:?}; still in VMX operation, CR4.VMXE left set.");
        result = result.and(Err(TeardownError::Vmxoff(fail)));
    }

    output::set_phase(Phase::BootServices);
    if firmware.interrupts_enabled {
        // SAFETY: firmware had interrupts on, and its IDT is loaded again, so
        // every interrupt reaches a firmware handler.
        unsafe { asm!("sti", options(nostack)) };
    }

    report(firmware);
    result
}

/// Prints whether teardown left the CPU as firmware expects. Reaches the
/// console too: the phase is boot services again.
fn report(firmware: &FirmwareState) {
    let vmxe = cr::read_cr4() & CR4_VMXE != 0;
    let cr3_restored = cr::read_cr3() == firmware.cr3;
    let tables_restored = segment::read_gdtr() == firmware.gdtr && segment::read_idtr() == firmware.idtr;
    log!(
        "Teardown: CR4.VMXE={} firmware CR3 restored={cr3_restored} firmware GDTR/IDTR restored={tables_restored} IF={}.",
        u8::from(vmxe),
        u8::from(interrupts_enabled()),
    );
}

`src/main.rs`:

```rs
// Host unit tests (`cargo test --target <host triple>`) build with std and
// the test harness; the UEFI build is no_std with a firmware entry point.
#![cfg_attr(not(test), no_main)]
#![cfg_attr(not(test), no_std)]
// Every `unsafe` block says why it is sound here (`// SAFETY:`), and every
// `unsafe fn` lists its callers' obligations (`# Safety`).
#![warn(clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks)]

use core::time::Duration;

use uefi::boot::{self, EventType, TimerTrigger, Tpl};
use uefi::prelude::*;

/// Prints a tagged line to the serial port (COM2), and to the firmware
/// console while still in boot services.
///
/// Safe in every context: outside the boot-services phase (see
/// `output::Phase`) the console half is skipped and only serial is written.
///
/// Defined above the `mod` lines on purpose: a `macro_rules!` macro is only
/// visible to code that comes after it, and `bring_up` uses it.
macro_rules! log {
    ($($arg:tt)*) => {
        crate::output::log_line(format_args!($($arg)*))
    };
}

mod bring_up;
mod output;
mod port;
mod resident;
mod serial;
mod vmx;

/// Prefix for every line this hypervisor prints, on screen and on serial.
pub const TAG: &str = "[Aleph0 Virtualization Hypervisor]";

/// Where Aleph0 prints: COM2, leaving COM1 to the guest.
const OUTPUT_PORT: serial::SerialPort = serial::SerialPort::COM2;

#[cfg_attr(not(test), entry)]
fn main() -> Status {
    // First, so every later line also reaches serial. Needs no firmware.
    let serial = serial::init(OUTPUT_PORT);

    log!("Initializing UEFI helpers...");

    uefi::helpers::init().unwrap();

    log!("UEFI helpers initialized successfully.");
    match serial {
        Ok(()) => log!("Serial output enabled on {OUTPUT_PORT}."),
        Err(error) => log!("Serial output disabled on {OUTPUT_PORT}: {error:?}; console only."),
    }

    // The firmware unloads this image when `main` returns, and the OS may
    // reuse its pages after ExitBootServices; the copy stays.
    // SAFETY: boot services are active, and the only statics written so far
    // are the serial port, its readiness, the output phase and the `uefi`
    // crate's image handle and system table: none an address in the image.
    match unsafe { resident::ResidentImage::copy() } {
        Ok(image) => {
            log!(
                "Image copied to resident memory: {:#018x} -> {:#018x}, {} bytes, {} fixups applied; running on from the copy.",
                image.loaded(),
                image.base(),
                image.size(),
                image.fixups(),
            );
            // SAFETY: `image` is this image's copy, and nothing below uses
            // this image's statics again.
            unsafe { image.call(run) }
        }
        Err(error) => {
            log!("Image not copied to resident memory: {error:?}; Aleph0 cannot outlive boot services.");
            Status::ABORTED
        }
    }
}

/// Everything after the copy, in the resident image: bring-up, and the
/// return to the firmware.
fn run() -> Status {
    // Bring-up returns once the test guest has stopped, once the firmware
    // runs as the guest, or at the first failure. In the first and last case
    // it has left VMX operation if it entered it, unless VMXOFF failed: then
    // the CPU is still in VMX root operation with CR4.VMXE set, teardown
    // printed that, and firmware takes over in that state. Once the firmware
    // runs as the guest, everything below runs in VMX non-root operation.
    let status = match bring_up::run() {
        Ok(bring_up::GuestRun::Finished { exits }) => {
            log!("Guest finished after {exits} VM exits; VMX operation left.");
            Status::SUCCESS
        }
        Ok(bring_up::GuestRun::Virtualized) => {
            log!("The firmware runs as the guest: Aleph0 returns to it in VMX non-root operation.");
            Status::SUCCESS
        }
        Err(error) => {
            bring_up::report_error(error);
            Status::ABORTED
        }
    };

    check_firmware_timer();
    log!("Returning to firmware with {status:?}.");
    status
}

/// How long [`check_firmware_timer`] waits.
const TIMER_CHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1);

/// Waits on a one-shot UEFI timer event. Only the firmware's timer
/// interrupt signals it, so getting past the wait shows that interrupts
/// reach the firmware's handlers: through the restored IDT, or, once the
/// firmware runs as the guest, through its own IDT in VMX non-root
/// operation, with no VM exit. If they do not, the wait never ends, and the
/// "Waiting" line is the last one on serial.
///
/// WaitForEvent may turn interrupts on by itself (through RestoreTPL), so
/// this does not show that teardown restored IF; teardown prints IF itself.
fn check_firmware_timer() {
    log!("Waiting {} s on a firmware timer event...", TIMER_CHECK.as_secs());

    // SAFETY: no notification function, so no callback can run with a bad
    // context pointer.
    let event = match unsafe { boot::create_event(EventType::TIMER, Tpl::APPLICATION, None, None) } {
        Ok(event) => event,
        Err(error) => {
            log!("Firmware timer event not created: {:?}.", error.status());
            return;
        }
    };

    let mut events = [event];
    if let Err(error) = boot::set_timer(&events[0], TimerTrigger::Relative(TIMER_CHECK)) {
        log!("Firmware timer not armed: {:?}.", error.status());
    } else if let Err(error) = boot::wait_for_event(&mut events) {
        log!("Waiting on the firmware timer failed: {:?}.", error.status());
    } else {
        log!("Firmware timer fired: interrupts reach the firmware again.");
    }

    let [event] = events;
    if let Err(error) = boot::close_event(event) {
        log!("Firmware timer event not closed: {:?}.", error.status());
    }
}

`src/output.rs`:

```rs
//! Where output may go, and what happens when the hypervisor panics.
//!
//! # Why Aleph0 has its own panic handler
//!
//! The `uefi` crate's handler (its `panic_handler` feature) prints with
//! `uefi::println!`, then calls `boot::stall` and `runtime::reset`: three
//! firmware calls. A panic inside the VM-exit handler would then enter
//! firmware from exit context, where interrupts are off and the firmware's
//! state is whatever the guest left behind. After `ExitBootServices` the
//! message would be lost entirely.
//!
//! This handler prints over serial first (no firmware needed), then on the
//! console, then halts the CPU. It never stalls, resets, or otherwise calls
//! into firmware.
//!
//! Host unit tests link `std`, which brings its own panic handler; two would
//! not link, so the handler and its state are compiled out under `cfg(test)`.

#[cfg(not(test))]
use core::sync::atomic::AtomicBool;
use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicU8, Ordering};

/// Set by the first panic. A second panic, raised while the first is still
/// printing (for example from a `Display` impl or the console driver), sees
/// `true` and halts at once instead of recursing forever.
#[cfg(not(test))]
static PANICKING: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);

/// Reports a panic and stops this CPU for good.
///
/// Runs in any context: ordinary UEFI code, the VM-exit handler, and later
/// after `ExitBootServices`. It must therefore not depend on firmware for
/// anything it needs to get the message out.
#[cfg(not(test))]
#[panic_handler]
fn panic(info: &core::panic::PanicInfo) -> ! {
    // `swap` reads the old value and stores `true` in one indivisible step,
    // so exactly one panic gets `false` back and goes on to print. That
    // guarantee comes from atomicity alone; the flag guards no other data,
    // so `Relaxed` would be enough and `SeqCst` is just the strictest choice.
    if PANICKING.swap(true, Ordering::SeqCst) {
        halt_forever();
    }

    // Serial first: it needs no firmware, so the message is already on serial
    // if the console call below hangs or faults. `PanicInfo`'s `Display`
    // prints "panicked at FILE:LINE:COL:" followed by the message.
    crate::serial_println!("{} PANIC: {info}", crate::TAG);
    // What led here, if the guest ran: its last VM exits. After the message,
    // so the message is out even if this goes wrong.
    crate::vmx::vmexit::report_exit_history(format_args!("PANIC"));

    // Firmware console: only in the boot-services phase. In the VM-exit
    // handler or after `ExitBootServices` the message goes to serial alone.
    if console_allowed() {
        uefi::println!("{} PANIC: {info}", crate::TAG);
    }

    halt_forever();
}

/// Stops this CPU permanently, with interrupts disabled.
///
/// Used wherever execution must end without firmware help: after a panic,
/// after an exception in VMX root operation (`vmx::host`), and after a stop
/// of the firmware guest, which has nothing to return to. The test guest's
/// stop does not halt; the VM-exit handler hands it back to bring-up.
///
/// * `CLI` clears RFLAGS.IF, so maskable interrupts (timer, devices) are no
///   longer delivered. During boot services UEFI runs with interrupts on and
///   its timer fires regularly; without CLI, firmware interrupt handlers
///   would keep running. After a VM exit IF is already 0 (host RFLAGS is
///   loaded as 0x2), so there CLI only makes sure.
/// * `HLT` stops executing until an interrupt arrives. With IF = 0 only
///   non-maskable events wake it: NMI, SMI, machine check, INIT/reset.
/// * After an NMI handler returns, execution continues after `HLT`; the loop
///   sends it straight back to `CLI; HLT`.
///
/// `HLT` instead of an empty `loop {}`: a busy loop keeps the core at 100%,
/// while under Hyper-V a `HLT` is itself a VM exit that lets Hyper-V
/// deschedule the vCPU, so a halted Aleph0 costs the host no CPU time.
///
/// `-> !` ("never") tells the compiler this function does not return, which
/// is what lets the panic handler end with a call to it.
pub fn halt_forever() -> ! {
    loop {
        // SAFETY: CLI and HLT only stop this CPU, which is what this
        // function is for; they touch no memory (`nomem`) and no stack
        // (`nostack`). `preserves_flags` is deliberately absent, because CLI
        // changes RFLAGS.
        unsafe { core::arch::asm!("cli", "hlt", options(nomem, nostack)) };
    }
}

/// Which context the hypervisor is running in, as far as output is concerned.
///
/// `#[repr(u8)]` with explicit values makes `phase as u8` a fixed number, so
/// the phase can live in an [`AtomicU8`].
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[repr(u8)]
pub enum Phase {
    /// Ordinary UEFI code before `ExitBootServices`: `main` and bring-up,
    /// and again once teardown has left VMX operation. The only phase in
    /// which the firmware console may be used.
    BootServices = 0,
    /// After `ExitBootServices`: the firmware console is gone and the OS
    /// owns the machine. The exit handler sets it for good at the VMCALL of
    /// Aleph0's `ExitBootServices` event (`resident`).
    Runtime = 1,
    /// The VM-exit handler, which puts the phase it found back when it
    /// resumes the guest (in place, the guest is Aleph0's own code too, which
    /// may use the console again); after a stop that returns to bring-up,
    /// bring-up until teardown has left VMX operation. Interrupts off,
    /// firmware state unknown.
    VmExit = 2,
}

impl Phase {
    /// The phase stored as `value`.
    fn from_u8(value: u8) -> Self {
        match value {
            0 => Self::BootServices,
            1 => Self::Runtime,
            _ => Self::VmExit,
        }
    }
}

/// The current [`Phase`], stored as its `u8` value. Starts in boot services,
/// because that is where `main` begins.
///
/// `SeqCst` below is stronger than needed: the phase guards no other data and
/// only one CPU runs this code, so `Relaxed` would do.
static PHASE: AtomicU8 = AtomicU8::new(Phase::BootServices as u8);

/// Switches the output phase, and returns the one it replaces; later `log!`
/// lines and panics follow it.
pub fn set_phase(phase: Phase) -> Phase {
    Phase::from_u8(PHASE.swap(phase as u8, Ordering::SeqCst))
}

/// Whether the firmware console may be used right now.
fn console_allowed() -> bool {
    PHASE.load(Ordering::SeqCst) == Phase::BootServices as u8
}

/// Implementation of the `log!` macro in `main.rs`. Taking `Arguments` means
/// the caller's expressions are evaluated once, then formatted once per
/// destination.
///
/// Serial is written in every phase. The firmware console only in
/// [`Phase::BootServices`]; elsewhere calling it is unsafe (VM-exit handler)
/// or pointless (after `ExitBootServices` it silently prints nothing).
pub fn log_line(args: core::fmt::Arguments) {
    let tag = crate::TAG;
    if console_allowed() {
        uefi::println!("{tag} {args}");
    }
    crate::serial_println!("{tag} {args}");
}

`src/port.rs`:

```rs
//! Port I/O: the `in` and `out` instructions, 1, 2 and 4 bytes wide.
//!
//! Used by the serial driver (`serial.rs`) and by the VM-exit handler, which
//! runs a guest's intercepted IN/OUT for it. Background: `docs/PORT_IO.md`.
//!
//! The `asm!` options are promises to the compiler:
//! - `nostack`: the instruction does not push or pop;
//! - `preserves_flags`: `in`/`out` do not change RFLAGS;
//! - `nomem`: the instruction does not read or write memory, so the compiler
//!   may move ordinary memory accesses across it. True for the UART, which
//!   never touches RAM. Do NOT copy `nomem` into port I/O for a DMA device
//!   (one that reads a buffer in RAM after an `out` command): the compiler
//!   could then move the buffer writes after the command. The guest's IN/OUT
//!   are emulated with these functions too; they reach no RAM through Aleph0
//!   (string I/O stops the guest instead).

use core::arch::asm;

/// Writes one byte to an I/O port: `out dx, al`.
///
/// `in("dx") port` loads the 16-bit port number into DX and `in("al") value`
/// loads the byte into AL before the instruction runs; the CPU then sends an
/// I/O write for that port to the chipset.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// Port writes reach hardware directly; the port must belong to a device
/// the caller owns, or be one a guest asked to write.
pub unsafe fn outb(port: u16, value: u8) {
    // SAFETY: OUT touches only the I/O port, which the caller guarantees it
    // may write.
    unsafe { asm!("out dx, al", in("dx") port, in("al") value, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) }
}

/// Writes two bytes to an I/O port: `out dx, ax`.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// As for [`outb`].
pub unsafe fn outw(port: u16, value: u16) {
    // SAFETY: as for `outb`.
    unsafe { asm!("out dx, ax", in("dx") port, in("ax") value, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) }
}

/// Writes four bytes to an I/O port: `out dx, eax`.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// As for [`outb`].
pub unsafe fn outl(port: u16, value: u32) {
    // SAFETY: as for `outb`.
    unsafe { asm!("out dx, eax", in("dx") port, in("eax") value, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) }
}

/// Reads one byte from an I/O port: `in al, dx`.
///
/// `in("dx") port` loads the port number into DX; afterwards `out("al")`
/// copies the byte the device returned from AL into `value`. A port no
/// device claims reads as `0xFF`.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// Some device registers change state when read (reading the UART's data
/// register removes the received byte); the port must belong to a device
/// the caller owns, or be one a guest asked to read.
pub unsafe fn inb(port: u16) -> u8 {
    let value: u8;
    // SAFETY: IN touches only the I/O port, which the caller guarantees it
    // may read.
    unsafe { asm!("in al, dx", out("al") value, in("dx") port, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) }
    value
}

/// Reads two bytes from an I/O port: `in ax, dx`.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// As for [`inb`].
pub unsafe fn inw(port: u16) -> u16 {
    let value: u16;
    // SAFETY: as for `inb`.
    unsafe { asm!("in ax, dx", out("ax") value, in("dx") port, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) }
    value
}

/// Reads four bytes from an I/O port: `in eax, dx`.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// As for [`inb`].
pub unsafe fn inl(port: u16) -> u32 {
    let value: u32;
    // SAFETY: as for `inb`.
    unsafe { asm!("in eax, dx", out("eax") value, in("dx") port, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) }
    value
}

`src/resident/memory.rs`:

```rs
//! Which UEFI memory the OS may take for itself once `ExitBootServices`
//! has returned, after the UEFI spec's table "Memory Type Usage after
//! ExitBootServices()".
//!
//! Aleph0 checks every allocation it keeps against [`is_reclaimable`]
//! (`bring_up`), and the `ExitBootServices` test harness
//! (`tools/ebs-harness`) overwrites what it names, to show that nothing
//! Aleph0 needs is there. This file depends on nothing but `uefi`, because
//! the harness includes it too.

use uefi::boot::MemoryType;

/// Whether the OS may reuse memory of type `memory_type` as its own once
/// `ExitBootServices` has returned:
///
/// | Type | After `ExitBootServices` |
/// |---|---|
/// | `LOADER_CODE`, `LOADER_DATA` | the OS loader and the OS use it as they see fit |
/// | `BOOT_SERVICES_CODE`, `BOOT_SERVICES_DATA`, `CONVENTIONAL` | available for general use |
/// | `ACPI_RECLAIM` | general use once the OS has enabled ACPI |
/// | `PERSISTENT_MEMORY` | works as conventional memory that keeps its contents |
/// | `UNACCEPTED` | general use once the OS has accepted it |
///
/// Everything else is kept: `RESERVED`, `RUNTIME_SERVICES_CODE`,
/// `RUNTIME_SERVICES_DATA`, `ACPI_NON_VOLATILE` and `PAL_CODE`, which the OS
/// preserves, `UNUSABLE` memory, which it avoids, MMIO and MMIO port space,
/// which are not memory, and the OEM and OS-loader types (`0x7000_0000` and
/// up), whose use only their owner knows.
pub fn is_reclaimable(memory_type: MemoryType) -> bool {
    use MemoryType as Type;
    [
        Type::LOADER_CODE,
        Type::LOADER_DATA,
        Type::BOOT_SERVICES_CODE,
        Type::BOOT_SERVICES_DATA,
        Type::CONVENTIONAL,
        Type::ACPI_RECLAIM,
        Type::PERSISTENT_MEMORY,
        Type::UNACCEPTED,
    ]
    .contains(&memory_type)
}

`src/resident/mod.rs`:

```rs
//! Staying resident after `ExitBootServices`: what lets Aleph0 go on
//! handling VM exits once the OS owns the machine. docs/RESIDENT.md has the
//! whole design.
//!
//! - Its pages: everything Aleph0 keeps is allocated as a resident type
//!   (`vmx::page`), and bring-up checks each allocation's type in the
//!   memory map ([`memory_type_at`], [`memory::is_reclaimable`]).
//! - Its image: the firmware loads Aleph0 as an application, in
//!   `LOADER_CODE`, and unloads it when `main` returns. `main` therefore
//!   copies the image into resident code pages, applies its base
//!   relocations for the new address ([`pe`]), and runs everything else
//!   from the copy ([`ResidentImage`]): its code and its statics.
//! - Knowing when boot services end: an `EVT_SIGNAL_EXIT_BOOT_SERVICES`
//!   event, whose notify function lives in the copy, makes a VMCALL in the
//!   guest ([`watch_exit_boot_services`]); the exit handler then switches
//!   the output phase to runtime.

pub mod memory;
pub mod pe;

use core::arch::asm;
use core::ffi::c_void;
use core::ptr::NonNull;

use uefi::boot::{self, EventType, MemoryType, Tpl};
use uefi::proto::loaded_image::LoadedImage;
use uefi::{Event, Status};

use crate::vmx::page::{self, PAGE_SIZE, RESIDENT_CODE};
use crate::vmx::vmcall;
use pe::{Headers, PeError};

/// Why the image could not be copied.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum ImageError {
    /// The firmware's LoadedImage protocol for Aleph0's image could not be
    /// opened.
    LoadedImageUnavailable(Status),
    /// The image the firmware reports is smaller than its headers say.
    ImageTruncated { loaded: usize, size_of_image: usize },
    /// UEFI could not provide the pages for the copy.
    AllocationFailed,
    /// The headers or the base relocation table are not usable.
    Pe(PeError),
}

impl From<PeError> for ImageError {
    fn from(error: PeError) -> Self {
        Self::Pe(error)
    }
}

/// Aleph0's image, copied into [`RESIDENT_CODE`] pages and relocated for
/// its address there. The pages are never freed.
pub struct ResidentImage {
    /// Where the firmware loaded the image.
    loaded: u64,
    /// Where the copy is.
    base: u64,
    /// Bytes copied: the loaded image's size.
    size: usize,
    /// DIR64 fixups applied to the copy.
    fixups: usize,
}

impl ResidentImage {
    /// Copies the running image, statics included, into resident code
    /// pages, and applies its base relocations for the copy's address.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// Boot services must still be active, with memory identity-mapped.
    /// No static may hold an address inside the image that the code stored
    /// at run time: relocation moves only the addresses the linker listed,
    /// so such a value would still point into the loaded image in the copy.
    pub unsafe fn copy() -> Result<Self, ImageError> {
        let (loaded, size) = {
            let image = boot::open_protocol_exclusive::<LoadedImage>(boot::image_handle())
                .map_err(|error| ImageError::LoadedImageUnavailable(error.status()))?;
            let (base, size) = image.info();
            (base as u64, size as usize)
        };
        // SAFETY: the firmware loaded the image at `loaded`, `size` bytes,
        // and keeps it there until `main` returns; nothing writes it
        // concurrently.
        let image = unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts(loaded as *const u8, size) };
        let headers = Headers::parse(image)?;
        if headers.size_of_image > size {
            return Err(ImageError::ImageTruncated {
                loaded: size,
                size_of_image: headers.size_of_image,
            });
        }

        let base =
            page::allocate_zeroed_pages_of_type(size.div_ceil(PAGE_SIZE), RESIDENT_CODE, ImageError::AllocationFailed)?;
        // SAFETY: a fresh allocation of at least `size` bytes, which nothing
        // else refers to; never freed.
        let copy = unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(base.as_ptr(), size) };
        copy.copy_from_slice(image);
        let base = base.as_ptr() as u64;
        let fixups = pe::relocate(copy, headers.relocations, base.wrapping_sub(loaded))?;
        Ok(Self {
            loaded,
            base,
            size,
            fixups,
        })
    }

    /// Where the copy is.
    pub fn base(&self) -> u64 {
        self.base
    }

    /// Where the firmware loaded the image.
    pub fn loaded(&self) -> u64 {
        self.loaded
    }

    /// Bytes copied.
    pub fn size(&self) -> usize {
        self.size
    }

    /// DIR64 fixups applied to the copy.
    pub fn fixups(&self) -> usize {
        self.fixups
    }

    /// Calls the copy of `function`, a function of this image, and returns
    /// what it returns.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// `self` must come from [`ResidentImage::copy`] of this image. From
    /// the call on, the copy's statics are the live ones, so the caller must
    /// not rely on its own afterwards.
    pub unsafe fn call(&self, function: fn() -> Status) -> Status {
        let offset = (function as usize as u64).wrapping_sub(self.loaded);
        assert!(offset < self.size as u64, "the function is not in the image");
        // SAFETY: the copy holds this image byte for byte, relocated for its
        // address, so the same offset there is the same function, with the
        // same signature.
        let copied = unsafe { core::mem::transmute::<usize, fn() -> Status>((self.base + offset) as usize) };
        copied()
    }
}

/// The type of the memory-map region holding `address`, among `regions`
/// (start, pages, type), or `None` if no region holds it.
pub fn memory_type_at(mut regions: impl Iterator<Item = (u64, u64, MemoryType)>, address: u64) -> Option<MemoryType> {
    regions
        .find(|&(start, pages, _)| address >= start && address - start < pages.saturating_mul(PAGE_SIZE as u64))
        .map(|(_, _, memory_type)| memory_type)
}

/// Has the firmware call [`on_exit_boot_services`] during
/// `ExitBootServices`: the event that tells Aleph0 when boot services end.
///
/// The firmware calls it in the guest, from the copy, so this must run in
/// the resident image, and the event must be closed if the firmware never
/// becomes the guest: outside VMX operation its VMCALL would raise #UD.
pub fn watch_exit_boot_services() -> uefi::Result<Event> {
    // SAFETY: the notify function takes no context, and only makes its
    // VMCALL, which needs nothing from the firmware.
    unsafe {
        boot::create_event(
            EventType::SIGNAL_EXIT_BOOT_SERVICES,
            Tpl::CALLBACK,
            Some(on_exit_boot_services),
            None,
        )
    }
}

/// Called by the firmware inside `ExitBootServices`, in the guest: tells
/// Aleph0 with a VMCALL ([`vmcall::BOOT_SERVICES_ENDED`]), which it resumes
/// past (`ExitEvent::BootServicesEnded`).
unsafe extern "efiapi" fn on_exit_boot_services(_event: Event, _context: Option<NonNull<c_void>>) {
    // SAFETY: the event exists only while the firmware runs as Aleph0's
    // guest (bring-up closes it when the launch fails), so the VMCALL exits
    // to Aleph0, which changes no guest register for it and resumes past
    // it. It touches no memory and no stack.
    unsafe {
        asm!(
            "vmcall",
            inout("rcx") vmcall::BOOT_SERVICES_ENDED => _,
            options(nomem, nostack),
        );
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
#[path = "../../tests/unit/resident.rs"]
mod tests;

`src/resident/pe.rs`:

```rs
//! Base relocation of a loaded PE32+ image: what moving Aleph0's image to
//! another address needs (Microsoft PE format specification, "The .reloc
//! Section (Image Only)").
//!
//! The linker writes every absolute address in the image (a vtable entry,
//! a pointer in a static) for one base address, and lists where each one
//! is in the base relocation table. A loader that puts the image `delta`
//! bytes away from that base adds `delta` to each listed address. The
//! firmware did that when it loaded Aleph0, and `ResidentImage::copy` does
//! it again, from the loaded image to its copy.
//!
//! ```text
//! 0x00  "MZ"
//! 0x3C  offset of the PE signature ──▶ "PE\0\0"
//!                                      COFF file header, 20 bytes
//!                                      optional header, magic 0x20B (PE32+):
//!                                        +56   SizeOfImage
//!                                        +108  NumberOfRvaAndSizes
//!                                        +112  data directories, 8 bytes each;
//!                                              #5: base relocation table (RVA, size)
//!
//! base relocation table: one block per 4 KiB page that has fixups
//!   page RVA (4 bytes) │ block size (4 bytes) │ entries, 2 bytes each: type 15:12, offset 11:0
//!
//!   type 10 (DIR64):    add delta to the 8 bytes at page RVA + offset
//!   type 0 (ABSOLUTE):  nothing; pads the block
//! ```
//!
//! An RVA is an offset from the image's start: once loaded, every section
//! sits at its RVA. An x86-64 image has no fixup type but these two.

use core::ops::Range;

/// Why an image could not be relocated.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum PeError {
    /// The headers are not a PE32+ image's, or lie outside the image.
    NotPe32Plus,
    /// The image has no base relocation table, so it cannot move.
    NoRelocations,
    /// The base relocation table lies outside the image.
    TableOutsideImage,
    /// The block at `offset` in the table is shorter than its header, has
    /// an odd size, or runs past the table's end.
    BadBlock { offset: usize },
    /// The DIR64 fixup at `rva` would write outside the image.
    FixupOutsideImage { rva: usize },
    /// The entry for `rva` has a type other than DIR64 and ABSOLUTE.
    UnsupportedFixup { kind: u8, rva: usize },
}

/// "MZ": the DOS header every PE image starts with.
const DOS_MAGIC: &[u8] = b"MZ";
/// Offset of the field holding the PE signature's offset.
const PE_OFFSET_FIELD: usize = 0x3C;
const PE_SIGNATURE: &[u8] = b"PE\0\0";
const COFF_HEADER_SIZE: usize = 20;
/// The optional header's magic for a PE32+ (64-bit) image.
const PE32_PLUS_MAGIC: u16 = 0x20B;
// Offsets in the PE32+ optional header.
const SIZE_OF_IMAGE: usize = 56;
const NUMBER_OF_RVA_AND_SIZES: usize = 108;
const DATA_DIRECTORIES: usize = 112;
/// Data directory #5: the base relocation table.
const BASE_RELOCATION_DIRECTORY: usize = 5;
const DATA_DIRECTORY_SIZE: usize = 8;
/// A block's page RVA and size.
const BLOCK_HEADER_SIZE: usize = 8;
const FIXUP_ABSOLUTE: u8 = 0;
const FIXUP_DIR64: u8 = 10;

/// What relocating a loaded image needs from its headers.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Headers {
    /// SizeOfImage: how many bytes the loaded image takes.
    pub size_of_image: usize,
    /// Where the base relocation table lies in the loaded image.
    pub relocations: Range<usize>,
}

impl Headers {
    /// Reads the headers at the start of the loaded `image`.
    pub fn parse(image: &[u8]) -> Result<Self, PeError> {
        if image.get(..DOS_MAGIC.len()) != Some(DOS_MAGIC) {
            return Err(PeError::NotPe32Plus);
        }
        let signature = read_u32(image, PE_OFFSET_FIELD).ok_or(PeError::NotPe32Plus)? as usize;
        if image.get(signature..signature.saturating_add(PE_SIGNATURE.len())) != Some(PE_SIGNATURE) {
            return Err(PeError::NotPe32Plus);
        }
        let optional = signature + PE_SIGNATURE.len() + COFF_HEADER_SIZE;
        if read_u16(image, optional) != Some(PE32_PLUS_MAGIC) {
            return Err(PeError::NotPe32Plus);
        }
        let size_of_image = read_u32(image, optional + SIZE_OF_IMAGE).ok_or(PeError::NotPe32Plus)? as usize;
        let directories = read_u32(image, optional + NUMBER_OF_RVA_AND_SIZES).ok_or(PeError::NotPe32Plus)? as usize;
        if directories <= BASE_RELOCATION_DIRECTORY {
            return Err(PeError::NoRelocations);
        }
        let directory = optional + DATA_DIRECTORIES + BASE_RELOCATION_DIRECTORY * DATA_DIRECTORY_SIZE;
        let rva = read_u32(image, directory).ok_or(PeError::NotPe32Plus)? as usize;
        let size = read_u32(image, directory + 4).ok_or(PeError::NotPe32Plus)? as usize;
        if size == 0 {
            return Err(PeError::NoRelocations);
        }
        let relocations = rva..rva + size;
        if relocations.end > image.len() {
            return Err(PeError::TableOutsideImage);
        }
        Ok(Self {
            size_of_image,
            relocations,
        })
    }
}

/// Adds `delta` to every DIR64 fixup the base relocation table at `table`
/// lists in the loaded `image`, and returns how many there were.
///
/// On an error the image is left partly relocated, so it must not run.
pub fn relocate(image: &mut [u8], table: Range<usize>, delta: u64) -> Result<usize, PeError> {
    let mut fixups = 0;
    let mut block = table.start;
    while block < table.end {
        let bad_block = PeError::BadBlock {
            offset: block - table.start,
        };
        let page = read_u32(image, block).ok_or(bad_block)? as usize;
        let size = read_u32(image, block + 4).ok_or(bad_block)? as usize;
        if size < BLOCK_HEADER_SIZE || !size.is_multiple_of(2) || size > table.end - block {
            return Err(bad_block);
        }
        for entry in (block + BLOCK_HEADER_SIZE..block + size).step_by(2) {
            let entry = read_u16(image, entry).ok_or(bad_block)?;
            let rva = page + usize::from(entry & 0xFFF);
            match (entry >> 12) as u8 {
                FIXUP_ABSOLUTE => {}
                FIXUP_DIR64 => {
                    let address = read(image, rva)
                        .map(u64::from_le_bytes)
                        .ok_or(PeError::FixupOutsideImage { rva })?;
                    // In bounds: `read` just read these 8 bytes.
                    image[rva..rva + size_of::<u64>()].copy_from_slice(&address.wrapping_add(delta).to_le_bytes());
                    fixups += 1;
                }
                kind => return Err(PeError::UnsupportedFixup { kind, rva }),
            }
        }
        block += size;
    }
    Ok(fixups)
}

/// The `N` bytes at `offset` in `bytes`, if they are all there.
fn read<const N: usize>(bytes: &[u8], offset: usize) -> Option<[u8; N]> {
    bytes.get(offset..offset.checked_add(N)?)?.try_into().ok()
}

fn read_u16(bytes: &[u8], offset: usize) -> Option<u16> {
    read(bytes, offset).map(u16::from_le_bytes)
}

fn read_u32(bytes: &[u8], offset: usize) -> Option<u32> {
    read(bytes, offset).map(u32::from_le_bytes)
}

#[cfg(test)]
#[path = "../../tests/unit/resident/pe.rs"]
mod tests;

`src/serial.rs`:

```rs
//! Firmware-independent debug output over a serial port: COM2, so COM1
//! stays free for the guest.
//!
//! Further reading, kept in the repository so it is not forgotten:
//!
//! * `docs/SERIAL_LOGGING.md`: a beginner walkthrough of this file. Its
//!   step numbers match the `Step N` comments below.
//! * `docs/PORT_IO.md`: how `in`/`out` and the 16-bit I/O port space work,
//!   and how a hypervisor intercepts them.
//!
//! # Why not `uefi::println!`?
//!
//! `uefi::println!` calls the firmware's console driver. That is fine in
//! `main`, but this hypervisor will soon print from places where calling
//! firmware is unsafe or impossible:
//!
//! * the VM-exit handler, which runs with interrupts off, on its own stack,
//!   in the middle of whatever the firmware was doing when the guest started;
//! * anything after `ExitBootServices`, when the firmware console is gone.
//!
//! This module drives the serial hardware directly with `in`/`out`
//! instructions. It needs no allocator, no firmware, no interrupts and no
//! locks, so it works in every one of those contexts. Every VMM (QEMU,
//! Hyper-V, VMware, Bochs) emulates this device, which is why it is the
//! standard debug channel for OS and hypervisor work.
//!
//! # The device: a 16550 UART
//!
//! A UART turns bytes into a bit stream on a wire. A PC has its UARTs at
//! fixed I/O port bases, `0x3F8` for COM1 and `0x2F8` for COM2, and each
//! exposes eight byte-wide registers at `base + 0` through `base + 7`
//! ([`SerialPort`]). Aleph0 writes to COM2: the guest OS will want COM1 for
//! its own console (Linux's `ttyS0`), and two writers on one UART would
//! interleave their output.
//!
//! # Port I/O in short
//!
//! x86 has two address spaces. Memory is reached with ordinary instructions
//! (`mov`). The **I/O space** is separate and **16 bits wide**: port numbers
//! run from `0x0000` to `0xFFFF` (65,536 ports, one byte each), and only the
//! `in`/`out` instructions reach it. Port `0x3F8` and memory address `0x3F8`
//! are unrelated.
//!
//! * `out dx, al` sends the byte in AL to the port numbered by DX;
//!   `in al, dx` reads a byte from port DX into AL.
//! * The port must be in DX here: the other form, with the port written
//!   into the instruction, only reaches ports `0x00`–`0xFF`, and the UARTs
//!   are above that.
//! * Data can be 8, 16 or 32 bits (AL, AX, EAX). The UART's registers are
//!   all 8-bit, so this file only uses byte access ([`outb`], [`inb`]).
//! * The CPU sends the access to the chipset as an I/O transaction, and the
//!   device that claims that port answers. No device means a read of `0xFF`.
//! * Ports are not memory: a read can change device state, and writing and
//!   reading the same port can reach two different registers.
//! * Ring 0 may use any port; this code always runs at ring 0.
//!
//! Under Hyper-V, every `in`/`out` here causes a VM exit (reason 30) and
//! Hyper-V's emulated UART answers. Details: `docs/PORT_IO.md`.
//!
//! The registers used here, by offset from the base:
//!
//! | Offset | DLAB=0 (normal)         | DLAB=1 (setup)          |
//! |--------|-------------------------|-------------------------|
//! | 0      | transmit/receive byte   | divisor latch, low byte |
//! | 1      | interrupt enable        | divisor latch, high byte|
//! | 2      | FIFO control (write)    |                         |
//! | 3      | line control; bit 7 is DLAB                       |
//! | 4      | modem control; bit 4 is loopback                  |
//! | 5      | line status; bit 5 = ready for another byte       |
//!
//! DLAB ("divisor latch access bit") reuses offsets 0 and 1 for the baud
//! divisor while it is set. The UART clock runs at 115200 × 16 Hz, so the
//! divisor is `115200 / baud`; 1 selects the maximum, 115200 baud. Virtual
//! UARTs ignore the speed entirely, but real ones and terminal software
//! expect the usual "115200 8N1": 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit.
//!
//! # Sending a byte
//!
//! Poll line status bit 5 ("transmit holding register empty") until it is
//! set, then write the byte to offset 0. That is all [`write_byte`] does. The
//! poll is bounded, so a missing or wedged UART slows output down instead
//! of hanging the hypervisor.
//!
//! # Seeing the output
//!
//! * QEMU: `scripts/run.ps1` sends COM2 to `run\qemu-serial.log` and COM1
//!   to the terminal. OVMF mirrors its console to every serial port, so on
//!   COM2 each `log!` line would show twice; COM1 shows it once.
//! * Hyper-V: `scripts/run-hyperv.ps1` attaches COM2 to the named pipe
//!   `aleph0-com2` and COM1 to `aleph0-com1`, and reads both; see that
//!   script and the README.
//!
//! # Concurrency
//!
//! There is no lock. That is sound while exactly one CPU runs this code and
//! nothing interrupts a print with another print: true today, because the
//! exit handler runs with interrupts off and only between guest instructions.
//! Once several vCPUs exist, output needs a spinlock (not one that can
//! deadlock if an exit handler interrupts its own holder).

use core::fmt;
use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicU16, Ordering};

use crate::port::{inb, outb};

// Step 1: where the chip lives. COM2 claims the 8 ports 0x2F8..=0x2FF and
// uses the low 3 bits of the port number to pick one of its registers.

/// A 16550 UART, named by the I/O port base its eight registers start at.
/// A `u16` because port numbers are 16-bit.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct SerialPort(u16);

impl SerialPort {
    /// COM1, ports `0x3F8..=0x3FF`: the guest's. The test guest's
    /// port-I/O test uses its scratch register.
    pub const COM1: Self = Self(0x3F8);
    /// COM2, ports `0x2F8..=0x2FF`: Aleph0's own output.
    pub const COM2: Self = Self(0x2F8);

    /// The first of the eight ports.
    pub const fn base(self) -> u16 {
        self.0
    }

    /// The port of the register at `offset` (0 to 7) from the base.
    const fn register(self, offset: u16) -> u16 {
        self.0 + offset
    }
}

impl fmt::Display for SerialPort {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match *self {
            Self::COM1 => write!(f, "COM1 ({:#x})", self.0),
            Self::COM2 => write!(f, "COM2 ({:#x})", self.0),
            Self(base) => write!(f, "the UART at {base:#x}"),
        }
    }
}

/// Register offsets from the port base. See the module table.
/// Offset 0 is two registers: writing it sends a byte, reading it receives.
const DATA: u16 = 0;
const INTERRUPT_ENABLE: u16 = 1;
const FIFO_CONTROL: u16 = 2;
const LINE_CONTROL: u16 = 3;
const MODEM_CONTROL: u16 = 4;
const LINE_STATUS: u16 = 5;

/// Line control: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit.
const LINE_8N1: u8 = 0b0000_0011;
/// Line control bit 7: offsets 0 and 1 address the baud divisor.
const LINE_DLAB: u8 = 1 << 7;
/// FIFO control: enable FIFOs, clear both, 14-byte receive threshold.
const FIFO_ENABLE_AND_CLEAR: u8 = 0b1100_0111;
/// Modem control: DTR + RTS + OUT2, the normal "ready" state.
const MODEM_READY: u8 = 0b0000_1011;
/// Modem control bit 4: internal loopback, transmitted bytes are received.
const MODEM_LOOPBACK: u8 = 1 << 4;
/// Line status bit 0: a received byte is waiting.
const STATUS_DATA_READY: u8 = 1 << 0;
/// Line status bit 5: the transmit register can take another byte.
const STATUS_TRANSMIT_EMPTY: u8 = 1 << 5;

/// Polls before giving up on a byte. Virtual UARTs are ready immediately;
/// this only bounds the wait when the device is missing or stuck.
const SPIN_LIMIT: u32 = 100_000;

/// Set once [`init`] has found a working UART. Writes before that, or
/// after a failed init, are dropped instead of touching an unknown device.
static READY: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);

/// The base of the UART [`init`] found, which [`write_byte`] writes to. Set
/// before [`READY`], so a writer that sees `READY` also sees it.
static PORT: AtomicU16 = AtomicU16::new(0);

/// Baud-rate divisor for the 115200 Hz UART reference rate.
pub const fn divisor(baud: u32) -> u16 {
    (115_200 / baud) as u16
}

// Step 0: the only two ways this driver touches hardware are
// `port::outb` and `port::inb` (`src/port.rs`). Everything else in the file
// is calls to these.

/// Why [`init`] did not enable serial output.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum SerialError {
    /// The loopback test did not return the byte it sent: no UART at this
    /// port, or one that does not behave like a 16550.
    LoopbackFailed,
}

/// Programs `port` for 115200 8N1 with polling (no interrupts), then proves
/// a UART is really there with a loopback test before sending output to it.
/// If the test fails, output stays off: it never falls back to another port.
///
/// Safe to call more than once; firmware may already have configured the
/// same port, and reprogramming it with the same settings is harmless.
pub fn init(port: SerialPort) -> Result<(), SerialError> {
    let [divisor_low, divisor_high] = divisor(115_200).to_le_bytes();
    let register = |offset| port.register(offset);

    // SAFETY: every port below is a register of `port`, the UART this
    // driver is given to own.
    unsafe {
        // Step 2a: no UART interrupts. This driver polls the status
        // register instead, and no interrupt handler exists.
        outb(register(INTERRUPT_ENABLE), 0);

        // Step 2b: set the speed. Baud = bits per second on the wire, and
        // the chip produces it as 115200 / divisor. The divisor is 16 bits,
        // split across offsets 0 (low) and 1 (high), which only hold it
        // while DLAB (line control bit 7) is set, like holding Shift.
        outb(register(LINE_CONTROL), LINE_DLAB); // 0b1000_0000: DLAB on
        outb(register(DATA), divisor_low); // offset 0 = divisor low
        outb(register(INTERRUPT_ENABLE), divisor_high); // offset 1 = divisor high

        // Step 2c: frame format 8N1 (8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit).
        // Writing 0b0000_0011 also clears bit 7, turning DLAB off, so
        // offsets 0/1 are data and interrupt enable again. Forgetting this
        // is the classic bug: every "send" would change the speed instead.
        outb(register(LINE_CONTROL), LINE_8N1);

        // Step 2d: enable and empty the 16-byte transmit/receive queues.
        outb(register(FIFO_CONTROL), FIFO_ENABLE_AND_CLEAR);

        // Step 3: prove a UART is here. Loopback makes the chip feed its
        // transmitter into its own receiver, so a byte written must come
        // straight back. A port no device claims reads as 0xFF and fails
        // this check. Nothing leaves the chip while loopback is on.
        const PROBE: u8 = 0xAE;
        outb(register(MODEM_CONTROL), MODEM_READY | MODEM_LOOPBACK);
        outb(register(DATA), PROBE);
        let mut received = None;
        for _ in 0..SPIN_LIMIT {
            if inb(register(LINE_STATUS)) & STATUS_DATA_READY != 0 {
                received = Some(inb(register(DATA)));
                break;
            }
        }

        // End of step 3, and step 2e: leave loopback whatever the result
        // and signal "ready" (DTR + RTS + OUT2). Step 2e lives here because
        // the loopback test also writes modem control. From here on, bytes
        // leave the chip normally, and the firmware's own console driver
        // can use the port again.
        outb(register(MODEM_CONTROL), MODEM_READY);

        if received != Some(PROBE) {
            return Err(SerialError::LoopbackFailed);
        }
    }

    PORT.store(port.base(), Ordering::Relaxed);
    READY.store(true, Ordering::Release);
    Ok(())
}

/// Sends one byte, waiting (boundedly) for the transmitter.
/// Does nothing until [`init`] has succeeded.
///
/// Step 4. Line status bit 5 is a light the chip controls: writing a byte
/// turns it off (busy), and the chip turns it back on by itself once it has
/// taken the byte. Reading the status only looks at the light; it does not
/// make the chip ready. Under Hyper-V the light is back on instantly.
pub fn write_byte(byte: u8) {
    if !READY.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
        return;
    }

    let port = SerialPort(PORT.load(Ordering::Relaxed));
    // SAFETY: the status and data registers of the UART this driver owns;
    // `init` found it there.
    unsafe {
        // Wait for "can take a byte", but never forever: a missing or
        // stuck UART must not hang the hypervisor.
        for _ in 0..SPIN_LIMIT {
            if inb(port.register(LINE_STATUS)) & STATUS_TRANSMIT_EMPTY != 0 {
                break;
            }
        }
        outb(port.register(DATA), byte);
    }
}

/// Sends a string, expanding `\n` to `\r\n`: terminals need the carriage
/// return to move back to column 0.
///
/// Step 5: a string is only bytes, so this is [`write_byte`] in a loop.
pub fn write_str(text: &str) {
    for byte in text.bytes() {
        if byte == b'\n' {
            write_byte(b'\r');
        }
        write_byte(byte);
    }
}

/// Zero-sized handle that lets `core::fmt` format straight to the port,
/// with no buffer or allocation.
///
/// Step 6: `core::fmt` can write to anything implementing `fmt::Write`.
/// It hands over the formatted output in pieces as it produces them, and
/// each piece goes straight to [`write_str`]. No heap is needed, which is
/// why `serial_println!` is safe in the VM-exit handler.
pub struct Serial;

impl fmt::Write for Serial {
    fn write_str(&mut self, text: &str) -> fmt::Result {
        write_str(text);
        Ok(())
    }
}

/// Implementation detail of [`serial_print!`] and [`serial_println!`].
#[doc(hidden)]
pub fn _print(args: fmt::Arguments) {
    // Serial never reports an error, so the result carries no information.
    let _ = fmt::Write::write_fmt(&mut Serial, args);
}

/// Like `print!`, but to the serial port only. Safe in the VM-exit handler.
#[macro_export]
macro_rules! serial_print {
    ($($arg:tt)*) => {
        $crate::serial::_print(format_args!($($arg)*))
    };
}

/// Like `println!`, but to the serial port only. Safe in the VM-exit handler.
#[macro_export]
macro_rules! serial_println {
    () => {
        $crate::serial::write_str("\n")
    };
    ($($arg:tt)*) => {{
        $crate::serial::_print(format_args!($($arg)*));
        $crate::serial::write_str("\n");
    }};
}

#[path = "../tests/unit/serial.rs"]

`src/vmx/apic.rs`:

```rs
//! The Local APIC, as far as Aleph0 needs it: where IA32_APIC_BASE puts its
//! registers, which mode it is in, and the register the test guest reads.
//!
//! In xAPIC mode the registers are a 4 KiB page of MMIO at the base
//! address, `0xFEE00000` unless firmware moved it: device memory outside
//! RAM, which EPT maps UC to itself (`ept::MapLayout`). In x2APIC mode they
//! are MSRs instead, and the page decodes nothing (Intel SDM Vol. 3A, "Local
//! APIC Status and Location" and "x2APIC Mode").

use core::fmt;
use core::ops::RangeInclusive;

use super::ept::WalkEnd;
use super::mtrr::MemoryType;
use super::paging::{Mapping, WalkError};

/// IA32_APIC_BASE: the Local APIC's base address and mode.
pub const IA32_APIC_BASE: u32 = 0x1B;
/// IA32_APIC_BASE bit 8: this CPU is the bootstrap processor.
const APIC_BASE_BSP: u64 = 1 << 8;
/// IA32_APIC_BASE bits 11:10, EN and EXTD: the mode ([`LapicMode`]).
pub const APIC_BASE_MODE: u64 = 0b11 << 10;
/// [`APIC_BASE_MODE`] in xAPIC mode: EN = 1, EXTD = 0.
pub const APIC_BASE_XAPIC: u64 = 0b10 << 10;
/// [`APIC_BASE_MODE`] in x2APIC mode: EN = 1, EXTD = 1.
const APIC_BASE_X2APIC: u64 = 0b11 << 10;
/// [`APIC_BASE_MODE`] with the Local APIC off: EN = 0, EXTD = 0.
const APIC_BASE_DISABLED: u64 = 0;

/// Offset of the version register in the xAPIC's register page.
pub const LAPIC_VERSION: u64 = 0x30;
/// Bits 7:0 of the version register on an integrated APIC, which every
/// CPU since the Pentium has (Intel SDM Vol. 3A, "Local APIC Version
/// Register"). A read of nothing gives `0xFF`, outside the range.
pub const INTEGRATED_APIC_VERSIONS: RangeInclusive<u8> = 0x10..=0x15;

/// The mode bits 11:10 of IA32_APIC_BASE set, named as KVM's `enum
/// lapic_mode` names them.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum LapicMode {
    Disabled,
    /// The registers are the MMIO page at the base address.
    Xapic,
    /// The registers are MSRs; the MMIO page decodes nothing.
    X2apic,
    /// EXTD without EN, which the CPU never takes.
    Invalid,
}

impl LapicMode {
    pub fn name(self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::Disabled => "disabled",
            Self::Xapic => "xAPIC",
            Self::X2apic => "x2APIC",
            Self::Invalid => "invalid mode",
        }
    }
}

/// An IA32_APIC_BASE value.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct ApicBase(pub u64);

impl ApicBase {
    /// The physical address of the register page, bits MAXPHYADDR-1:12 on a
    /// CPU with `physical_address_bits` (MAXPHYADDR).
    pub fn address(self, physical_address_bits: u8) -> u64 {
        let below_maxphyaddr = u64::MAX
            .checked_shr(64u32.saturating_sub(physical_address_bits.into()))
            .unwrap_or(0);
        self.0 & below_maxphyaddr & !0xFFF
    }

    pub fn mode(self) -> LapicMode {
        match self.0 & APIC_BASE_MODE {
            APIC_BASE_DISABLED => LapicMode::Disabled,
            APIC_BASE_XAPIC => LapicMode::Xapic,
            APIC_BASE_X2APIC => LapicMode::X2apic,
            _ => LapicMode::Invalid,
        }
    }

    /// Whether this CPU is the bootstrap processor (bit 8).
    pub fn bsp(self) -> bool {
        self.0 & APIC_BASE_BSP != 0
    }
}

impl fmt::Display for ApicBase {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "{:#x} ({}", self.0, self.mode().name())?;
        if self.bsp() {
            f.write_str(", BSP")?;
        }
        f.write_str(")")
    }
}

/// Why the test guest could not read the Local APIC's registers, in xAPIC
/// mode.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum LocalApicError {
    /// The page tables the guest shares with bring-up do not map the
    /// register page at `address` to itself: how they translate it instead.
    GuestMapping {
        address: u64,
        translation: Result<Mapping, WalkError>,
    },
    /// EPT does not map the register page at `address` to itself, UC: how
    /// the walk of it ended instead.
    EptMapping { address: u64, end: WalkEnd },
}

/// Checks that the test guest can read the registers of a Local APIC in
/// xAPIC mode, at `address`: the guest's page tables translating the page
/// to itself (`translation`, as `paging::walk_current` gives it), since the
/// guest reads it through that linear address, and EPT mapping it to
/// itself, UC, readable, as the walk of it ended (`walk_end`). In any other
/// mode there is no register page, and the guest skips its read.
pub fn check_registers(
    address: u64,
    translation: Result<Mapping, WalkError>,
    walk_end: WalkEnd,
) -> Result<(), LocalApicError> {
    if translation.map(|mapping| mapping.physical) != Ok(address) {
        return Err(LocalApicError::GuestMapping { address, translation });
    }
    match walk_end {
        WalkEnd::Mapped {
            hpa,
            memory_type: MemoryType::Uncacheable,
            access,
            ..
        } if hpa == address && access & super::ept::EPT_READ != 0 => Ok(()),
        end => Err(LocalApicError::EptMapping { address, end }),
    }
}

`src/vmx/context_tables.rs`:

```rs
//! The GDT and TSS the firmware context runs on, and the TSS layout both
//! TSSs share.
//!
//! Firmware may leave TR unset (Hyper-V's does), but the guest state copies
//! TR, and VM entry refuses a guest TR that is not usable. So Aleph0 copies
//! the firmware's GDT into a page of its own, appends a 64-bit TSS
//! descriptor, and loads both ([`GdtRegion::activate`]). Bring-up and the
//! test guest run on them.
//!
//! VMX root operation does not: every VM exit loads Aleph0's own GDT, TSS
//! and IDT (`vmx::host`), whose TSS comes from
//! [`TssRegion::allocate_with_interrupt_stacks`].
//!
//! This TSS's stack fields (RSP0-2, IST1-7) stay 0: the firmware context
//! never changes privilege level, and `activate` refuses an IDT with a gate
//! that would switch to an IST stack.

use crate::vmx::segment::{
    self, DescriptorTable, GATE_IST_MASK, GATE_SIZE, SegmentDescriptor, descriptor_offset, read_cs, read_gdtr,
    read_idtr, read_ss, read_tr, segment_base_from_gdt, system_descriptor_base,
};
use core::{
    arch::asm,
    ptr::{NonNull, copy_nonoverlapping},
};
use uefi::boot;

use super::page::{PAGE_SIZE, allocate_zeroed_page};
/// The 64-bit TSS. In long mode it holds only stack pointers: RSP0-2 for a
/// change of privilege level, and IST1-7, the stacks an IDT gate can name.
#[repr(C, packed)]
pub(crate) struct Tss {
    reserved1: u32,
    rsp0: u64,
    rsp1: u64,
    rsp2: u64,
    reserved2: u64,
    ist1: u64,
    ist2: u64,
    ist3: u64,
    ist4: u64,
    ist5: u64,
    ist6: u64,
    ist7: u64,
    reserved3: u64,
    reserved4: u16,
    iomap_base: u16,
}

/// Bytes of a [`Tss`]; its descriptor's limit is one less (0x67).
pub(crate) const TSS_SIZE: usize = core::mem::size_of::<Tss>();

const _: () = {
    assert!(TSS_SIZE == 0x68);
    assert!(core::mem::offset_of!(Tss, rsp0) == 0x04);
    assert!(core::mem::offset_of!(Tss, ist1) == 0x24);
    assert!(core::mem::offset_of!(Tss, iomap_base) == 0x66);
};

impl Tss {
    /// A TSS whose IST1-IST7 fields hold `interrupt_stacks` (0 for an unused
    /// one), with RSP0-2 at 0, and the I/O-map base past the limit, so it has
    /// no I/O permission bitmap.
    pub(crate) fn new(interrupt_stacks: [u64; 7]) -> Self {
        let [ist1, ist2, ist3, ist4, ist5, ist6, ist7] = interrupt_stacks;
        Self {
            reserved1: 0,
            rsp0: 0,
            rsp1: 0,
            rsp2: 0,
            reserved2: 0,
            ist1,
            ist2,
            ist3,
            ist4,
            ist5,
            ist6,
            ist7,
            reserved3: 0,
            reserved4: 0,
            iomap_base: TSS_SIZE as u16,
        }
    }
}

/// Why setting up a TSS failed.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum TssError {
    /// UEFI could not allocate the TSS page.
    AllocationFailed,
}

pub struct TssRegion {
    page: NonNull<u8>,
}

impl TssRegion {
    /// Allocate a page that stays live while the CPU may use this TSS, and
    /// write a TSS with no stacks in it ([`Tss::new`]).
    /// Return `TssError::AllocationFailed` if UEFI cannot provide a page.
    pub fn allocate() -> Result<Self, TssError> {
        Self::allocate_with_interrupt_stacks([0; 7])
    }

    /// Like [`allocate`](Self::allocate), with IST1-IST7 set to
    /// `interrupt_stacks`.
    pub fn allocate_with_interrupt_stacks(interrupt_stacks: [u64; 7]) -> Result<Self, TssError> {
        let page = allocate_zeroed_page(TssError::AllocationFailed)?;
        // SAFETY: `page` is a fresh page, larger than a `Tss`, which nothing
        // else refers to yet. The write is unaligned because `Tss` is packed.
        unsafe { page.cast::<Tss>().as_ptr().write_unaligned(Tss::new(interrupt_stacks)) };
        Ok(Self { page })
    }

    /// Return the TSS linear address for its GDT descriptor and VMCS host state.
    pub fn base(&self) -> u64 {
        self.page.as_ptr() as u64
    }
}

/// Why setting up the host GDT failed.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum GdtError {
    /// UEFI could not allocate the GDT page.
    AllocationFailed,
    /// The current GDT plus alignment and a 16-byte TSS descriptor cannot fit in one page.
    TooLarge,
    /// The active GDTR has a null base address.
    InvalidSource,
    /// A TSS descriptor has already been appended to this GDT.
    AlreadyInstalled,
    /// The TSS descriptor could not be verified after being appended.
    TssVerificationFailed,
    /// The prepared GDTR could not be verified after appending the TSS descriptor.
    GdtrPreparationFailed,
    /// The active IDT is missing or does not contain complete 16-byte gates.
    InvalidIdt,
    /// A present IDT gate needs an IST stack, but the host TSS has none.
    IdtRequiresIst,
    /// The CPU state did not match the prepared GDT and TSS after loading them.
    ActivationVerificationFailed,
}

/// Descriptor byte 5 of an available 64-bit TSS: present (bit 7), DPL 0,
/// S = 0, type 0x9.
const TSS_AVAILABLE_PRESENT: u8 = 0x89;
/// Size of a 64-bit system descriptor (TSS).
const SYSTEM_DESCRIPTOR_SIZE: usize = 16;
/// IDT gate byte 5, bit 7: the gate is present.
const GATE_PRESENT: u8 = 0x80;

/// Encode a present, available 64-bit TSS descriptor (type 0x9, DPL 0)
/// with byte granularity. Only the low 20 bits of `limit` are encodable.
pub(crate) fn tss_descriptor(base: u64, limit: u32) -> [u8; SYSTEM_DESCRIPTOR_SIZE] {
    let mut descriptor = [0u8; SYSTEM_DESCRIPTOR_SIZE];
    descriptor[0..2].copy_from_slice(&(limit as u16).to_le_bytes());
    descriptor[2..4].copy_from_slice(&(base as u16).to_le_bytes());
    descriptor[4] = (base >> 16) as u8;
    descriptor[5] = TSS_AVAILABLE_PRESENT;
    descriptor[6] = ((limit >> 16) & 0x0f) as u8;
    descriptor[7] = (base >> 24) as u8;
    descriptor[8..12].copy_from_slice(&((base >> 32) as u32).to_le_bytes());
    descriptor
}

pub struct GdtRegion {
    page: NonNull<u8>,
    original_length: usize,
    tss_selector: Option<u16>,
}

impl GdtRegion {
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// The active GDTR must describe readable memory for `limit + 1` bytes,
    /// and that table must remain stable while it is copied.
    pub unsafe fn copy_active() -> Result<Self, GdtError> {
        let page = allocate_zeroed_page(GdtError::AllocationFailed)?;
        // SAFETY: `page` was just allocated and nothing refers to it, so it
        // may be freed; the copy reads the active GDT, which the caller
        // guarantees is readable through its limit, into the page, which it
        // fits (checked first).
        unsafe {
            let descriptor_table = read_gdtr();
            let original_length = descriptor_table.limit as usize + 1;
            let offset = (original_length + 7) & !7;
            if offset + SYSTEM_DESCRIPTOR_SIZE > PAGE_SIZE {
                boot::free_pages(page, 1).expect("failed to free oversized GDT page");
                return Err(GdtError::TooLarge);
            }
            if descriptor_table.base == 0 {
                boot::free_pages(page, 1).expect("failed to free unused GDT page");
                return Err(GdtError::InvalidSource);
            }

            copy_nonoverlapping(descriptor_table.base as *const u8, page.as_ptr(), original_length);

            Ok(Self {
                page,
                original_length,
                tss_selector: None,
            })
        }
    }

    /// Return the linear address of the copied GDT.
    pub fn base(&self) -> u64 {
        self.page.as_ptr() as u64
    }

    /// Return the copied GDT's base and limit once its TSS descriptor exists.
    pub fn prepared_gdtr(&self) -> Option<DescriptorTable> {
        let selector = self.tss_selector?;
        Some(DescriptorTable {
            base: self.base(),
            limit: selector + SYSTEM_DESCRIPTOR_SIZE as u16 - 1,
        })
    }

    /// Append an available 64-bit TSS descriptor and return its selector.
    /// This does not load the GDT or change TR; the TSS must remain live when it is loaded.
    pub fn append_tss_descriptor(&mut self, tss_region: &TssRegion) -> Result<u16, GdtError> {
        if self.tss_selector.is_some() {
            return Err(GdtError::AlreadyInstalled);
        }

        let offset = self.original_length.next_multiple_of(8);
        if offset + SYSTEM_DESCRIPTOR_SIZE > PAGE_SIZE {
            return Err(GdtError::TooLarge);
        }

        let descriptor = tss_descriptor(tss_region.base(), (TSS_SIZE - 1) as u32);

        // SAFETY: the 16 bytes at `offset` lie within the GDT page (checked
        // above), which this region owns; the CPU does not use the copy yet.
        unsafe {
            copy_nonoverlapping(descriptor.as_ptr(), self.page.as_ptr().add(offset), descriptor.len());
        }

        let selector = offset as u16;
        self.tss_selector = Some(selector);
        Ok(selector)
    }

    /// Check the TSS descriptor in the copied GDT before it is loaded.
    pub fn verify_tss_descriptor(&self, tss_region: &TssRegion) -> bool {
        let Some(selector) = self.tss_selector else {
            return false;
        };
        let offset = selector as usize;
        if selector == 0 || selector & segment::SELECTOR_RPL_TI != 0 || offset + SYSTEM_DESCRIPTOR_SIZE > PAGE_SIZE {
            return false;
        }

        // SAFETY: the descriptor lies within the GDT page (checked above),
        // which this region owns and nothing else writes.
        let descriptor = unsafe { &*self.page.as_ptr().add(offset).cast::<[u8; SYSTEM_DESCRIPTOR_SIZE]>() };
        // G is 0 in a TSS descriptor Aleph0 writes, so this is the raw limit.
        let low = SegmentDescriptor(u64::from_le_bytes(descriptor[..8].try_into().expect("8 bytes")));

        low.limit() == (TSS_SIZE - 1) as u32
            && system_descriptor_base(descriptor) == tss_region.base()
            && descriptor[5] == TSS_AVAILABLE_PRESENT
            && descriptor[6] & 0xF0 == 0
            && descriptor[12..16] == [0; 4]
    }

    /// Check the active tables, load this GDT and TSS, and verify the CPU state.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// The GDT and TSS must remain live while the CPU uses them. The caller
    /// must ensure the active selectors and IDT remain usable after the switch.
    /// The active IDT must be readable and stable through its reported limit
    /// while its gates are inspected. Call only once: LTR marks the TSS
    /// descriptor busy, so the pre-load verifier will reject a second call.
    /// If post-load verification fails, the CPU still uses the new tables.
    pub unsafe fn activate(&self, tss_region: &TssRegion) -> Result<(), GdtError> {
        if !self.verify_tss_descriptor(tss_region) {
            return Err(GdtError::TssVerificationFailed);
        }
        let gdtr = self.prepared_gdtr().ok_or(GdtError::GdtrPreparationFailed)?;

        // The selectors in use must name descriptors inside the copied part of
        // the GDT. SS may be null in 64-bit mode.
        let (cs, ss) = (read_cs(), read_ss());
        let copied = DescriptorTable {
            base: self.base(),
            limit: (self.original_length - 1) as u16,
        };
        let ss_is_null = ss & !segment::SELECTOR_RPL == 0;
        if descriptor_offset(&copied, cs, 8).is_none() || !(ss_is_null || descriptor_offset(&copied, ss, 8).is_some()) {
            return Err(GdtError::GdtrPreparationFailed);
        }

        let idtr = read_idtr();
        let idt_length = idtr.limit as usize + 1;
        if idtr.base == 0 || !idt_length.is_multiple_of(GATE_SIZE) {
            return Err(GdtError::InvalidIdt);
        }
        let idt = idtr.base as *const u8;
        for offset in (0..idt_length).step_by(GATE_SIZE) {
            // SAFETY: the gate lies within the IDT limit, and the caller
            // guarantees the IDT is readable through it.
            let (ist, attributes) =
                unsafe { (idt.add(offset + 4).read_volatile(), idt.add(offset + 5).read_volatile()) };
            if attributes & GATE_PRESENT != 0 && ist & GATE_IST_MASK != 0 {
                return Err(GdtError::IdtRequiresIst);
            }
        }

        let selector = self.tss_selector.ok_or(GdtError::GdtrPreparationFailed)?;
        // SAFETY: the copied GDT keeps the active CS/SS descriptors (checked
        // above) and holds the verified TSS descriptor at `selector`; the
        // caller keeps both pages live.
        unsafe {
            segment::load_gdtr(&gdtr);
            asm!("ltr {selector:x}", selector = in(reg) selector, options(nostack, preserves_flags));
        }

        let loaded_gdtr = read_gdtr();
        let loaded_tr = read_tr();
        if loaded_gdtr != gdtr || loaded_tr != selector {
            return Err(GdtError::ActivationVerificationFailed);
        }
        // SAFETY: `loaded_gdtr` is the copied GDT (checked above), which this
        // region owns.
        if unsafe { segment_base_from_gdt(&loaded_gdtr, loaded_tr) } != tss_region.base() {
            return Err(GdtError::ActivationVerificationFailed);
        }

        Ok(())
    }
}
