`src/vmx/paging.rs`:

```rs
//! A read-only walk of the current 4-level page tables.
//!
//! Answers one question: for a given address, what do the page tables say
//! about it? Is it mapped, can it be written, can code run from it?
//!
//! With guest CR3 = host CR3, the guest translates linear addresses through
//! exactly these tables, so what they say about a page is what the guest's
//! first translation stage gives. EPT (`vmx::ept`) then translates the
//! result a second time and may refuse the access on its own.
//!
//! In 64-bit mode the CPU translates every address through 4 levels of
//! tables, splitting the address into pieces:
//!
//! ```text
//!  47      39 38      30 29      21 20      12 11         0
//! [ PML4 idx | PDPT idx |  PD idx  |  PT idx  |   offset   ]
//!    9 bits     9 bits     9 bits     9 bits     12 bits
//! ```
//!
//! CR3 points to the first table (PML4). Each index picks one 8-byte entry
//! in the current table, and that entry points to the next table. The last
//! entry points to the page itself, and the offset is added to it.
//!
//! [`walk`] is pure logic over a "read the entry at this physical address"
//! function, so it can be tested on the host with fake tables.
//! [`walk_current`] runs it on the live CR3.
//!
//! A longer walkthrough with more examples is in `docs/PAGE_TABLE_WALK.md`.
//!
//! # Why the pieces are 12 and 9 bits
//!
//! A page is 4096 = 2^12 bytes, so 12 bits pick a byte inside it. A table
//! fills exactly one page with 8-byte entries: 4096 / 8 = 512 = 2^9
//! entries, so 9 bits pick an entry. 4 * 9 + 12 = 48 bits; bits 63:48 of
//! the address must be copies of bit 47 ("canonical").
//!
//! # The levels
//!
//! The names are historical: 32-bit x86 had only PD -> PT, and each wider
//! mode added a level on top. An entry is named after its table: PML4E,
//! PDPTE, PDE, PTE.
//!
//! ```text
//! CR3 ──► PML4  Page Map Level 4             one entry covers 512 GiB
//!          │
//!          ▼
//!         PDPT  Page Directory Pointer Table one entry covers   1 GiB ──(PS=1)──► 1 GiB page
//!          │
//!          ▼
//!         PD    Page Directory               one entry covers   2 MiB ──(PS=1)──► 2 MiB page
//!          │
//!          ▼
//!         PT    Page Table                   one entry covers   4 KiB = the page
//! ```
//!
//! Each level splits its region into 512 pieces. The tree only needs tables
//! for regions that are actually used: an unused 512 GiB region is just a
//! PML4 entry with P = 0. A flat table for 48 bits would itself be 512 GiB.
//!
//! At every level, two different things decide where to look:
//! - *which row* comes from the virtual address (that level's 9 bits);
//! - *where the table is* comes from the row read one level up (or CR3).
//!
//! # CR3
//!
//! One register per CPU core, holding the root of the tree in use right
//! now. It does not change per address: every lookup starts from the same
//! CR3 and only takes different rows. An OS gives each process its own tree
//! and loads that process's CR3 on a switch; VM entry/exit load GUEST_CR3 /
//! HOST_CR3 from the VMCS. The UEFI firmware built the (identity-mapped)
//! tables this walk reads and loaded CR3 before the `.efi` started. VM exits
//! load Aleph0's own tables instead (`vmx::host`).
//!
//! ```text
//!  63      52 51                     12 11     5  4   3  2  0
//! ┌──────────┬─────────────────────────┬────────┬───┬───┬────┐
//! │ reserved │  PML4 table address     │ ignored│PCD│PWT│ign │
//! └──────────┴─────────────────────────┴────────┴───┴───┴────┘
//! ```
//!
//! The low 12 address bits are always 0 (tables are 4 KiB-aligned), so they
//! are not stored. With CR4.PCIDE = 1, bits 11:0 hold a process-context ID.
//!
//! # Entry format
//!
//! Every entry is one 64-bit number: an address plus flag bits. `*` marks
//! the bits [`walk`] reads.
//!
//! An entry that points to the next table (any PML4E; PDPTE/PDE with PS=0):
//!
//! ```text
//!  63  62    52 51                    12 11  8  7   6  5   4   3   2   1   0
//! ┌───┬────────┬────────────────────────┬─────┬───┬───┬──┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
//! │XD │ ignored│  next table address    │ ign │PS │ign│A │PCD│PWT│U/S│R/W│ P │
//! └───┴────────┴────────────────────────┴─────┴───┴───┴──┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
//!   *                    *                      *                      *   *
//! ```
//!
//! A PTE (4 KiB page):
//!
//! ```text
//!  63  62 59 58 52 51                    12 11 9  8   7   6  5   4   3   2   1   0
//! ┌───┬─────┬─────┬────────────────────────┬────┬───┬───┬───┬──┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
//! │XD │PKey │ ign │   4 KiB page address   │ign │ G │PAT│ D │A │PCD│PWT│U/S│R/W│ P │
//! └───┴─────┴─────┴────────────────────────┴────┴───┴───┴───┴──┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
//! ```
//!
//! A PDE with PS = 1 (2 MiB page) looks like a PTE, except bit 7 is PS = 1,
//! PAT moves to bit 12, bits 20:13 are reserved (0), and the page address is
//! bits 51:21. A PDPTE with PS = 1 (1 GiB page) is the same with the page
//! address in bits 51:30 and bits 29:13 reserved.
//!
//! | Bit     | Name | Meaning                                                    |
//! |---------|------|------------------------------------------------------------|
//! | 0       | P    | Present. 0 = nothing mapped; all other bits are ignored.   |
//! | 1       | R/W  | Writes allowed in this region.                             |
//! | 2       | U/S  | User (ring 3) may access. 0 = kernel only.                 |
//! | 3, 4    | PWT, PCD | Caching: write-through, cache-disable.                 |
//! | 5       | A    | Accessed; set by the CPU when the entry is used.           |
//! | 6       | D    | Dirty (page entries only); set when the page is written.   |
//! | 7       | PS   | In PDPTE/PDE: 1 = this entry is a 1 GiB/2 MiB page.        |
//! | 7 or 12 | PAT  | Memory type (bit 7 in a PTE, bit 12 in a large page).      |
//! | 8       | G    | Global: keep in the TLB across CR3 changes (pages only).   |
//! | 51:12   | addr | Next table or page. Bits above MAXPHYADDR must be 0.       |
//! | 62:59   | PKey | Protection key (pages only); unused here.                  |
//! | 63      | XD   | No instruction fetch in this region (if EFER.NXE = 1).     |
//!
//! # Combining permissions
//!
//! The CPU checks every level and the strictest one wins, like doors in a
//! row: a page is writable only if R/W = 1 at *every* level (AND), and one
//! XD = 1 at *any* level blocks execution (OR). A PTE saying "writable"
//! under a read-only PDE is read-only.
//!
//! U/S works like R/W: a page is a *user* page only if U/S = 1 at every
//! level (AND); one U/S = 0 makes it a *supervisor* page. That matters even
//! for ring-0 code, through two CR4 bits:
//! - SMEP (bit 20): ring 0 may not *execute* from user pages.
//! - SMAP (bit 21): ring 0 may not *read or write* user pages unless
//!   RFLAGS.AC = 1.
//!
//! So for a ring-0 guest, "XD clear" alone does not prove a page is
//! executable, and "R/W set" alone does not prove it is writable.
//!
//! The CPU caches finished lookups in the TLB, so it does not walk on every
//! access; writing CR3 flushes most of that cache.
//!
//! # Worked example: the guest code page on Hyper-V
//!
//! Table locations and entry values are illustrative; the result matches
//! the Hyper-V log (`phys=0x7eb19000 size=Size4K writable=true xd=false`).
//!
//! ```text
//! virtual_address = 0x7eb19000
//!   47:39 = 000000000  PML4 index 0
//!   38:30 = 000000001  PDPT index 1
//!   29:21 = 111110101  PD   index 0x1F5
//!   20:12 = 100011001  PT   index 0x119
//!   11:0  = 0          offset 0
//!
//! CR3 = 0x7f801000                      -> table 0x7f801000
//! L4: row 0     at 0x7f801000 = 0x7f802023  P R/W A, PS=0 -> table 0x7f802000
//! L3: row 1     at 0x7f802008 = 0x7f803023  P R/W A, PS=0 -> table 0x7f803000
//! L2: row 0x1F5 at 0x7f803fa8 = 0x7f9a0023  P R/W A, PS=0 -> table 0x7f9a0000
//! L1: row 0x119 at 0x7f9a08c8 = 0x7eb19063  P R/W A D     -> page  0x7eb19000
//!
//! physical = 0x7eb19000 | (0x7eb19000 & 0xFFF) = 0x7eb19000
//! ```
//!
//! Each row address is `table + index * 8`; each next table is
//! `entry & ADDRESS_MASK`. The low bits `0x023` = `0b0010_0011` are P, R/W
//! and A; `0x063` adds D.
//!
//! Had the PD row been `0x7ea000E3` (`0xE3` sets PS), the walk would stop
//! at level 2 with a 2 MiB page and a 21-bit offset: physical =
//! `0x7ea00000 | (0x7eb19000 & 0x1FFFFF)` = the same `0x7eb19000`. The PT
//! index bits simply become part of the offset.

use super::cr::{CR4_LA57, read_cr3, read_cr4};

// Entry bits used by the walk; the full layout is in the module docs.

/// Bit 0 (P): the entry is valid. If 0, nothing is mapped below it.
const PRESENT: u64 = 1 << 0;
/// Bit 1 (R/W): writes allowed in this entry's region.
const WRITABLE: u64 = 1 << 1;
/// Bit 2 (U/S): user mode (ring 3) may access this entry's region.
const USER: u64 = 1 << 2;
/// Bit 7 (PS), in a PDPTE or PDE: this entry maps a 1 GiB or 2 MiB page
/// directly instead of pointing to a table.
const PAGE_SIZE_BIT: u64 = 1 << 7;
/// Bit 63 (XD): no instruction fetch in this entry's region.
const EXECUTE_DISABLE: u64 = 1 << 63;
/// Bits 51:12: physical address of the next table or of the page. Strips
/// the flag bits that share the same 8 bytes.
const ADDRESS_MASK: u64 = 0x000F_FFFF_FFFF_F000;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum PageSize {
    Size4K,
    Size2M,
    Size1G,
}

/// How one virtual address translates, with permissions combined over
/// every level of the walk.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Mapping {
    pub physical: u64,
    pub size: PageSize,
    /// R/W is set at every level. (Supervisor code may also write a
    /// read-only page while CR0.WP = 0; this does not count that.)
    pub writable: bool,
    /// U/S is set at every level: a user page. Ring 0 cannot execute it
    /// under CR4.SMEP, nor read or write it under CR4.SMAP (with AC = 0).
    pub user: bool,
    /// XD is set at some level. Blocks instruction fetch when EFER.NXE = 1;
    /// when NXE = 0 the bit is reserved and any access faults.
    pub execute_disable: bool,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum WalkError {
    /// CR4.LA57 is set; 5-level paging is not supported here.
    FiveLevelPaging,
    /// The entry at `level` (4 = PML4, 3 = PDPT, 2 = PD, 1 = PT) has P clear.
    NotPresent { level: u8 },
}

/// Translates `virtual_address` through the 4-level tables rooted at `cr3`.
///
/// `read_entry` returns the 8-byte entry at a physical address. The walker
/// never touches memory itself; the caller decides how entries are read,
/// which is what lets the tests use fake tables. Bits 11:0 of `cr3` (PCID
/// or cache flags) are ignored.
pub fn walk(cr3: u64, virtual_address: u64, read_entry: impl Fn(u64) -> u64) -> Result<Mapping, WalkError> {
    let mut table = cr3 & ADDRESS_MASK;
    // Permissions are combined over the whole walk, starting permissive.
    let mut writable = true;
    let mut user = true;
    let mut execute_disable = false;

    // Level 4 (PML4) down to level 1 (PT).
    for level in (1..=4u8).rev() {
        // This level's 9-bit index: bits 47:39 at level 4, 38:30 at level 3,
        // 29:21 at level 2, 20:12 at level 1.
        let shift = 12 + 9 * (level as u32 - 1);
        let index = (virtual_address >> shift) & 0x1FF;
        let entry = read_entry(table + index * 8);

        if entry & PRESENT == 0 {
            return Err(WalkError::NotPresent { level });
        }
        // Writable or user only if R/W or U/S is set at every level; one XD
        // bit at any level is enough to block execution.
        writable &= entry & WRITABLE != 0;
        user &= entry & USER != 0;
        execute_disable |= entry & EXECUTE_DISABLE != 0;

        // Does this entry map a page (end of the walk) or point to the next
        // table? At levels 3 and 2, the PS bit means "this entry is the
        // page": 1 GiB or 2 MiB, with a 30- or 21-bit offset instead of 12.
        // A level-1 entry is always a 4 KiB page.
        let size = match level {
            3 if entry & PAGE_SIZE_BIT != 0 => Some(PageSize::Size1G),
            2 if entry & PAGE_SIZE_BIT != 0 => Some(PageSize::Size2M),
            1 => Some(PageSize::Size4K),
            _ => None,
        };
        if let Some(size) = size {
            // Large-page entries keep the PAT bit at bit 12, inside the
            // offset range, so clear the offset bits from the frame.
            let offset_mask = (1u64 << shift) - 1;
            let frame = entry & ADDRESS_MASK & !offset_mask;
            return Ok(Mapping {
                physical: frame | (virtual_address & offset_mask),
                size,
                writable,
                user,
                execute_disable,
            });
        }

        // Not a page yet: the entry holds the next table's address.
        table = entry & ADDRESS_MASK;
    }

    unreachable!("a level-1 entry always ends the walk")
}

/// Translates `virtual_address` through the page tables the CPU is using now.
///
/// Reads the real CR3 and gives [`walk`] a function that reads each entry
/// straight from memory at its physical address. Refuses 5-level paging,
/// which [`walk`] does not handle.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// Reads the tables through their physical addresses, so the tables
/// themselves must be identity-mapped. UEFI guarantees that while boot
/// services are active; after `ExitBootServices` it no longer holds.
pub unsafe fn walk_current(virtual_address: u64) -> Result<Mapping, WalkError> {
    if read_cr4() & CR4_LA57 != 0 {
        return Err(WalkError::FiveLevelPaging);
    }
    let cr3 = read_cr3();
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees boot services are active, so the tables
    // are identity-mapped and each entry is readable at its physical address.
    walk(cr3, virtual_address, |physical| unsafe {
        (physical as *const u64).read_volatile()
    })
}

/// The tests build small fake page tables in a `HashMap` (physical address
/// to entry) and check translation, permission combining, large pages, and
/// missing entries.
#[cfg(test)]
#[path = "../../tests/unit/vmx/paging.rs"]
mod tests;

`src/vmx/region.rs`:

```rs
//! The 4 KiB regions VMX instructions take by physical address: the VMXON
//! region and each VMCS. Both start with the VMCS revision identifier from
//! IA32_VMX_BASIC and are otherwise left to the CPU.

use super::msr;
use super::page::allocate_zeroed_page;

/// IA32_VMX_BASIC bits 30:0: the revision identifier both regions start with.
const REVISION_ID_MASK: u64 = 0x7FFF_FFFF;

/// The VMCS revision identifier, from IA32_VMX_BASIC bits 30:0.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// The CPU must support VMX, or reading IA32_VMX_BASIC raises #GP.
pub unsafe fn vmcs_revision_id() -> u32 {
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX support, so the MSR exists.
    (unsafe { msr::rdmsr(msr::IA32_VMX_BASIC) } & REVISION_ID_MASK) as u32
}

/// One zeroed, page-aligned 4 KiB page with the revision identifier in its
/// first four bytes. Never freed: no `Drop`, because the CPU may use the
/// page for as long as VMX operation lasts.
pub struct VmxRegion {
    /// Physical address. Equal to the virtual address under UEFI's identity
    /// mapping.
    phys_addr: u64,
}

impl VmxRegion {
    /// Allocates the page and writes the revision identifier.
    /// `allocation_error` is returned if UEFI has no page.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// The CPU must support VMX (see [`vmcs_revision_id`]).
    pub unsafe fn allocate<E>(allocation_error: E) -> Result<Self, E> {
        let page = allocate_zeroed_page(allocation_error)?;
        // SAFETY: the page is freshly allocated, page-aligned and zeroed, so a
        // u32 write at its start is in bounds and aligned; the CPU does not
        // use it yet. VMX support is the caller's obligation.
        unsafe { page.cast::<u32>().as_ptr().write_volatile(vmcs_revision_id()) };
        Ok(Self {
            phys_addr: page.as_ptr() as u64,
        })
    }

    /// The memory operand VMXON, VMCLEAR and VMPTRLD take: a pointer to the
    /// 64-bit physical address, not the address itself.
    pub fn phys_addr_ref(&self) -> &u64 {
        &self.phys_addr
    }
}

```

`src/vmx/segment.rs`:

```rs
//! Reading the CPU's segmentation state.
//!
//! Long mode barely uses segmentation — most bases are 0 and limits are
//! ignored — but the registers still exist, and VM entry checks the values
//! written into the VMCS for both host and guest. So the state has to be read
//! out of the running CPU and copied in.
//!
//! Three kinds of value are needed per segment:
//!
//! * the **selector** — an index into the GDT, held in CS/SS/DS/ES/FS/GS/TR;
//! * the **base** — the real 64-bit start address. Only FS, GS and TR matter
//!   in long mode; the rest are architecturally 0.
//! * the **limit** and **access rights** — needed for guest state, not for
//!   host state. They are decoded from the segment's GDT descriptor by
//!   [`SegmentDescriptor::limit`] and [`SegmentDescriptor::access_rights`].
//!
//! Host state has two extra rules the CPU enforces at VM entry, both common
//! causes of "invalid host state" (error 8):
//!
//! * every host selector must have its RPL and TI bits (the low 3) clear;
//! * the host TR selector must not be 0 — it has to point at a real TSS.
//!
//! Nothing here needs VMX, so [`read_all`] can be called and printed under
//! plain QEMU/TCG to sanity-check the values before any VMCS work.

use super::msr;
use core::arch::asm;

/// Contents of GDTR or IDTR: where a descriptor table starts and how big it is.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct DescriptorTable {
    /// Address of the first descriptor.
    pub base: u64,
    /// Size of the table in bytes, minus one.
    pub limit: u16,
}

impl DescriptorTable {
    /// The 10-byte memory operand of LGDT/LIDT and SGDT/SIDT: the limit,
    /// then the base, both little-endian.
    pub fn to_operand(self) -> [u8; 10] {
        let mut operand = [0u8; 10];
        operand[..2].copy_from_slice(&self.limit.to_le_bytes());
        operand[2..].copy_from_slice(&self.base.to_le_bytes());
        operand
    }

    /// The inverse of [`DescriptorTable::to_operand`].
    pub fn from_operand(operand: [u8; 10]) -> Self {
        let [limit_low, limit_high, base @ ..] = operand;
        Self {
            base: u64::from_le_bytes(base),
            limit: u16::from_le_bytes([limit_low, limit_high]),
        }
    }
}

/// Reads GDTR, the pointer to the Global Descriptor Table.
pub fn read_gdtr() -> DescriptorTable {
    let mut operand = [0u8; 10];
    // SAFETY: SGDT writes exactly 10 bytes to `operand`, which is ours and
    // 10 bytes long; it has no other effect. No `nomem`: claiming it lets the
    // compiler drop the buffer and fold the decoding to zero, which it does
    // in release.
    unsafe { asm!("sgdt [{0}]", in(reg) operand.as_mut_ptr(), options(nostack, preserves_flags)) };
    DescriptorTable::from_operand(operand)
}

/// Reads IDTR, the pointer to the Interrupt Descriptor Table.
pub fn read_idtr() -> DescriptorTable {
    let mut operand = [0u8; 10];
    // SAFETY: as in `read_gdtr`, with SIDT.
    unsafe { asm!("sidt [{0}]", in(reg) operand.as_mut_ptr(), options(nostack, preserves_flags)) };
    DescriptorTable::from_operand(operand)
}

/// Loads GDTR. Segment registers keep their cached descriptors until they
/// are reloaded, so nothing visible changes until then.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// `table` must describe a live GDT with valid descriptors for the
/// selectors in CS, SS, DS, ES, FS and GS, in case they are reloaded.
pub unsafe fn load_gdtr(table: &DescriptorTable) {
    let operand = table.to_operand();
    // SAFETY: LGDT only reads the 10-byte operand; the caller guarantees the
    // table it names is live and valid.
    unsafe { asm!("lgdt [{0}]", in(reg) operand.as_ptr(), options(readonly, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
}

/// Loads IDTR.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// `table` must describe a live IDT whose gates handle every interrupt and
/// exception that may arrive.
pub unsafe fn load_idtr(table: &DescriptorTable) {
    let operand = table.to_operand();
    // SAFETY: LIDT only reads the 10-byte operand; the caller guarantees the
    // table it names is live and handles every vector that may arrive.
    unsafe { asm!("lidt [{0}]", in(reg) operand.as_ptr(), options(readonly, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
}

/// Defines a safe reader for one selector register. Reading a selector (or
/// TR with STR) has no side effects, and Aleph0 always runs in ring 0, where
/// neither instruction can fault.
macro_rules! selector_reader {
    ($(#[$doc:meta])* $name:ident, $instruction:literal) => {
        $(#[$doc])*
        pub fn $name() -> u16 {
            let selector: u16;
            // SAFETY: a read of a selector register: no memory access, no
            // side effects, no fault in ring 0.
            unsafe { asm!($instruction, out(reg) selector, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
            selector
        }
    };
}

selector_reader!(
    /// Reads the CS selector, which also carries the current privilege level.
    read_cs,
    "mov {:x}, cs"
);
selector_reader!(
    /// Reads the SS selector.
    read_ss,
    "mov {:x}, ss"
);
selector_reader!(
    /// Reads the DS selector.
    read_ds,
    "mov {:x}, ds"
);
selector_reader!(
    /// Reads the ES selector.
    read_es,
    "mov {:x}, es"
);
selector_reader!(
    /// Reads the FS selector.
    read_fs,
    "mov {:x}, fs"
);
selector_reader!(
    /// Reads the GS selector.
    read_gs,
    "mov {:x}, gs"
);
selector_reader!(
    /// Reads the Task Register selector, which points at the TSS descriptor.
    ///
    /// A zero value here is a problem: VM entry rejects a host TR selector of
    /// 0. Firmware may leave TR unset, so check it before preparing VMCS host
    /// state.
    read_tr,
    "str {:x}"
);

/// Reads the FS base from [`msr::IA32_FS_BASE`].
///
/// # Safety
///
/// The CPU must support long mode, so that the MSR exists.
pub unsafe fn read_fs_base() -> u64 {
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees long mode, which has IA32_FS_BASE.
    unsafe { msr::rdmsr(msr::IA32_FS_BASE) }
}

/// Reads the GS base from [`msr::IA32_GS_BASE`].
///
/// # Safety
///
/// The CPU must support long mode, so that the MSR exists.
pub unsafe fn read_gs_base() -> u64 {
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees long mode, which has IA32_GS_BASE.
    unsafe { msr::rdmsr(msr::IA32_GS_BASE) }
}

/// Selector bits 1:0 (RPL): the requested privilege level. Selectors 0-3
/// all name the null descriptor.
pub const SELECTOR_RPL: u16 = 0b11;
/// Selector bit 2 (TI): the selector names the LDT, not the GDT.
pub const SELECTOR_TI: u16 = 1 << 2;
/// Selector bits 2:0, TI and RPL. Clearing them leaves the byte offset of
/// the descriptor in the table.
pub const SELECTOR_RPL_TI: u16 = 0b111;

/// Byte offset in `gdt` of the `size`-byte descriptor `selector` names.
///
/// The selector's index is bits 15:3 and each GDT slot is 8 bytes, so the
/// selector with its low 3 bits cleared is already the byte offset. `None`
/// for a null selector (any RPL), an LDT selector (TI = 1), or a descriptor
/// that does not end within the GDT limit.
pub fn descriptor_offset(gdt: &DescriptorTable, selector: u16, size: usize) -> Option<usize> {
    let offset = usize::from(selector & !SELECTOR_RPL_TI);
    let fits = offset + size <= usize::from(gdt.limit) + 1;
    (selector & SELECTOR_TI == 0 && offset != 0 && fits).then_some(offset)
}

/// Size of one 64-bit IDT gate.
pub const GATE_SIZE: usize = 16;
/// Gate byte 5: present (bit 7), DPL 0, type 0xE (64-bit interrupt gate,
/// which clears RFLAGS.IF on delivery).
const INTERRUPT_GATE_PRESENT: u8 = 0x8E;
/// Gate byte 4, bits 2:0: the IST index (0 = the current stack).
pub(crate) const GATE_IST_MASK: u8 = 0b111;

/// A 64-bit interrupt gate to `handler` through code segment `selector`:
/// present, DPL 0, on interrupt stack `ist` (1-7 name the TSS's IST1-IST7;
/// 0 keeps the stack the CPU is on). Only bits 2:0 of `ist` are encodable.
///
/// ```text
/// bytes 0-1    handler bits 15:0
/// bytes 2-3    code segment selector
/// byte  4      bits 2:0: IST index
/// byte  5      0x8E: present, DPL 0, type 0xE (64-bit interrupt gate)
/// bytes 6-7    handler bits 31:16
/// bytes 8-11   handler bits 63:32
/// bytes 12-15  reserved, 0
/// ```
pub fn interrupt_gate(handler: u64, selector: u16, ist: u8) -> [u8; GATE_SIZE] {
    let mut gate = [0u8; GATE_SIZE];
    gate[0..2].copy_from_slice(&(handler as u16).to_le_bytes());
    gate[2..4].copy_from_slice(&selector.to_le_bytes());
    gate[4] = ist & GATE_IST_MASK;
    gate[5] = INTERRUPT_GATE_PRESENT;
    gate[6..8].copy_from_slice(&((handler >> 16) as u16).to_le_bytes());
    gate[8..12].copy_from_slice(&((handler >> 32) as u32).to_le_bytes());
    gate
}

/// Base address in a 16-byte system descriptor (a 64-bit TSS). Bits 31:0
/// are scattered as in a code/data descriptor; bits 63:32 follow in bytes
/// 8-11:
///
/// ```text
/// bytes 2..4    base 15:0
/// byte  4       base 23:16
/// byte  7       base 31:24
/// bytes 8..12   base 63:32
/// ```
pub fn system_descriptor_base(bytes: &[u8; 16]) -> u64 {
    let (low, high) = bytes.split_at(8);
    let low = SegmentDescriptor(u64::from_le_bytes(low.try_into().expect("8 bytes")));
    let high = u32::from_le_bytes(high[..4].try_into().expect("4 bytes"));
    low.base() | (u64::from(high) << 32)
}

/// Extracts a segment's base address from its 16-byte GDT descriptor, or 0
/// if [`descriptor_offset`] refuses the selector.
///
/// Needed for TR, whose base is not available from any register or MSR — it
/// has to be read out of the descriptor the selector points at.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// `gdt` must describe a live, readable GDT through its reported limit.
pub unsafe fn segment_base_from_gdt(gdt: &DescriptorTable, selector: u16) -> u64 {
    let Some(offset) = descriptor_offset(gdt, selector, 16) else {
        return 0;
    };
    // SAFETY: `descriptor_offset` checked that the 16 bytes lie within the
    // limit, and the caller guarantees the table is readable.
    let bytes = unsafe { ((gdt.base + offset as u64) as *const [u8; 16]).read_unaligned() };
    system_descriptor_base(&bytes)
}

// An 8-byte code/data descriptor, as a little-endian u64. The base and limit
// are scattered for backwards compatibility with the 286:
//
//  63    56 55 54 53 52 51  48 47 46 45 44 43  40 39             16 15       0
// ┌────────┬──┬──┬──┬───┬─────┬──┬─────┬──┬──────┬─────────────────┬──────────┐
// │base    │G │D │L │AVL│limit│P │ DPL │S │ type │ base 23:0       │limit 15:0│
// │31:24   │  │/B│  │   │19:16│  │     │  │      │                 │          │
// └────────┴──┴──┴──┴───┴─────┴──┴─────┴──┴──────┴─────────────────┴──────────┘
//
// The VMCS stores access rights as bits 55:52 and 47:40 of this, packed
// together with the limit bits removed:
//
//  31     17  16     15 14 13 12  11  8  7  6 5  4  3   0
// ┌─────────┬────────┬──┬──┬──┬───┬─────┬──┬───┬──┬──────┐
// │reserved │unusable│G │D │L │AVL│ res │P │DPL│S │ type │
// └─────────┴────────┴──┴──┴──┴───┴─────┴──┴───┴──┴──────┘

/// VMCS access-rights bit 16: the segment register is unusable, as after
/// loading a null selector. VM entry then ignores the other bits.
pub const ACCESS_RIGHTS_UNUSABLE: u32 = 1 << 16;

/// Descriptor bit 55 (G): the limit counts 4 KiB units, not bytes.
const DESCRIPTOR_GRANULARITY: u64 = 1 << 55;

/// An 8-byte code or data descriptor from the GDT, as a little-endian u64
/// (see the layout above).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct SegmentDescriptor(pub u64);

impl SegmentDescriptor {
    /// Base bits 31:0.
    ///
    /// Enough for CS, SS, DS and ES, whose bases are 32-bit (and ignored in
    /// 64-bit mode). FS and GS take their 64-bit base from MSRs instead; TR
    /// needs [`segment_base_from_gdt`], since a TSS descriptor is 16 bytes.
    pub fn base(self) -> u64 {
        ((self.0 >> 16) & 0xFF_FFFF) | ((self.0 >> 32) & 0xFF00_0000)
    }

    /// The segment limit in bytes, as the VMCS wants it.
    ///
    /// The descriptor stores 20 bits. With G = 1 they count 4 KiB pages, so
    /// the byte limit is `raw * 4096 + 4095`: 0xFFFFF becomes 0xFFFF_FFFF.
    pub fn limit(self) -> u32 {
        let raw = (self.0 & 0xFFFF) as u32 | ((self.0 >> 32) as u32 & 0xF_0000);
        if self.0 & DESCRIPTOR_GRANULARITY != 0 {
            (raw << 12) | 0xFFF
        } else {
            raw
        }
    }

    /// The access rights in VMCS format: descriptor bits 47:40 become bits
    /// 7:0, descriptor bits 55:52 become bits 15:12, and the limit bits in
    /// between (11:8 here) are cleared, since VM entry requires them to be 0.
    pub fn access_rights(self) -> u32 {
        (self.0 >> 40) as u32 & 0xF0FF
    }
}

/// Reads the 8-byte descriptor `selector` names, or `None` if
/// [`descriptor_offset`] refuses it.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// `gdt` must describe a live, readable GDT through its reported limit.
pub unsafe fn read_descriptor(gdt: &DescriptorTable, selector: u16) -> Option<SegmentDescriptor> {
    let offset = descriptor_offset(gdt, selector, 8)?;
    // SAFETY: `descriptor_offset` checked that the 8 bytes lie within the
    // limit, and the caller guarantees the table is readable.
    let raw = unsafe { ((gdt.base + offset as u64) as *const u64).read_unaligned() };
    Some(SegmentDescriptor(raw))
}

/// Everything about the current segmentation state, for printing or for
/// filling in the VMCS.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
pub struct SegmentState {
    pub cs: u16,
    pub ss: u16,
    pub ds: u16,
    pub es: u16,
    pub fs: u16,
    pub gs: u16,
    pub tr: u16,
    pub fs_base: u64,
    pub gs_base: u64,
    pub tr_base: u64,
    pub gdtr: DescriptorTable,
    pub idtr: DescriptorTable,
}

/// Snapshots the current segmentation state.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// The current GDT must be live and readable through its limit (TR's base is
/// read from it), and the CPU must be in long mode (FS/GS bases are MSRs).
pub unsafe fn read_all() -> SegmentState {
    // Both are needed before the struct can be built: TR's base is only
    // reachable by indexing the GDT with the TR selector.
    let gdtr = read_gdtr();
    let tr = read_tr();

    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees long mode and a readable GDT.
    unsafe {
        SegmentState {
            cs: read_cs(),
            ss: read_ss(),
            ds: read_ds(),
            es: read_es(),
            fs: read_fs(),
            gs: read_gs(),
            tr,
            fs_base: read_fs_base(),
            gs_base: read_gs_base(),
            tr_base: segment_base_from_gdt(&gdtr, tr),
            gdtr,
            idtr: read_idtr(),
        }
    }
}

`src/vmx/vmcall.rs`:

//! Aleph0's own VMCALLs: a VMCALL whose RCX holds one of these values is a
//! call to Aleph0, which `exit_decision::decide` handles for the firmware
//! and the OS after it. Every other VMCALL is a Hyper-V hypercall, whose
//! input value is in RCX too (`vmx::hyperv`), and Aleph0 forwards it.
//!
//! Each value is eight ASCII bytes read big-endian, so a register dump
//! shows it as text: `0x416c657068304542` is "Aleph0EB". Its top byte, 'A'
//! (0x41), sets bit 62, which is reserved in a hypercall input value (bits
//! 63:60, TLFS "Hypercall Inputs"), so no valid hypercall is ever taken for
//! one of these.
//!
//! This file depends on nothing, because the `ExitBootServices` test
//! harness (`tools/ebs-harness`) includes it too.

/// Boot services have ended: Aleph0's `ExitBootServices` event makes this
/// VMCALL in the guest (`resident::watch_exit_boot_services`), and Aleph0
/// switches its output to the runtime phase. "Aleph0EB".
pub const BOOT_SERVICES_ENDED: u64 = u64::from_be_bytes(*b"Aleph0EB");

/// Does nothing but exit: Aleph0 resumes past it. The `ExitBootServices`
/// harness makes it to see a VMCALL handled. "Aleph0TS".
pub const TEST: u64 = u64::from_be_bytes(*b"Aleph0TS");

/// Bits 63:60 of a hypercall input value, reserved: Hyper-V refuses a
/// hypercall with any of them set.
const HYPERCALL_RESERVED_TOP: u64 = 0xF << 60;

const _: () = assert!(BOOT_SERVICES_ENDED & HYPERCALL_RESERVED_TOP != 0 && TEST & HYPERCALL_RESERVED_TOP != 0);

`src/vmx/vmcs/fields.rs`:

```rs
//! VMCS field encodings, and the bits inside the control fields.
//!
//! [`super::vmread`] and [`super::vmwrite`] name a field by a 32-bit
//! *encoding*, not by an offset into the VMCS region (whose layout is
//! undocumented). The encoding packs what kind of field it is:
//!
//! ```text
//!  14  13  12  11  10  9            1   0
//! ┌───────┬───┬───────┬──────────────┬──────┐
//! │ width │ 0 │ type  │    index     │access│
//! └───────┴───┴───────┴──────────────┴──────┘
//! ```
//!
//! - width: 0 = 16-bit, 1 = 64-bit, 2 = 32-bit, 3 = natural (64-bit here)
//! - type: 0 = control, 1 = read-only data, 2 = guest state, 3 = host state
//! - access: 0 = the full field, 1 = the high 32 bits of a 64-bit field
//!
//! So the leading hex digits already say what a field is: `0x08xx` is a
//! 16-bit guest field, `0x6Cxx` a natural-width host field.

/// Pin-based VM-execution controls.
pub const PIN_BASED_VM_EXEC_CONTROL: u32 = 0x4000;
/// Primary processor-based VM-execution controls.
pub const PRIMARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL: u32 = 0x4002;
/// Pin-based control bit 3: an NMI that arrives while the guest runs causes
/// a VM exit (reason 0, interruption type NMI) instead of being delivered
/// through the guest's IDT.
pub const PIN_BASED_NMI_EXITING: u32 = 1 << 3;
/// Pin-based control bit 5, "virtual NMIs": the CPU tracks the guest's NMI
/// blocking, so an injected NMI blocks further ones until the guest's IRET.
/// Requires NMI exiting.
pub const PIN_BASED_VIRTUAL_NMIS: u32 = 1 << 5;
/// Primary processor-based control bit 7: HLT causes a VM exit (reason 12).
pub const CPU_BASED_HLT_EXITING: u32 = 1 << 7;
/// Primary processor-based control bit 22: a VM exit (reason 8) as soon as
/// the guest can take an NMI. Requires virtual NMIs.
pub const CPU_BASED_NMI_WINDOW_EXITING: u32 = 1 << 22;
/// Primary processor-based control bit 25: IN/OUT exit only for ports whose
/// bit is set in the I/O bitmaps ([`IO_BITMAP_A`], [`IO_BITMAP_B`]). While
/// set, the CPU ignores bit 24 (unconditional I/O exiting).
pub const CPU_BASED_USE_IO_BITMAPS: u32 = 1 << 25;
/// Primary processor-based control bit 28: RDMSR/WRMSR exit only for MSRs
/// whose bit is set in the MSR bitmap ([`MSR_BITMAP`]). Without it, every
/// RDMSR and WRMSR exits.
pub const CPU_BASED_USE_MSR_BITMAPS: u32 = 1 << 28;
/// Primary processor-based control bit 31: the CPU also uses the secondary
/// controls ([`SECONDARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL`]). Without it they all count as 0.
pub const CPU_BASED_ACTIVATE_SECONDARY_CONTROLS: u32 = 1 << 31;
/// Secondary control bit 1: guest-physical addresses are translated through
/// the EPT tables named by [`EPT_POINTER`].
pub const SECONDARY_ENABLE_EPT: u32 = 1 << 1;
/// Secondary control bit 5: the guest's TLB entries are tagged with a
/// virtual-processor identifier. Aleph0 does not enable it; the EPT/VPID
/// capability MSR exists if either this or EPT is allowed.
pub const SECONDARY_ENABLE_VPID: u32 = 1 << 5;
/// Exception bitmap: bit N set makes guest exception vector N cause a VM exit
/// (reason 0) instead of being delivered through the guest's IDT.
pub const EXCEPTION_BITMAP: u32 = 0x4004;
/// Page-fault error-code mask and match: with bit 14 of the exception bitmap
/// set, a guest #PF exits only if (error code & mask) == match, so 0 and 0
/// make every #PF exit.
pub const PAGE_FAULT_ERROR_CODE_MASK: u32 = 0x4006;
/// See [`PAGE_FAULT_ERROR_CODE_MASK`].
pub const PAGE_FAULT_ERROR_CODE_MATCH: u32 = 0x4008;
/// CR3-target count: how many CR3-target values are valid; VM entry requires
/// at most 4.
pub const CR3_TARGET_COUNT: u32 = 0x400A;
/// VM-exit controls.
pub const VM_EXIT_CONTROLS: u32 = 0x400C;
/// VM-exit MSR-store count: entries in the MSR-store list; nonzero needs a
/// valid list address.
pub const VM_EXIT_MSR_STORE_COUNT: u32 = 0x400E;
/// VM-exit MSR-load count: entries in the MSR-load list; nonzero needs a
/// valid list address.
pub const VM_EXIT_MSR_LOAD_COUNT: u32 = 0x4010;
/// VM-entry controls.
pub const VM_ENTRY_CONTROLS: u32 = 0x4012;
/// VM-entry MSR-load count: entries in the MSR-load list; nonzero needs a
/// valid list address.
pub const VM_ENTRY_MSR_LOAD_COUNT: u32 = 0x4014;
/// VM-entry interruption-information field: bit 31 set injects an event on
/// entry, so 0 means no injection.
pub const VM_ENTRY_INTERRUPTION_INFO: u32 = 0x4016;
/// VM-entry exception error code (32-bit): the error code delivered with an
/// injected exception whose interruption info has bit 11 set.
pub const VM_ENTRY_EXCEPTION_ERROR_CODE: u32 = 0x4018;
/// VM-entry instruction length (32-bit): the length the CPU charges when it
/// injects a software interrupt or software exception (interruption types 4,
/// 5 and 6), so RIP ends past the INT/INT3/INTO that was being delivered.
pub const VM_ENTRY_INSTRUCTION_LEN: u32 = 0x401A;
/// Secondary processor-based VM-execution controls. The CPU reads this field
/// only while primary bit 31 ([`CPU_BASED_ACTIVATE_SECONDARY_CONTROLS`]) is
/// set.
pub const SECONDARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL: u32 = 0x401E;

/// Physical addresses of the I/O bitmaps: A covers ports 0x0000–0x7FFF,
/// B ports 0x8000–0xFFFF, one bit per port (64-bit).
pub const IO_BITMAP_A: u32 = 0x2000;
pub const IO_BITMAP_B: u32 = 0x2002;
/// Physical address of the 4 KiB MSR bitmap (64-bit).
pub const MSR_BITMAP: u32 = 0x2004;
/// EPT pointer (EPTP): the physical address of the EPT PML4 table, with the
/// memory type and page-walk length in its low bits (see `vmx::ept::Eptp`).
pub const EPT_POINTER: u32 = 0x201A;

/// VM-exit control bit 9: the host runs in 64-bit mode after a VM exit.
pub const VM_EXIT_HOST_ADDRESS_SPACE_SIZE: u32 = 1 << 9;
/// VM-exit control bit 2: save the guest's DR7 and IA32_DEBUGCTL into the
/// VMCS (GUEST_DR7, GUEST_IA32_DEBUGCTL). Every exit sets DR7 to 0x400, so
/// without it the guest's DR7 is gone after the exit.
pub const VM_EXIT_SAVE_DEBUG_CONTROLS: u64 = 1 << 2;

/// GUEST_IA32_PAT and GUEST_IA32_EFER.
pub const VM_EXIT_SAVE_IA32_PAT: u64 = 1 << 18;
pub const VM_EXIT_SAVE_IA32_EFER: u64 = 1 << 20;

pub const VM_EXIT_LOAD_IA32_PAT: u64 = 1 << 19;
pub const VM_EXIT_LOAD_IA32_EFER: u64 = 1 << 21;

pub const VM_ENTRY_IA32E_MODE_GUEST: u32 = 1 << 9;
/// VM-entry control bits that load guest PAT and EFER from the VMCS. When a
/// bit is 0, the guest keeps the value the CPU already has, and the matching
/// guest field may not even exist.
pub const VM_ENTRY_LOAD_IA32_PAT: u64 = 1 << 14;
pub const VM_ENTRY_LOAD_IA32_EFER: u64 = 1 << 15;

/// Why the last VMX instruction failed (32-bit; valid after VMfailValid).
pub const VM_INSTRUCTION_ERROR: u32 = 0x4400;
/// Why the last VM exit happened (32-bit).
pub const VM_EXIT_REASON: u32 = 0x4402;
/// VM-exit interruption information (32-bit), for exception exits (reason 0):

`src/vmx/vmcs/launch.rs`:

```rs
//! Entering the guest with VMLAUNCH, and coming back when it stops.
//!
//! A successful VMLAUNCH never falls through: the CPU runs the guest, and
//! every VM exit starts the VM-exit stub in `vmx::vmexit` on its own stack.
//! To let bring-up go on after the guest stops, [`launch`] first saves the
//! caller's registers and stack pointer, like C's `setjmp`. When the guest
//! should stop, the exit stub jumps to `vmx_return_to_launcher`, which
//! restores them and returns, like `longjmp`. To the Rust caller, `launch`
//! is an ordinary function that returns a [`GuestStop`].
//!
//! Every way back from the guest carries a *stop value*. Bits 63:62 say
//! which kind it is, and the rest is the payload:
//!
//! | bits 63:62 | payload | meaning |
//! |---|---|---|
//! | 0 | RFLAGS right after VMLAUNCH | VMLAUNCH failed |
//! | 1 | number of exits | all planned exits arrived |
//! | 2 | exit number (61:32), raw exit reason (31:0) | an exit the handler does not resume |
//! | 3 | RFLAGS right after VMRESUME | VMRESUME failed |
//!
//! Kind 0 is RFLAGS itself, so the launch stub returns it without encoding:
//! RFLAGS bits 63:22 are reserved and read as 0. No stop value is 0, because
//! RFLAGS bit 1 always reads as 1, so the exit handler can return 0 to mean
//! "resume the guest".
//!
//! [`launch_in_place`] is the other way in, for the firmware: there is no
//! guest code to jump to and no stop to come back from. It writes the RIP,
//! RSP and RFLAGS it runs with into the guest state just before VMLAUNCH,
//! so the guest starts at the instruction after VMLAUNCH, on the same stack.
//! The code that called it then goes on as the guest, in VMX non-root
//! operation, and returns to its own caller. Nothing jumps back into its
//! frame, so it saves none.

use core::arch::asm;
use core::sync::atomic::AtomicU64;

use super::fields::{GUEST_RFLAGS, GUEST_RIP, GUEST_RSP};
use super::{VmcsError, instruction_error_for, launch_failure, resume_failure};
use crate::vmx::exit_decision::ExitReason;

/// RSP inside `vmx_launch`, saved after it pushed the caller's registers;
/// `vmx_return_to_launcher` reloads it to get back into that frame.
///
/// Only the stub below reads and writes it, once per launch, on the one CPU
/// that runs the guest. The atomic just gives it a fixed, writable home
/// without `static mut`, and `no_mangle` keeps the name the asm uses.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
static VMX_LAUNCH_RSP: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);

// `vmx_launch` is called with the Microsoft x64 ABI (`efiapi`). A callee
// must preserve RBX, RBP, RDI, RSI, R12-R15 and RSP, so the stub pushes the
// eight registers and saves RSP. The ABI also makes XMM6-XMM15
// callee-saved, but the x86_64-unknown-uefi target is soft-float with SSE
// disabled, so neither the caller nor the exit handler uses them (see the
// VM-exit stub in `vmx::vmexit`).
//
// While the guest runs, this frame on the firmware stack stays untouched:
// the exit handler runs on the VM-exit stack, and the guest on its own page.
//
// No call happens here, so stack alignment does not matter. On the way
// back, RFLAGS are what VMLAUNCH left (failure), or host RFLAGS as loaded
// by the VM exit, 0x2 (stop), so IF stays 0 until teardown.
core::arch::global_asm!(
    r#"
    .globl vmx_launch
vmx_launch:
    push rbx
    push rbp
    push rdi
    push rsi
    push r12
    push r13
    push r14
    push r15
    mov [rip + VMX_LAUNCH_RSP], rsp
    vmlaunch

    // Reached only if VMLAUNCH failed. Its RFLAGS are the stop value
    // (kind 0); fall through to return them.
    pushfq
    pop rax

    // RAX holds the stop value. The VM-exit stub also jumps here when the
    // guest stops: back into vmx_launch's frame, then return to its caller.
    .globl vmx_return_to_launcher
vmx_return_to_launcher:
    mov rsp, [rip + VMX_LAUNCH_RSP]
    pop r15
    pop r14
    pop r13
    pop r12
    pop rsi
    pop rdi
    pop rbp
    pop rbx
    ret
"#
);

unsafe extern "efiapi" {
    /// The stub above. Returns a stop value.
    fn vmx_launch() -> u64;
}

/// Why the guest stopped, or why it never ran.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum GuestStop {
    /// All planned VMCALL exits arrived as expected.
    Finished { exits: u64 },
    /// Exit `number` was not one the handler resumes.
    Unexpected { number: u64, reason: ExitReason },
    /// VMLAUNCH fell through; the guest never ran.
    LaunchFailed {
        error: VmcsError,
        instruction_error: Option<u32>,
    },
    /// VMRESUME fell through after an exit the handler resumed.
    ResumeFailed {
        error: VmcsError,
        instruction_error: Option<u32>,
    },
}

const KIND_SHIFT: u32 = 62;
const PAYLOAD_MASK: u64 = (1 << KIND_SHIFT) - 1;
const KIND_LAUNCH_FAILED: u64 = 0;
const KIND_FINISHED: u64 = 1;
const KIND_UNEXPECTED: u64 = 2;
const KIND_RESUME_FAILED: u64 = 3;

/// Width of the exit-number field (bits 61:32) of an unexpected-exit stop
/// value. A larger number keeps only its low 30 bits, so it can never spill
/// into the kind.
const EXIT_NUMBER_BITS: u32 = 30;
const EXIT_NUMBER_MASK: u64 = (1 << EXIT_NUMBER_BITS) - 1;

/// Stop value for "all planned exits arrived", after `exits` exits.
pub fn encode_finished(exits: u64) -> u64 {
    (KIND_FINISHED << KIND_SHIFT) | (exits & PAYLOAD_MASK)
}

/// Stop value for exit `number`, whose raw VM_EXIT_REASON is `raw_reason`.
pub fn encode_unexpected(number: u64, raw_reason: u32) -> u64 {
    (KIND_UNEXPECTED << KIND_SHIFT) | ((number & EXIT_NUMBER_MASK) << 32) | u64::from(raw_reason)
}

/// Stop value for a VMRESUME that fell through and left `rflags`.
pub fn encode_resume_failed(rflags: u64) -> u64 {
    (KIND_RESUME_FAILED << KIND_SHIFT) | (rflags & PAYLOAD_MASK)
}

/// Decodes a stop value. `instruction_error` is always `None` here: reading
/// it needs the current VMCS, which only `launch` can do.
fn decode(value: u64) -> GuestStop {
    let payload = value & PAYLOAD_MASK;
    match value >> KIND_SHIFT {
        KIND_LAUNCH_FAILED => GuestStop::LaunchFailed {
            error: launch_failure(payload),
            instruction_error: None,
        },
        KIND_FINISHED => GuestStop::Finished { exits: payload },
        KIND_UNEXPECTED => GuestStop::Unexpected {
            number: payload >> 32,
            reason: ExitReason::from_raw(payload as u32),
        },
        // KIND_RESUME_FAILED: `value >> 62` is at most 3.
        _ => GuestStop::ResumeFailed {
            error: resume_failure(payload),
            instruction_error: None,
        },
    }
}

/// Enters the guest described by the current VMCS, and returns once the
/// guest has stopped or VMLAUNCH has failed.
///
/// The guest runs between VMLAUNCH and the stop: the exit handler resumes
/// it after each planned VMCALL, and stops it after the last one or at any
/// exit or VMRESUME failure it does not handle. The module docs explain how
/// execution gets back here.
///
/// For a VmFailValid of VMLAUNCH or VMRESUME, the VM-instruction error is
/// read here, while the VMCS is still current; teardown clears it.
///
/// Invalid *guest* state is not a launch failure: the CPU reports it as a
/// VM exit with bit 31 of the exit reason set (basic reason 33), which
/// arrives as [`GuestStop::Unexpected`].
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX root operation, with a current VMCS whose controls, host state and
/// guest state are fully written. HOST_RSP and HOST_RIP must point at a live
/// exit stack and handler, and the guest's pages must stay allocated.
pub unsafe fn launch() -> GuestStop {
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX root operation with a fully written
    // current VMCS, HOST_RSP/HOST_RIP at a live exit stack and handler, and
    // guest pages that stay allocated.
    let value = unsafe { vmx_launch() };
    match decode(value) {
        GuestStop::LaunchFailed { error, .. } => GuestStop::LaunchFailed {
            error,
            // SAFETY: still in VMX operation with the VMCS current; teardown
            // has not run yet.
            instruction_error: unsafe { instruction_error_for(error) },
        },
        GuestStop::ResumeFailed { error, .. } => GuestStop::ResumeFailed {
            error,
            // SAFETY: as above.
            instruction_error: unsafe { instruction_error_for(error) },
        },
        stop => stop,
    }
}

/// Decodes what the in-place launch's asm leaves: 0 when it runs on as the
/// guest, or the RFLAGS of the VMWRITE or VMLAUNCH that failed, which are
/// never 0 (bit 1 always reads as 1).
fn decode_in_place(value: u64) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    match value {
        0 => Ok(()),
        rflags => Err(launch_failure(rflags)),
    }
}

/// Enters the guest described by the current VMCS in place: the guest is
/// this code, from the instruction after VMLAUNCH on, with the RSP and
/// RFLAGS it had there, IF included. So this returns `Ok` in VMX non-root
/// operation, to its caller, as if VMLAUNCH had been an instruction that did
/// nothing. The registers VM entry does not load (the general-purpose ones)
/// keep their values across it.
///
/// Returns [`GuestStop::LaunchFailed`] in root operation if VMLAUNCH, or a
/// VMWRITE of GUEST_RIP, GUEST_RSP or GUEST_RFLAGS just before it, failed:
/// the guest never ran. A failed VMWRITE reads as VmFailValid with error 12
/// (unsupported VMCS component).
///
/// An interrupt that arrives after RFLAGS is copied runs the firmware's
/// handler in root operation, on the stack below the copied RSP, and is
/// gone by VMLAUNCH; the guest starts with that same RSP.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// As for [`launch`], except for RIP, RSP and RFLAGS, which this writes:
/// VMX root operation, with a current VMCS whose controls, host state and
/// other guest state are fully written, and HOST_RSP and HOST_RIP at a live
/// exit stack and handler. The guest state must describe the running
/// context (`guest_state::GuestEntry::InPlace`), so that the code after
/// VMLAUNCH runs the same as before it. No VM exit may jump back here: the
/// exit handler must halt on a stop (`GuestKind::Firmware`).
pub unsafe fn launch_in_place() -> Result<(), GuestStop> {
    let value: u64;
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX root operation with a fully written
    // current VMCS and a guest state that is this context's. VMWRITE changes
    // only the VMCS. Each `jbe` leaves at the first VMfail (CF = 1 or
    // ZF = 1). PUSHFQ and POP balance, so RSP at VMLAUNCH, and at `2:` where
    // the guest starts, is the one written to GUEST_RSP. VM entry keeps the
    // general-purpose registers, so every operand still holds its value
    // there; flags are clobbered either way (no `preserves_flags`).
    unsafe {
        asm!(
            "lea {value}, [rip + 2f]",
            "vmwrite {rip_field}, {value}",
            "jbe 3f",
            "vmwrite {rsp_field}, rsp",
            "jbe 3f",
            "pushfq",
            "pop {value}",
            "vmwrite {rflags_field}, {value}",
            "jbe 3f",
            "vmlaunch",
            // VMLAUNCH or a VMWRITE failed: its RFLAGS say how.
            "3:",
            "pushfq",
            "pop {value}",
            "jmp 4f",
            // The guest starts here, in VMX non-root operation.
            "2:",
            "xor {value:e}, {value:e}",
            "4:",
            // `out`, not `lateout`: written before the inputs are last read.
            value = out(reg) value,
            rip_field = in(reg) u64::from(GUEST_RIP),
            rsp_field = in(reg) u64::from(GUEST_RSP),
            rflags_field = in(reg) u64::from(GUEST_RFLAGS),
        );
    }
    decode_in_place(value).map_err(|error| GuestStop::LaunchFailed {
        error,
        // SAFETY: the launch failed, so this is still root operation with the
        // VMCS current; teardown has not run yet.
        instruction_error: unsafe { instruction_error_for(error) },
    })
}

mod tests;

`src/vmx/vmcs/mod.rs`:

```rs
//! The Virtual Machine Control Structure (VMCS).
//!
//! A VMCS describes one virtual CPU: the guest's register state, the host
//! state to return to on a VM exit, and which events cause those exits.
//! One VMCS per vCPU; one "current" VMCS per logical processor.
//!
//! The region looks exactly like the VMXON region — 4 KiB, 4 KiB-aligned,
//! revision identifier in the first four bytes — but it is used differently.
//! Apart from that revision identifier, **never touch it with ordinary loads
//! and stores**: the internal layout is undocumented and the CPU caches
//! fields internally. [`vmread`] and [`vmwrite`] are the only legal access.
//!
//! Lifecycle:
//!
//! 1. [`VmxRegion::allocate`] — a page with the revision identifier, same
//!    as the VMXON region.
//! 2. [`VmcsRegion::vmclear`] — initialise it and flush any cached data the
//!    CPU holds for that physical address. Required once before first use,
//!    even on a freshly zeroed page.
//! 3. [`VmcsRegion::vmptrld`] — make it the *current* VMCS. From here on
//!    [`vmread`]/[`vmwrite`] act on it implicitly, with no address operand.
//! 4. [`vmwrite`] the fields, then [`launch`] or [`launch_in_place`]
//!    (VMLAUNCH).
//!
//! [`VmcsRegion::create_current`] runs steps 1-3.
//!
//! Fields are addressed by a 32-bit **encoding**, not by an offset. The
//! encoding packs the field's width, type (control / read-only / guest /
//! host) and index; every encoding this hypervisor uses is in [`fields`].
//!
//! Like VMXON, these instructions report failure through RFLAGS rather than
//! exceptions: CF=1 is VMfailInvalid, ZF=1 is VMfailValid. The difference is
//! that once a current VMCS exists, VMfailValid also stores a numeric reason
//! readable via [`vm_instruction_error`].

use crate::vmx::ept::Eptp;
use crate::vmx::instruction::{VmxFail, check_rflags, vmx_asm};
use crate::vmx::msr::{self, UnsupportedControl, VmcsControlMsrs};
use crate::vmx::region::VmxRegion;
use crate::vmx::{cr, segment};
use core::arch::asm;

pub mod fields;
mod launch;

pub use launch::{GuestStop, encode_finished, encode_resume_failed, encode_unexpected, launch, launch_in_place};

// Private glob: this file uses dozens of encodings. Callers elsewhere import
// from `vmcs::fields` themselves, so each constant has a single path.
use fields::*;

/// Requested control bits; CPU-required bits are added by `configure_controls`.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
pub struct DesiredControls {
    pub pin: u32,
    pub primary: u32,
    /// Secondary processor-based controls. Nonzero also turns on primary
    /// bit 31, without which the CPU ignores them.
    pub secondary: u32,
    pub exit: u32,
    pub entry: u32,
    /// EXCEPTION_BITMAP: the guest exception vectors that exit instead of
    /// going through the guest's IDT ([`exception_bitmap`]).
    pub exception_bitmap: u32,
}

impl DesiredControls {
    /// Minimal requests for a 64-bit guest on this 64-bit host, plus NMI
    /// exiting with virtual NMIs, so Aleph0 sees the guest's NMIs and can
    /// reinject them, EPT, so guest memory goes through Aleph0's tables, the
    /// MSR and I/O bitmaps, so only the MSRs and ports Aleph0 chooses exit
    /// (`vmx::exit_bitmaps`), and HLT exiting. Hyper-V forces HLT exiting
    /// anyway; requesting it means a guest HLT with IF = 0 exits on every
    /// CPU instead of halting it for good. The exception bitmap depends on
    /// `kind`.
    pub const fn minimal_64_bit_guest(kind: GuestKind) -> Self {
        Self {
            pin: PIN_BASED_NMI_EXITING | PIN_BASED_VIRTUAL_NMIS,
            primary: CPU_BASED_HLT_EXITING | CPU_BASED_USE_IO_BITMAPS | CPU_BASED_USE_MSR_BITMAPS,
            secondary: SECONDARY_ENABLE_EPT,
            exit: VM_EXIT_HOST_ADDRESS_SPACE_SIZE,
            entry: VM_ENTRY_IA32E_MODE_GUEST,
            exception_bitmap: exception_bitmap(kind),
        }
    }
}

/// Which guest Aleph0 runs. The kind decides where the guest starts
/// (`guest_state::GuestEntry`), which exceptions exit ([`exception_bitmap`]),
/// how its exits are decided (`exit_decision::decide`), and where a stop
/// ends.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum GuestKind {
    /// Aleph0's built-in test guest (`vmx::guest`), the regression mode. Its
    /// IDT has only the NMI gate, and its scripted VMCALLs end the run. A
    /// stop returns to bring-up ([`launch`]), and bring-up then leaves VMX
    /// operation.
    BuiltInTest,
    /// The running firmware, virtualized in place ([`launch_in_place`]). It
    /// has its own full IDT and handles its own faults. It never finishes,
    /// and a stop halts: the firmware has reused the stack the launch ran
    /// on.
    Firmware,
}

impl GuestKind {
    /// The guest this build runs: the built-in test guest with the
    /// `test-guest` Cargo feature, the firmware otherwise.
    pub const SELECTED: Self = if cfg!(feature = "test-guest") {
        Self::BuiltInTest
    } else {
        Self::Firmware
    };

    /// Whether a stop of this guest returns to bring-up, through the frame
    /// [`launch`] saved. [`launch_in_place`] saves none, so a stop of the
    /// firmware halts.
    pub const fn stop_returns_to_bring_up(self) -> bool {
        matches!(self, Self::BuiltInTest)
    }
}

/// The exception bitmap for `kind`.
///
/// The built-in test guest's IDT has only vector 2 (NMI). Without an exit, a
/// fault there would hit a missing gate (#GP, then #DF, then a triple
/// fault), so the host would see nothing useful. All ones makes every
/// exception arrive as exit reason 0, where the handler prints the vector;
/// its `ud2` paths rely on that.
///
/// The firmware has its own IDT and takes its own faults, as an OS will
/// (Linux builds its early page tables from #PF), so nothing exits. NMIs
/// still exit, through the NMI-exiting pin control, not this bitmap; a fault
/// the guest cannot handle ends in a triple fault (reason 2), which stops it.
pub const fn exception_bitmap(kind: GuestKind) -> u32 {
    match kind {
        GuestKind::BuiltInTest => u32::MAX,
        GuestKind::Firmware => 0,
    }
}

/// The VM-exit controls that, with [`PAT_SWITCH_ENTRY`], give the guest an
/// IA32_PAT of its own: VM exit saves the guest's into GUEST_IA32_PAT and
/// loads HOST_IA32_PAT.
const PAT_SWITCH_EXIT: u32 = (VM_EXIT_SAVE_IA32_PAT | VM_EXIT_LOAD_IA32_PAT) as u32;
/// The VM-entry control that loads GUEST_IA32_PAT.
const PAT_SWITCH_ENTRY: u32 = VM_ENTRY_LOAD_IA32_PAT as u32;

/// The VM-exit and VM-entry controls to add to a request so that IA32_PAT
/// is switched between the guest and Aleph0, or none when the CPU does not
/// allow all three.
///
/// The MSR bitmap does not intercept IA32_PAT (`exit_bitmaps`), so the
/// guest's WRMSR of it reaches the CPU. Without the switch the value stays
/// after VM exit, and Aleph0's page tables select PAT entry 0 (PWT = PCD =
/// PAT = 0): a guest that made it UC or WC would set the memory type of all
/// of Aleph0's own accesses, as a guest write to the MTRRs did before they
/// were intercepted. With it, VM exit saves the guest's PAT and loads
/// Aleph0's, and VM entry loads the guest's back (Intel SDM Vol. 3C,
/// "VM-Exit Controls" and "VM-Entry Controls"). The three only work
/// together: without the save, VM entry would undo the guest's writes;
/// without the loads, one PAT would still serve both.
///
/// On a CPU without them the PAT stays shared, as before: the stop dump
/// shows `(MSR, not switched)`, and `docs/HOST_ENVIRONMENT.md` lists it as
/// not covered.
fn pat_switch(capabilities: &VmcsControlMsrs) -> (u32, u32) {
    if capabilities.exit.allows(PAT_SWITCH_EXIT) && capabilities.entry.allows(PAT_SWITCH_ENTRY) {
        (PAT_SWITCH_EXIT, PAT_SWITCH_ENTRY)
    } else {
        (0, 0)
    }
}

/// The primary controls to request for `desired`: its own bits, plus
/// "activate secondary controls" when it asks for any secondary control.
fn primary_request(desired: DesiredControls) -> u32 {
    if desired.secondary != 0 {
        desired.primary | CPU_BASED_ACTIVATE_SECONDARY_CONTROLS
    } else {
        desired.primary
    }
}

/// Why a VMCS operation failed.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum VmcsError {
    /// UEFI could not provide a page.
    AllocationFailed,
    /// CF=1: the instruction failed with no current VMCS to record why.
    VmFailInvalid,
    /// ZF=1: the instruction failed and stored a reason in the current VMCS;
    /// read it with [`vm_instruction_error`].
    VmFailValid,
    /// [`write_verified`] read `read` back from `field` after writing
    /// `written`. Both instructions reported success, so this is not a VMX
    /// failure.
    ReadbackMismatch { field: u32, written: u64, read: u64 },
    /// The requested control value is not supported by the processor.
    UnsupportedControlValue,
    /// A host-state value failed its check before being written: a selector
    /// with RPL or TI set, a null CS or TR, or a null or misaligned
    /// HOST_RSP/HOST_RIP.
    HostStateValidation,
    /// VMLAUNCH fell through to the next instruction with CF and ZF both
    /// clear. A successful VMLAUNCH never falls through, so the guest was
    /// not entered, for a reason the flags do not say.
    LaunchReturned,
    /// VMRESUME fell through to the next instruction with CF and ZF both
    /// clear. Like [`VmcsError::LaunchReturned`], the guest was not entered.
    ResumeReturned,
    /// The CPU does not allow NMI-window exiting, which the exit handler
    /// needs to inject an NMI that arrived while the guest blocked NMIs.
    NmiWindowExitingUnsupported,
}

impl From<VmxFail> for VmcsError {
    fn from(fail: VmxFail) -> Self {
        match fail {
            VmxFail::Invalid => Self::VmFailInvalid,
            VmxFail::Valid => Self::VmFailValid,
        }
    }
}

impl From<UnsupportedControl> for VmcsError {
    fn from(_: UnsupportedControl) -> Self {
        Self::UnsupportedControlValue
    }
}

/// A VMCS: a [`VmxRegion`] used as a VMCS, through VMCLEAR and VMPTRLD.
pub struct VmcsRegion {
    region: VmxRegion,
}

impl VmcsRegion {
    /// Initialises the VMCS and flushes CPU-cached data for its address.
    ///
    /// Must run once before the region is first used, and again whenever a
    /// VMCS stops being current on this processor.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// The CPU must be in VMX root operation.
    pub unsafe fn vmclear(&self) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
        // SAFETY: VMCLEAR reads only the 8-byte operand and works on a region
        // this value owns; the caller guarantees VMX root operation.
        Ok(unsafe { vmx_asm!("vmclear [{0}]", in(reg) self.region.phys_addr_ref()) }?)
    }

    /// Allocates a VMCS, initialises it, and makes it the current VMCS.
    ///
    /// Runs lifecycle steps 1-3. The region must stay allocated for as long
    /// as it is current or may become current again.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// The CPU must be in VMX root operation.
    pub unsafe fn create_current() -> Result<Self, VmcsError> {
        // SAFETY: VMX root operation (the caller's obligation) implies VMX
        // support. The revision identifier is written before VMPTRLD, not
        // just before use: VMPTRLD rejects a region whose identifier does
        // not match the CPU (error 11).
        unsafe {
            let vmcs = Self {
                region: VmxRegion::allocate(VmcsError::AllocationFailed)?,
            };
            vmcs.vmclear()?;
            vmcs.vmptrld()?;
            Ok(vmcs)
        }
    }

    /// Makes this VMCS the current one for this logical processor.
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// The CPU must be in VMX root operation, and the region must have been
    /// cleared with [`VmcsRegion::vmclear`].
    pub unsafe fn vmptrld(&self) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
        // SAFETY: VMPTRLD reads only the 8-byte operand; the caller
        // guarantees VMX root operation and a cleared region.
        Ok(unsafe { vmx_asm!("vmptrld [{0}]", in(reg) self.region.phys_addr_ref()) }?)
    }
}

/// Reads a field from the current VMCS.
///
/// Operand order is the opposite of [`vmwrite`]: `VMREAD dest, field`, so the
/// destination register comes first and the encoding second.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation must be active and a VMCS current on this CPU; outside VMX
/// operation VMREAD raises #UD.
pub unsafe fn vmread(field_encoding: u32) -> Result<u64, VmcsError> {
    let value: u64;
    let rflags: u64;

    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS;
    // VMREAD writes only `value` and RFLAGS.
    unsafe {
        asm!(
            "vmread {value}, {field:r}",
            "pushfq",
            "pop {rflags}",
            value = out(reg) value,
            // Cast to u64 like vmwrite does: `{field:r}` names the full
            // 64-bit register, and a u32 input leaves its upper half
            // undefined, which the CPU would read as part of the encoding.
            field = in(reg) field_encoding as u64,
            rflags = lateout(reg) rflags,
        );
    }

    check_rflags(rflags)?;

    Ok(value)
}

/// Writes a field in the current VMCS.
///
/// Operand order is `VMWRITE field, value` — the encoding comes first, which
/// reads backwards compared to a normal `mov`.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation must be active and a VMCS current on this CPU. The value
/// takes effect at the next VM entry or exit, so it must be one the rest of
/// Aleph0 expects in that field.
pub unsafe fn vmwrite(field_encoding: u32, value: u64) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    let rflags: u64;

    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS,
    // and that the value suits the field; VMWRITE changes only the VMCS.
    unsafe {
        asm!(
            "vmwrite {field:r}, {value}",
            "pushfq",
            "pop {rflags}",
            value = in(reg) value,
            field = in(reg) field_encoding as u64,
            rflags = lateout(reg) rflags,
        );
    }

    Ok(check_rflags(rflags)?)
}

/// Writes a field in the current VMCS and reads it back, so a value that did
/// not land as written is caught here rather than as a VM-entry failure.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation must be active and a VMCS current on this CPU.
pub unsafe fn write_verified(field: u32, value: u64) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS.
    let read = unsafe {
        vmwrite(field, value)?;
        vmread(field)?
    };
    if read != value {
        return Err(VmcsError::ReadbackMismatch {
            field,
            written: value,
            read,
        });
    }
    Ok(())
}

/// Decodes the RFLAGS left behind when VMLAUNCH falls through. That only
/// happens on failure, so clear flags become [`VmcsError::LaunchReturned`]
/// instead of success.
fn launch_failure(rflags: u64) -> VmcsError {
    fall_through_failure(rflags, VmcsError::LaunchReturned)
}

/// Decodes the RFLAGS left behind when VMRESUME falls through. VMRESUME runs
/// in the VM-exit entry stub (`vmx::vmexit`), which passes RFLAGS here, so
/// this is public; clear flags become [`VmcsError::ResumeReturned`].
pub fn resume_failure(rflags: u64) -> VmcsError {
    fall_through_failure(rflags, VmcsError::ResumeReturned)
}

/// VMLAUNCH and VMRESUME reach the next instruction only when they fail:
/// CF=1 and ZF=1 say how, and clear flags mean `clear`.
fn fall_through_failure(rflags: u64, clear: VmcsError) -> VmcsError {
    match check_rflags(rflags) {
        Err(fail) => fail.into(),
        Ok(()) => clear,
    }
}

/// Derive legal pin, primary, exit, and entry controls from the CPU masks,
/// write them to the current VMCS, and verify each field by reading it back.
/// When `desired.secondary` is nonzero, the secondary controls are chosen,
/// written and verified the same way, and primary bit 31 activates them.
/// Always request 64-bit host mode on VM exit, regardless of `desired.exit`,
/// and the IA32_PAT switch when the CPU allows it ([`pat_switch`]).
/// Also zeroes the counts and fields VM entry checks, and writes
/// `desired.exception_bitmap`. It also checks that the CPU
/// allows NMI-window exiting (`VmcsError::NmiWindowExitingUnsupported`
/// otherwise), which the exit handler switches on at run time.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation must be active and a VMCS must be current on this CPU.
pub unsafe fn configure_controls(capabilities: &VmcsControlMsrs, desired: DesiredControls) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    let pin = capabilities.pinbased.choose(desired.pin)?;
    let primary = capabilities.primary.choose(primary_request(desired))?;
    let secondary = if desired.secondary != 0 {
        Some(capabilities.secondary.choose(desired.secondary)?)
    } else {
        None
    };
    // NMI-window exiting is only switched on while an NMI waits for
    // injection (`set_nmi_window_exiting`), but the CPU must allow it.
    if !capabilities.primary.allows(CPU_BASED_NMI_WINDOW_EXITING) {
        return Err(VmcsError::NmiWindowExitingUnsupported);
    }
    let (pat_exit, pat_entry) = pat_switch(capabilities);
    let exit = capabilities
        .exit
        .choose(desired.exit | VM_EXIT_HOST_ADDRESS_SPACE_SIZE | pat_exit)?;
    let entry = capabilities.entry.choose(desired.entry | pat_entry)?;

    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS.
    unsafe {
        write_verified(PIN_BASED_VM_EXEC_CONTROL, pin.into())?;
        write_verified(PRIMARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL, primary.into())?;
        write_verified(VM_EXIT_CONTROLS, exit.into())?;
        write_verified(VM_ENTRY_CONTROLS, entry.into())?;
        if let Some(secondary) = secondary {
            write_verified(SECONDARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL, secondary.into())?;
        }

        // VM entry checks these fields, and VMCLEAR does not guarantee that
        // a fresh VMCS holds zeros in them, so write the zeros explicitly:
        // no CR3 targets, no MSR load/store lists, no event injection. The
        // #PF mask and match are not entry checks, but they decide which
        // page faults the exception bitmap below catches: 0 and 0 mean all.
        for field in [
            CR3_TARGET_COUNT,
            VM_EXIT_MSR_STORE_COUNT,
            VM_EXIT_MSR_LOAD_COUNT,
            VM_ENTRY_MSR_LOAD_COUNT,
            VM_ENTRY_INTERRUPTION_INFO,
            PAGE_FAULT_ERROR_CODE_MASK,
            PAGE_FAULT_ERROR_CODE_MATCH,
        ] {
            write_verified(field, 0)?;
        }

        write_verified(EXCEPTION_BITMAP, desired.exception_bitmap.into())?;
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// The selectors a VM exit loads into the host's segment registers and TR.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct HostSelectors {
    pub cs: u16,
    pub ss: u16,
    pub ds: u16,
    pub es: u16,
    pub fs: u16,
    pub gs: u16,
    pub tr: u16,
}

/// The host state Aleph0 builds itself (`vmx::host`) instead of taking it
/// from the running firmware: page tables, descriptor tables, and the
/// selectors that index them.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct HostTables {
    pub cr3: u64,
    pub gdtr_base: u64,
    pub idtr_base: u64,
    pub tr_base: u64,
    pub selectors: HostSelectors,
}

/// Write the host state to the current VMCS: `tables` for CR3, the
/// descriptor tables and the selectors; the running CPU for CR0, CR4, the FS
/// and GS bases and the SYSENTER MSRs, which VM exits restore as they are now.
/// Do not use this as evidence that VM entry is ready until all host fields
/// required by the selected VM-exit controls have been populated.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation must be active and a VMCS current on this CPU. `tables`
/// must describe page tables, a GDT, a TSS and an IDT that stay live and
/// usable for as long as a VM exit can load them.
pub unsafe fn configure_host_state(tables: &HostTables) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    let selectors = tables.selectors;
    let cr0 = cr::read_cr0();
    let cr4 = cr::read_cr4();
    // SAFETY: UEFI runs in long mode, which has both MSRs.
    let (fs_base, gs_base) = unsafe { (segment::read_fs_base(), segment::read_gs_base()) };
    // SAFETY: the SYSENTER MSRs exist on every x86_64 CPU, and reading
    // them has no side effects.
    let (sysenter_cs, sysenter_esp, sysenter_eip) = unsafe {
        (
            u64::from(msr::rdmsr(msr::IA32_SYSENTER_CS) as u32),
            msr::rdmsr(msr::IA32_SYSENTER_ESP),
            msr::rdmsr(msr::IA32_SYSENTER_EIP),
        )
    };

    // VM entry requires every host selector to have RPL and TI clear, and
    // CS and TR to be non-null.
    {
        let selectors = [
            selectors.es,
            selectors.cs,
            selectors.ss,
            selectors.ds,
            selectors.fs,
            selectors.gs,
            selectors.tr,
        ];

        if selectors
            .iter()
            .any(|selector| selector & segment::SELECTOR_RPL_TI != 0)
        {
            return Err(VmcsError::HostStateValidation);
        }
    }

    if selectors.cs == 0 || selectors.tr == 0 {
        return Err(VmcsError::HostStateValidation);
    }
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS.
    let exit_controls = unsafe { vmread(VM_EXIT_CONTROLS)? };

    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS. PAT
    // and EFER are read only when the exit controls load them, which the CPU
    // allows only if it has them.
    // Host PAT and EFER are written only when the exit controls load them.
    // HOST_RSP and HOST_RIP come later, from `configure_host_entry`.
    unsafe {
        write_verified(HOST_ES_SELECTOR, selectors.es.into())?;
        write_verified(HOST_CS_SELECTOR, selectors.cs.into())?;
        write_verified(HOST_SS_SELECTOR, selectors.ss.into())?;
        write_verified(HOST_DS_SELECTOR, selectors.ds.into())?;
        write_verified(HOST_FS_SELECTOR, selectors.fs.into())?;
        write_verified(HOST_GS_SELECTOR, selectors.gs.into())?;
        write_verified(HOST_TR_SELECTOR, selectors.tr.into())?;

        write_verified(HOST_CR0, cr0)?;
        write_verified(HOST_CR3, tables.cr3)?;
        write_verified(HOST_CR4, cr4)?;

        write_verified(HOST_FS_BASE, fs_base)?;
        write_verified(HOST_GS_BASE, gs_base)?;
        write_verified(HOST_TR_BASE, tables.tr_base)?;
        write_verified(HOST_GDTR_BASE, tables.gdtr_base)?;
        write_verified(HOST_IDTR_BASE, tables.idtr_base)?;

        write_verified(HOST_IA32_SYSENTER_CS, sysenter_cs)?;
        write_verified(HOST_IA32_SYSENTER_ESP, sysenter_esp)?;
        write_verified(HOST_IA32_SYSENTER_EIP, sysenter_eip)?;

        if exit_controls & VM_EXIT_LOAD_IA32_PAT != 0 {
            write_verified(HOST_IA32_PAT, msr::rdmsr(msr::IA32_PAT))?;
        }
        if exit_controls & VM_EXIT_LOAD_IA32_EFER != 0 {
            write_verified(HOST_IA32_EFER, msr::rdmsr(msr::IA32_EFER))?;
        }
    }

    Ok(())
}

/// Store the host stack top and VM-exit entry address without entering a guest.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation must be active and a VMCS current on this CPU. The stack
/// and entry code must remain mapped and valid whenever a VM exit can occur.
pub unsafe fn configure_host_entry(stack_top: u64, entry_address: u64) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    if stack_top == 0 || stack_top & 15 != 0 || entry_address == 0 {
        return Err(VmcsError::HostStateValidation);
    }

    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS.
    unsafe {
        write_verified(HOST_RSP, stack_top)?;
        write_verified(HOST_RIP, entry_address)?;
    }
    Ok(())
}

/// `primary` with NMI-window exiting turned on or off, other bits unchanged.
fn with_nmi_window_exiting(primary: u64, on: bool) -> u64 {
    let bit = u64::from(CPU_BASED_NMI_WINDOW_EXITING);
    if on { primary | bit } else { primary & !bit }
}

/// Turns NMI-window exiting on or off in the current VMCS. The exit handler
/// turns it on while an NMI waits until the guest can take it, and off once
/// the NMI is injected.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation with a current VMCS. `configure_controls` has checked that
/// the CPU allows the bit.
pub unsafe fn set_nmi_window_exiting(on: bool) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS.
    let primary = unsafe { vmread(PRIMARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL)? };
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS. Only
    // the NMI-window bit changes, which the caller checked the CPU allows.
    unsafe { vmwrite(PRIMARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL, with_nmi_window_exiting(primary, on)) }
}

/// Writes the EPT pointer and reads it back. VM entry checks it only when
/// the "enable EPT" secondary control is set.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation with a current VMCS. The tables `eptp` names must stay
/// allocated for as long as the VMCS may be used.
pub unsafe fn set_ept_pointer(eptp: Eptp) -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS.
    unsafe { write_verified(EPT_POINTER, eptp.raw()) }
}

/// The numeric reason the last VMX instruction failed.
///
/// Only meaningful straight after a [`VmcsError::VmFailValid`], and only
/// while a current VMCS exists. The field keeps the last value the CPU wrote,
/// so reading it at any other time returns something stale with no way to
/// tell — that is the caller's responsibility, not something the hardware
/// flags.
///
/// Never call this to diagnose a failed [`vmread`]: this *is* a `vmread`, so
/// it would fail the same way and recurse.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation must be active and a VMCS current on this CPU.
pub unsafe fn vm_instruction_error() -> Result<u32, VmcsError> {
    // VM_INSTRUCTION_ERROR is a 32-bit field; VMREAD zero-extends it.
    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS.
    Ok(unsafe { vmread(VM_INSTRUCTION_ERROR)? } as u32)
}

/// The VM-instruction error number behind `error`: `Some` only for a
/// VmFailValid whose number is readable.
///
/// Call it right after the failure. The number lives in the current VMCS,
/// so it is gone once the VMCS is cleared or VMX operation is left, which
/// teardown does before bring-up prints its errors.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// A VmFailValid can only come from a VMX instruction executed in VMX
/// operation with a current VMCS, so the VMREAD here cannot raise #UD. That
/// holds only until the VMCS is cleared or VMXOFF runs: call this before
/// either.
pub unsafe fn instruction_error_for(error: VmcsError) -> Option<u32> {
    if error == VmcsError::VmFailValid {
        // SAFETY: a VmFailValid comes from a VMX instruction run in VMX
        // operation with a current VMCS, which the caller guarantees is still
        // current.
        unsafe { vm_instruction_error() }.ok()
    } else {
        None
    }
}

/// Human-readable name for a [`vm_instruction_error`] code.
///
/// Numbers from Intel SDM Vol. 3, "VM-Instruction Error Numbers"; only the
/// ones reachable from this code are spelled out.
pub fn vm_instruction_error_name(error: u32) -> &'static str {
    match error {
        2 => "VMCLEAR with invalid physical address",
        3 => "VMCLEAR with VMXON pointer",
        4 => "VMLAUNCH with non-clear VMCS",
        5 => "VMRESUME with non-launched VMCS",
        7 => "VM entry with invalid control field(s)",
        8 => "VM entry with invalid host-state field(s)",
        9 => "VMPTRLD with invalid physical address",
        10 => "VMPTRLD with VMXON pointer",
        11 => "VMPTRLD with incorrect VMCS revision identifier",
        12 => "VMREAD/VMWRITE from/to unsupported VMCS component",
        13 => "VMWRITE to read-only VMCS component",
        15 => "VMXON executed in VMX root operation",
        _ => "unknown VM-instruction error",
    }
}

/// Proves the access path to the current VMCS works: write a field, read
/// it back.
///
/// Leaves the test pattern in GUEST_RIP; guest-state setup overwrites it.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// VMX operation must be active and a VMCS current on this CPU
/// ([`VmcsRegion::create_current`]).
pub unsafe fn self_test() -> Result<(), VmcsError> {
    // Bits set in both halves, so a write that only lands in the low 32 bits
    // is caught. Canonical (bits 63:47 clear), which GUEST_RIP will need once
    // VM entry starts checking it.
    const PATTERN: u64 = 0x0000_7FFF_DEAD_BEEF;

    // SAFETY: the caller guarantees VMX operation with a current VMCS.
    unsafe { write_verified(GUEST_RIP, PATTERN) }
}
